However, directly applying centralized and static RQ-based recommendation to federated learning is non-trivial due to 1) private and biased historical interactions and 2) evolving collaborative information. We propose RQFedRec, an RQ-based federated recommendation framework for dynamic feature-embedding communication. To construct globally aligned codebooks without accessing private interactions, RQFedRec introduces an information distillation module. Each client first learns item embeddings that encode local collaborative information from private interactions, and then distills such information into feature-indexed codebooks under globally shared SIDs, making sparse and biased local signals more compatible with server aggregation. To adapt to evolving collaborative information, RQFedRec introduces a self-refining SID update module that dynamically refines global SID assignments from aggregated codebooks. Extensive experiments demonstrate that RQFedRec improves recommendation performance and reduces communication costs without relying on semantic information, while further benefiting from public semantics when available. Code is available at https://github.com/Mingzhe-Han/RQFedRec.
papers.venue: ACM International Conference on Information and Knowledge Management (CIKM)

papers.title: FDA-Opt: Federated Fine-Tuning via Dynamic Update Schedules
papers.abstract: Federated Learning (FL) enables the utilization of vast, previously inaccessible data sources. At the same time, pre-trained Language Models (LMs) have taken the world by storm and for good reason. They exhibit remarkable emergent abilities and are readily adapted to downstream tasks. This opens one of the most exciting frontiers in FL: fine-tuning LMs. Yet, a persistent challenge in FL is the frequent, rigid communication of parameters—a problem magnified by the sheer size of these contemporary models. The FedOpt family of algorithms has become the go-to approach for FL, relying on fixed but arbitrary intervals for model exchanges. Recently, the FDA algorithm prescribed a dynamic approach by monitoring the training progress. However, it introduced a hard-to-calibrate parameter and imposed a rigid synchronization scheme. In this work, we address these limitations by proposing the FDA-Opt family of algorithms—a unified generalization of both FDA and FedOpt. Our experimental evaluation focuses on fine-tuning LMs on downstream NLP tasks and demonstrates that FDA-Opt outperforms FedOpt even when it is configured with hyper-parameters specifically optimized for the latter. In other words, we show that FDA-Opt is a practical, drop-in replacement for FedOpt in modern FL libraries and systems: it requires no additional configuration and delivers superior performance out of the box.
papers.venue: ACM International Conference on Information and Knowledge Management (CIKM)

papers.title: Federated Personalization of Early-Exit Networks
papers.abstract: Personalized Federated Learning (PFL) excels at tailoring client specific models, which is particularly critical for decentralized and heterogeneous data environments, yet existing methods produce static models with a fixed tradeoff between accuracy and efficiency. This inherent static nature limits their ability to adapt to inference demands that vary with context and resource availability, posing a challenge for real-world deployment. Early-exit networks (EENs), which enable adaptive inference via intermediate classifiers, offer a promising solution. However, integrating EENs into PFL introduces two intertwined conflicts: client-wise heterogeneity across clients and depth-wise interference arising from conflicting exit objectives. Prior studies fail to resolve both conflicts simultaneously, leading to suboptimal performance. In this paper, we propose X-FED, a novel Conflict-Aware Cross-Client Federated Exit Distillation framework that jointly addresses both client- and depth-wise conflicts while extending PFL to early-exit networks. At its core, X-FED employs a progressive, depth-prioritized student coordination mechanism that mitigates interference among shallow and deep exits while enabling effective personalized knowledge transfer across clients. Furthermore, we introduce a client-decoupled formulation that reduces communication overhead with theoretical soundness. Extensive evaluations on various datasets show that compared to state-of-the-art PFL and PFL-EE methods, X-FED achieves higher accuracy while reducing inference costs by 30.79%–46.86%.
papers.venue: ACM International Conference on Information and Knowledge Management (CIKM)

papers.title: Understanding developer pain points in federated learning: insights from stack overflow and GitHub
When Is Shallow Enough? Adaptive Split Federated Learning with Client-Specific Sufficiency Estimation
papers.abstract: Split Federated Learning (SFL) enables distributed model training by splitting networks between the server and clients. However, under client heterogeneity, the conventional static split strategy may be suboptimal because clients can differ in data distributions, adaptation dynamics, and representation learning progress, making a single split point insufficient to accommodate client-specific training states. In this paper, we propose FedSGA , a S ufficiency- G uided A daptive split Fed erated learning framework that addresses this question through client-specific shallow sufficiency estimation. First, we introduce a client-specific adaptation channel based on private prompt tokens, which tracks local adaptation dynamics separately from the shared backbone and provides a lightweight signal for detecting whether client adaptation remains active. To further avoid repeated online probing over multiple candidate depths, we design a shallow sufficiency estimator that combines cross-client semantic alignment, temporal interface stability, and prompt-state variation to estimate whether the shallowest split is already sufficient. Finally, we introduce a split-compatible interface harmonization module that projects activations from different split depths into a shared semantic space, improving the comparability of heterogeneous client interfaces before server-side prediction. Extensive experiments on multiple heterogeneous benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness of FedSGA in improving model performance compared with state-of-the-art methods while reducing unnecessary client-side computation.
papers.venue: ACM International Conference on Information and Knowledge Management (CIKM)

papers.title: Federated Learning Security with FedEDAuth: Embedding-Distribution Authentication for Counterfeit IC Detection
papers.abstract: Abstract The globalization of the semiconductor supply chain has intensified the proliferation of counterfeit integrated circuits (ICs), posing severe threats to the reliability and security of safety critical systems. Federated Learning (FL) has emerged as a promising privacy preserving paradigm for collaborative counterfeit IC detection, enabling distributed entities to jointly train machine learning models without exchanging sensitive raw data. However, the decentralized nature of FL introduces critical security vulnerabilities. This work first demonstrates that standard FL aggregation defenses are insufficient against a novel Byzantine data poisoning attack. This attack embeds subtle hardware-specific triggers into IC training data, corrupting the global model while evading detection with access to an average of just 4.46% of the dataset. To counteract this vulnerability, we propose Federated Embedding Distribution Authentication (FedEDAuth), a lightweight and proactive authentication framework. FedEDAuth detects and filters malicious clients prior to aggregation by analyzing the statistical properties of client-side feature embeddings against a trusted golden reference. Experimental evaluation across 50 distributed clients and five random seeds demonstrates that FedEDAuth achieves a 100% malicious client detection rate against a stealthy Byzantine data poisoning attack on an IC image dataset. Post-filtering, the federated counterfeit IC detection model achieves an accuracy of 90.94% and an AUC-ROC of 0.91. The results of this experiment underscore the critical necessity of secure client authentication for ensuring resilient collaborative hardware security. While demonstrated on counterfeit IC detection, the architecture is directly applicable to tasks including IoT device attestation, hardware trojan detection, and broader supply-chain integrity verification.
papers.venue: Journal of Hardware and Systems Security

papers.title: Federated Learning for Privacy-Preserving Healthcare Analytics: Addressing Data Security, Model Accuracy, and Interoperability
papers.abstract: Healthcare data is abundant but siloed: privacy regulation and institutional boundaries prevent the pooling that machine learning needs, so models are trained on narrow single-site data and generalise poorly. Federated learning (FL) offers a route around this by moving the model to the data rather than the data to the model. This study developed and evaluated a federated analytics framework across five simulated hospital nodes for a clinical-outcome prediction task, comparing it against isolated single-site models and a (privacy-violating) centralised baseline, and assessing the accuracy cost of adding differential privacy and the burden of cross-site interoperability harmonisation. The federated model reached an AUROC of 0.911, recovering 98.3% of centralised performance while sharing no raw data, and improved mean single-site AUROC by 9.4 percentage points. Differential privacy at ε = 4.0 cost 1.8 points of AUROC. Interoperability mapping resolved 92.7% of feature-schema mismatches. Federated learning delivers near-centralised accuracy with strong privacy, provided interoperability is actively managed.
papers.venue: International Journal of Medical Research And Innovation in Applied Science (IJMRIAS)

papers.title: Radio-Aware Clustering and Multi-Relay Routing for D2D-Assisted Hierarchical Federated Learning
papers.abstract: Existing hierarchical federated learning (HFL) schemes commonly form device clusters based on geographic or logical proximity, even though these criteria may poorly represent effective connectivity in industrial wireless environments. To address this, we propose RaLeD-FL, a radio-aware clustering framework for device-to-device HFL that jointly exploits direct and multi-relay device-to-device (D2D) paths. RaLeD-FL constructs a weighted connectivity graph by evaluating admissible paths according to their bottleneck capacity, end-to-end (E2E) reliability, cumulative delay, and hop count. Then, it combines Leiden community detection with multicriteria cluster-head selection, synchronization constraints, and lower and upper cluster-size controls. We evaluate RaLeD-FL using an ns-3/ns3-ai/Python co-simulation that incorporates industrial 5G connectivity, device mobility, and strongly non-independent and identically distributed (non-IID) data. On MNIST dataset, RaLeD-FL reaches an accuracy of 0.95 twice faster than best-performing baselines and achieves a final accuracy of 0.98. On CIFAR-10 dataset, it is the only method that consistently exceeds 0.7 in accuracy. Compared with Edge-Vanilla, RaLeD-FL reduces E2E FL latency by 79 % on MNIST and 81% on CIFAR-10, while incurring a signaling overhead smaller than a single model update. These results suggest that radio-aware clustering and D2D multi-relay model-update routing can substantially improve the learning efficiency of HFL in industrial wireless environments.

papers.title: A hybrid machine learning framework for synthetic-augmented multimodal emotion recognition via EEG and facial expressions
papers.abstract: Emotion recognition from electroencephalography (EEG) and facial expressions is limited by small, imbalanced datasets and by differences between individuals. This study presents a hybrid framework combining synthetic data generation and multimodal fusion, evaluated on unseen participants and subjects. For EEG, federated learning with FedProx and participant-specific batch normalisation was combined with SMOTE (FedS-CNNReS). For facial expressions (CK+), synthetic images were generated with a conditional variational autoencoder (CC-Balanced). Because the two datasets come from different individuals, they were coupled through a shared valence–arousal label space and fused at the decision level with the proposed Contrastive Gated Attention Fusion model (CGA-Fusion). Synthetic EEG feature vectors preserved the performance obtained with real data, and training on synthetic data alone was equivalent to real-data training. Synthetic facial images raised the recall of the minority class (sadness) from 0.43 to 0.75. Fusion improved arousal and three-class recognition over the facial classifier alone (from 0.689 to 0.844 and from 0.765 to 0.888); the advantage of CGA-Fusion over a simple product rule came mainly from probability calibration. When both modalities were trained on synthetic data only, the fused model generalised to real data. These results show that synthetic data can support multimodal emotion recognition, especially for under-represented emotions.

papers.title: Release the Potential of Relative Feature Consistency for Data Heterogeneous Federated Learning
papers.abstract: Federated Learning is a promising paradigm to achieve privacy-preserving collaborative training. However, its performance degrades severely under data heterogeneity. A main obstacle is the divergent local representations induced by data heterogeneity, which will degrade the quality of the aggregated global representations. In this paper, we discover that although local representation spaces contain client-specific biases, their internal inter-class structure remains consistent across clients, which we identify as relative consistency. Through theoretical and empirical analyses, we further show that a proxy dataset can serve as a common anchor to translate class prototypes into a relative space, where client-specific shifts are suppressed and cross-client class centers become better aligned. Based on these findings, we propose a novel framework named Federated learning with Relative Representation Alignment (FedReRA) with Relative Knowledge Extraction (RKE) and Relative Ensemble Inference (REI) to extract and leverage the relative consistency to address data heterogeneity. Specifically, RKE debiases the prototypes by translating absolute prototypes into the aligned relative space via a flexible proxy dataset, while REI conducts collaborative inference with bias-reduced prediction in the relative space. Extensive experiments validate FedReRA's superiority over state-of-the-art methods, achieving a 3.83% average improvement under high heterogeneity and notably sustaining nearly 10% improvement on CIFAR-100 even when using random noise as the proxy data.
papers.venue: ACM International Conference on Information and Knowledge Management (CIKM)

papers.title: Transcending the Semantic Chasm: Knowledge-Graph Guided Aggregation for Cross-Silo Federated Session Recommendation
papers.abstract: Session-based Recommendation (SBR) achieves high performance in traditional centralized settings by using global item transition graphs to capture user intent. However, Federated Learning (FL) mandates collaborative training on isolated data, which makes the construction of such global structures unattainable. We identify this critical dilemma as ''Structure Collapse'', where the global graph remains fragmented despite model averaging. This collapse induces a ''Semantic Chasm,'' resulting in incompatible knowledge fusion and imprecise intent prediction. To break this impasse, we propose a novel Cross-Silo Federated Session-based Recommendation framework (CSFSR), which reconstructs global connectivity by harmonizing knowledge priors with local intents. Specifically, our Knowledge-Aware Initialization counteracts Structure Collapse by synthesizing shared attributes into a unified semantic space that anchors isolated clients. Further addressing the Semantic Chasm, the Graph-Guided Aggregation mechanism uses client signatures to direct personalized fusion, effectively filtering noise and ensuring robustness. Extensive experiments on three real-world datasets demonstrate that CSFSR significantly outperforms state-of-the-art federated baselines and exhibits superior noise robustness. Our code is available at https://github.com/Is-Jiejie/CSFSR.
papers.venue: ACM International Conference on Information and Knowledge Management (CIKM)

papers.title: Towards Efficient Federated Time Series Forecasting under Structural Data Heterogeneity across Nodes
papers.abstract: Time series data is highly valuable yet sharing-sensitive across nodes, making federated learning a promising paradigm to leverage distributed temporal data. However, varying sampling standards lead to heterogeneous data structures across nodes, with diverse time granularities and inconsistent variable sets being particularly prominent, posing significant challenges for conventional federated learning frameworks. In this paper, we propose PiXTime, a novel Transformer-based time series forecasting model designed to tolerate and exploit such structurally heterogeneous distributed data. Specifically, we redesign the internal modules and adopt the parameter-decoupling philosophy by carefully designating each module as either local or shared to handle the unique challenges of the federated scenario. To address granularity misalignments, PiXTime retains a personalized set of local modules for each node, acting as a crucial bridge between the node-specific raw temporal granularities and the unified feature dimension of the federated network. To tackle variable inconsistencies, we design a shared VE Table that explicitly injects globally unified variable categorical identities into specific auxiliary tokens, enhancing PiXTime's capability to collaboratively train under highly diverse auxiliary variable distributions. Extensive experiments demonstrate that PiXTime not only establishes state-of-the-art (SOTA) performance in handling structurally heterogeneous distributed data but also achieves superiority in conventional benchmarks. We open-source our code at https://github.com/WearTheClo/PiXTime.
papers.venue: ACM International Conference on Information and Knowledge Management (CIKM)

papers.title: FedCSOT: Model-Heterogeneous Personalized Federated Learning via Channel Semantic Optimal Transport
papers.abstract: Federated Learning (FL) provides a privacy-preserving paradigm for collaborative learning across distributed clients. In practical FL systems, clients often exhibit non-IID data distributions and deploy diverse model architectures under resource constraints. While model heterogeneity improves deployment flexibility under client resource constraints, it prevents direct parameter aggregation and makes cross-architecture knowledge transfer challenging. Existing methods mainly rely on shared structures, coarse-grained distillation, or projection-based feature alignment, which cannot explicitly capture channel-level semantic correspondences across heterogeneous architectures. This paper proposes FedCSOT, a model-heterogeneous personalized FL framework based on channel semantic optimal transport. FedCSOT induces sequence-driven channel semantics from channel responses over a shared unlabeled sequence, establishing a common semantic space for cross-architecture alignment. The framework models cross-architecture semantic alignment through entropy-regularized optimal transport to facilitate knowledge transfer. It further designs a divergence-aware personalized fusion strategy to adaptively balance consensus knowledge and local personalization under non-IID data distributions. Extensive experiments under diverse data and model heterogeneity settings demonstrate that FedCSOT consistently improves average test accuracy, convergence behavior, and robustness over representative baselines. The code is available at https://github.com/greenhead01/FedCSOT.
papers.venue: ACM International Conference on Information and Knowledge Management (CIKM)

papers.title: FedEMoE: Towards Class-Aware Federated Learning via Evidential Mixture-of-Experts
papers.abstract: Federated learning under non-IID data suffers from client drift. Recent work introduces Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architectures to handle data heterogeneity by routing inputs to specialized experts, but two problems remain. Softmax routing produces overconfident expert assignments with no reliability measure. The parameter space carries no class-level information, forcing the server to aggregate all clients uniformly and destroying the expert specialization built during local training. We call this class-level specialization invisibility. To address these problems, we propose FedEMoE. On the client side, Evidential Mixture-of-Experts equips router and experts with evidential heads, dynamically adjusts the number of active experts based on routing uncertainty, and compresses accumulated evidence into a per-client signature. On the server side, Evidence-Guided Class-Aware Aggregation takes the signatures as input and adaptively performs class-aware parameter fusion and component recombination. Experiments on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and FEMNIST show that FedEMoE consistently outperforms eight baseline methods across all settings. Our code is available at https://github.com/Stephen-Chow1/FedEMoE-CIKM.
papers.venue: ACM International Conference on Information and Knowledge Management (CIKM)

papers.title: DualFed-RCGC: Dual-Track Personalized Federated Learning via Covariance-Transferred Rare-Class Geometric Completion
papers.abstract: Personalized federated learning under extreme data heterogeneity suffers from two coupled structural issues: local majority-class gradients contaminate the globally shared representation, while rare classes lack sufficient local support, making reliable local discrimination difficult. To address these issues, we propose DualFed-RCGC, a dual-track personalized federated learning framework. First, it employs a Y-shaped architecture with explicit gradient-path isolation, decoupling global representation learning from local adaptation to mitigate majority-dominated gradients from biasing the shared backbone. Second, to improve discrimination for underrepresented classes, we introduce a Covariance-Transferred Rare-Class Geometric Completion (RCGC) module. It calibrates local decision boundaries by synthesizing geometry-aware virtual features using fixed Equiangular Tight Frame (ETF) anchors and covariance structures transferred from local majority classes. Finally, a class-aware masked distillation strategy selectively injects global knowledge to further improve rare-class discrimination. Extensive experiments on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and Tiny-ImageNet demonstrate that DualFed-RCGC consistently improves personalized local accuracy while retaining a usable shared branch for federated aggregation.
papers.venue: ACM International Conference on Information and Knowledge Management (CIKM)

papers.title: HiMAC: Hierarchical Federated Learning with Mobility-Aware Collaboration
papers.abstract: Mobility-aware hierarchical federated learning (MobiHFL) is an emerging paradigm to support urban applications where clients continuously move across edge-server coverage areas. Existing methods mainly treat mobility as a scheduling challenge and often train a single global model across all edge-servers. This overlooks the spatial non-IID characteristics of urban environments, where regions exhibit distinct yet correlated data distributions. Region-wise personalization is a natural remedy, but mobility makes it difficult. Each edge model is trained on its current client population, while future arriving and departing clients may follow different distributions, causing cold-start degradation and feature-classifier mismatch after handover. We propose \sysname, a personalized MobiHFL framework that turns predicted client movement into proactive inter-edge collaboration. \sysname uses per-client LSTM trajectory predictors to estimate future client flows and builds a round-level transition matrix to guide collaboration. With a decoupled backbone-classifier architecture, \sysname prepares each edge for expected incoming clients through incoming-aware classifier initialization and improves compatibility with likely destination edges through outgoing-regularized backbone training. Extensive experiments on image classification and object detection benchmarks show improvements of up to 12.18 percentage points in image-classification accuracy and 6.50 points in mAP@50 over state-of-the-art baselines across varying mobility intensities.
papers.venue: ACM International Conference on Information and Knowledge Management (CIKM)

papers.title: Knowledge-Driven Recommendations in Decentralized Systems: Integrating Federated Personal Data and Public Contexts
papers.abstract: Modern recommendation systems force a critical trade-off between user data sovereignty and algorithmic personalization, while decentralized alternatives often struggle with data sparsity and reactive interventions that fail during high-volatility events, like decentralized finance liquidations. This doctoral research outlines a comprehensive framework that bridges sovereignty-preserving collaborative learning with predictive risk management. By fusing private personal knowledge graphs with public contextual data through computationally efficient retrieval-augmented generation and federated learning, the system generates highly tailored recommendations without exposing raw user data. Concurrently, it develops proactive, agentic architectures utilizing Survival Analysis and the physics of self-organized criticality to forecast individual time-to-event risks and systemic network fragility. By integrating these macroscopic and microscopic topological signals, the framework empowers automated agents to dynamically shift from yield-maximizing recommendations to minimally invasive, protective interventions, safeguarding users against cascading failures in decentralized ecosystems.
papers.venue: ACM International Conference on Information and Knowledge Management (CIKM)

papers.title: FedCSN: Mitigating Skewed Feature via Class-wise Selective Normalization in Federated Learning
papers.abstract: Federated learning (FL) enables multiple distributed clients to collaboratively train a shared model without directly exchanging raw data. However, heterogeneous feature distributions across clients often lead to inconsistent local optimization and degraded model performance. Existing normalization-based augmentation methods attempt to alleviate this issue through cross-client statistic sharing. Nevertheless, most existing methods do not explicitly consider class consistency during normalization perturbation, where statistics from different classes may be indiscriminately applied to local samples. Through our investigation, we observe that class-consistent statistic sharing can improve model performance, while cross-class statistic perturbation may introduce noisy augmentation under heterogeneous edge environments. Motivated by these observations, we propose FedCSN, a lightweight normalization-based augmentation framework based on class-wise selective normalization for FL under feature distribution skew. Specifically, FedCSN constructs class-wise normalization statistics from local datasets and adopts an adaptive dominant-class statistic selection strategy to improve the reliability of uploaded class-wise statistics. During local training, each sample is augmented using normalization statistics associated with its class label, thereby reducing cross-class statistic mismatch. Extensive experiments demonstrate that FedCSN achieves the highest dataset-level average accuracy among the evaluated methods across all three datasets using both AlexNet and ResNet18 under severe Non-IID settings. In particular, using AlexNet, FedCSN improves the average accuracy on Office-Caltech-10 by 6.12 percentage points compared with the state-of-the-art normalization-based augmentation method. The source code is publicly available at https://github.com/MereIN0211/FedCSN.
papers.venue: ACM International Conference on Information and Knowledge Management (CIKM)

papers.title: ProRC: Prototype Personalization with Reliability Calibration in Heterogeneous Federated Learning
papers.abstract: Prototype-based federated learning (FL) provides a promising route for federated heterogeneity. By exchanging class prototypes rather than model parameters, it provides class-level semantic guidance under non-IID data and accommodates heterogeneous client backbones. Under severely skewed label distributions, however, two coupled limitations emerge. The broadcast global prototype is a cross-client average, and direct adoption can cause client semantic dilution. Meanwhile, local prototypes of rare classes are estimated from a few samples, leading to local margin erosion against well-supported neighbours. To address both, we propose ProRC, a prototype personalization framework grounded in shrinkage estimation. ProRC replaces naive alignment with a reliability-calibrated, margin-aware interpolation between global and local prototypes, and comprises two complementary client-side modules. The first module, Reliability-Calibrated Prototype Adaptation (RaPA), calibrates each global prototype by the reliability of its local counterpart, restoring client-specific semantics only to the extent the data warrant. The second module, Margin-Aware Prototype Refinement (MaPR), audits the candidate against the local true-class margin and attenuates margin-reducing steps. Together, the two modules are designed to mitigate client semantic dilution and local margin erosion, while preserving the prototype-exchange protocol and per-round payload of prior methods. Extensive experiments on label-skewed and real-world image benchmarks, together with ablation and reliability analyses, show that ProRC achieves the best overall average accuracy among the compared methods and improves the strongest prototype baseline in most heterogeneous settings.
papers.venue: ACM International Conference on Information and Knowledge Management (CIKM)

papers.title: Progressive Collaboration Pruning for Federated Learning
papers.abstract: Collaboration-based personalized federated learning (Co-PFL) mitigates data heterogeneity by enabling clients to selectively exchange knowledge through a learned collaboration graph. Despite their success, existing Co-PFL methods often update collaboration weights mainly from pairwise similarity, which can produce graphs that are either overly sparse and hinder knowledge propagation or overly dense and weaken personalization, leaving graph connectivity largely uncontrolled. In this paper, we propose FedPGP, a Co-PFL framework that explicitly schedules collaboration from dense to sparse over training rounds, enabling clients to first exploit broadly shared knowledge and then refine specialized knowledge aligned with their local distributions. FedPGP builds on a connectivity-aware similarity regularization that jointly accounts for global graph connectivity and client-model similarity, together with an efficient greedy pruning rule that removes edges with the least contribution to the regularized objective. We further present FedPGP+, a module-specific extension that learns different collaboration graphs for different model modules, allowing collaboration intensity to vary along model depth. Extensive experiments across diverse non-IID settings show that FedPGP and FedPGP+ consistently outperform state-of-the-art Co-PFL baselines, achieving up to 5.52% absolute accuracy improvement, while producing interpretable dense-to-sparse collaboration schedules.
papers.venue: ACM International Conference on Information and Knowledge Management (CIKM)

papers.title: Correlation-Guided Latent Sharing for Non-IID Federated Learning
papers.abstract: Federated learning (FL) enables collaborative model training across distributed clients without centralizing raw data, but its performance often degrades under non-independent and non-identically distributed (non-IID) data. This degradation is especially severe when clients observe only a limited subset of the global label space, causing biased local updates and client drift. Standard aggregation methods such as FedAvg and FedProx mainly address this problem at the optimization level, but they do not directly enrich the incomplete local data distributions that cause heterogeneity. This paper proposes Correlation-Guided Latent Sharing (CGLS), a federated learning framework that selectively augments client training using latent information received from statistically aligned peers. CGLS identifies compatible clients through gradient-direction correlation and mixes local training data with synthetic latent information from correlated neighbors. We formulate this process as a mixed-distribution federated objective and explain how targeted mixing can reduce gradient dispersion under severe label skew. Experiments on MNIST, FashionMNIST and CIFAR-10 under Dirichlet and balanced one-class non-IID partitions show that CGLS improves accuracy and macro-F1 over FedAvg and FedProx, with the largest gains appearing in the strongest heterogeneity settings.
papers.venue: ACM International Conference on Information and Knowledge Management (CIKM)

papers.title: QD-RDFL: Resources-decoupled Collaborative Computation for Data Assetization
papers.abstract: Computation is increasingly collaborative: data, models, and computing resources are indispensable yet rarely co-located. As their demands grow, especially the computational requirements of modern large language models, it is increasingly impractical for any participant to simultaneously possess high-quality data, advanced models, and sufficient computing resources. In settings such as federated learning (FL), participants typically control only one component; for example, a hospital may own patient data but lack powerful models or large-scale computing resources. We refer to this emerging paradigm as resource-decoupled collaborative computation. A key challenge to its sustainability is fair reward attribution, as data, ubiquitous yet critical to model quality, becomes a valuable digital asset. We propose a Resource-Decoupled FL framework (RDFL) that enables data owners, model owners, and computing centers to jointly train high-quality global models while maximizing data assetization value. We introduce a Tripartite Stackelberg Model for global utility optimization under strategic interaction and develop QD-RDFL, a Quality-aware Dynamic Resource-Decoupled FL algorithm that quantifies data-quality contributions and allocates rewards accordingly. Experiments demonstrate the effectiveness and robustness of our approach.
papers.venue: ACM International Conference on Information and Knowledge Management (CIKM)

papers.title: When Geometry Becomes Unreliable: Robust Federated Aggregation via Bounded Influence
papers.abstract: Robust aggregation in federated learning is often framed as down-weighting abnormal client updates. However, in realistic cross-device regimes, each round observes only a small number of high-dimensional updates, while benign updates can already be anisotropic, heavy-tailed, and strongly affected by non-IID data. In this setting, robustness depends not only on the final weighting rule, but also on whether the server-visible update geometry is estimable. We propose FedBIG (Federated Bounded-Influence Geometry), a server-side aggregation framework that separates geometry construction from influence control. Instead of scoring raw updates directly, FedBIG builds a stabilized sketch-space geometry using robust centering, low-dimensional projection, calibrated scatter estimation, shrinkage, and whitening. It then maps stabilized deviations to bounded-influence weights and aggregates the original client updates. Experiments on heterogeneous federated learning benchmarks show that FedBIG improves the robustness--utility trade-off under statistical and triggered poisoning. Ablations, boundary stress tests, and runtime analysis further support the central claim: robust aggregation is effective when server-visible geometry is estimable, and weakens when this geometry collapses under extreme heterogeneity or sparse participation. Our code is available at https://github.com/ytma-phoenix/FedBIG.
papers.venue: ACM International Conference on Information and Knowledge Management (CIKM)

papers.title: Fair to Federate? Two-Sided Prediction of Performance and Fairness Outcomes in Healthcare Federated Learning
papers.abstract: Federated learning (FL) has emerged as a promising paradigm for collaborative healthcare modeling under privacy constraints, yet institutions currently lack tools to anticipate how joining a federation will impact predictive performance and fairness. Existing work has primarily focused on post-hoc fairness mitigation, while overlooking the pre-collaboration decision itself. In this work, we introduce the Federation Assessment Problem, a two-sided prediction problem concerned with anticipating how federation would affect both a candidate institution seeking to join a federation and the institutions already participating in it, before collaboration occurs. To address this problem, we propose a two-stage meta-learning framework that predicts changes in performance and fairness metrics from institution-level metadata. We evaluate the framework on two healthcare imaging domains, across federations of varying sizes. Results show that federation-induced changes in both predictive performance and fairness can be estimated with high accuracy. The analysis further identifies label bias as one of the strongest predictors of fairness outcomes across both domains, often rivaling or exceeding demographic composition in importance. These findings demonstrate that informed federation assessment is possible without raw data sharing and highlight the need to explicitly measure multiple sources of bias when reasoning about fairness in healthcare FL.
papers.venue: ACM International Conference on Information and Knowledge Management (CIKM)

papers.title: Cross-Architecture Semantic Backdoor Attack in Data-Driven Federated Learning
papers.abstract: Traditional Federated Learning (FL) relies on iterative parameter exchange, which limits architectural flexibility and introduces high communication overhead for large foundation models. To address these issues, Data-Driven Federated Learning (DD-FL) has recently emerged as a scalable alternative. Instead of exchanging model parameters, DD-FL adopts a one-shot data-centric pipeline, where heterogeneous clients collaboratively annotate a shared unlabeled public dataset and the server performs knowledge distillation through soft-label aggregation. While DD-FL improves scalability and supports heterogeneous architectures, it also introduces a new attack surface on the shared public dataset. These public datasets are often collected from web crawlers or collaborative platforms with limited integrity validation, making data poisoning feasible. Moreover, since DD-FL removes parameter-level interactions and relies on soft-label aggregation across heterogeneous models, traditional FL backdoor attacks designed for individual models are easily diluted and exhibit poor cross-architecture transferability. In this paper, we propose a semantic backdoor attack for DD-FL. Our method generates poisoned samples by aligning image perturbations with target semantic directions in a shared vision-language space. This enables poisoned samples to induce semantically aligned target predictions across heterogeneous client models, making the backdoor more transferable during soft-label aggregation. We also study how biased aggregation weights further strengthen the attack effect. Experiments on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and TinyImageNet show that our method achieves higher attack success rates and robustness than existing baselines, while maintaining high clean accuracy and strong visual stealthiness.
papers.venue: ACM International Conference on Information and Knowledge Management (CIKM)

papers.title: Artificial Intelligence for Data Engineering and Management Of Networked Systems (AI4DEMONS)
papers.abstract: Modern networked systems generate massive volumes of heterogeneous and continuously evolving data, creating major challenges for data management, intelligent analysis, and cybersecurity. Traditional machine learning approaches often struggle to adapt to the scale, decentralization, and dynamic nature of contemporary network environments, motivating the need for adaptive, distributed, and knowledge-driven AI solutions. This workshop explores recent advances in AI-driven network intelligence and cybersecurity, with a particular focus on information and knowledge management techniques for distributed systems. Topics include Generative AI (GenAI) for synthetic network data generation and augmentation, Large Language Models (LLMs) and Natural Language Processing (NLP) for cybersecurity intelligence and threat analysis, continual and federated learning for privacy-preserving adaptive systems, adversarial learning and trustworthy AI, and agentic AI for autonomous and human-in-the-loop security workflows. The workshop also investigates retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), knowledge graphs, reasoning over structured and unstructured security data, intelligent orchestration, and scalable AI-enabled network analytics. By bringing together researchers and practitioners from AI, cybersecurity, networking, and knowledge management, the workshop aims to foster interdisciplinary discussion on resilient, intelligent, and trustworthy networked systems.
papers.venue: ACM International Conference on Information and Knowledge Management (CIKM)

papers.title: Artificial Intelligence for Pulmonary Disease Diagnosis: A Comparative Review of Medical Imaging Modalities and Deep Learning Approaches
papers.venue: Communications in computer and information science

papers.title: A comprehensive survey of malware detection across platforms
Adaptive noise-mitigated distributed variational quantum sensing with federated learning
Artificial intelligence–driven pharmacovigilance: transforming signal detection, real-world drug safety monitoring, and regulatory decision-making
papers.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Pharmacovigilance is undergoing rapid transformation due to the expansion of digital healthcare systems, biomedical data generation, and pharmaceutical innovation. Conventional drug-safety monitoring methods remain limited by underreporting, delayed signal identification, fragmented datasets, and restricted predictive capability. Artificial intelligence (AI) has emerged as a promising approach for improving signal detection, real-world drug-safety surveillance, and regulatory decision-making. AREAS COVERED: This review evaluates application of AI technologies in modern pharmacovigilance and regulatory science. It discusses use of machine learning, deep learning, neural networks, and natural language processing for adverse-event detection, literature mining, signal prioritization, and analysis of electronic health records (EHR) and social-media data. Emerging technologies, including large language models, federated learning, blockchain, digital twins, and Internet of Things (IoT)-enabled monitoring systems, are also explored. Literature was identified through structured searches of MEDLINE/PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, Embase, and Google Scholar, covering publications from January 2000 to February 2026. EXPERT OPINION: AI-driven pharmacovigilance has potential to improve real-time safety surveillance, predictive risk assessment, and automated regulatory workflows. However, broader implementation remains challenged by concerns related to interpretability, data quality, cybersecurity, algorithmic bias, and regulatory validation. Future progress will depend on transparent, explainable, and human-supervised AI systems integrated within globally interoperable healthcare infrastructures.

papers.title: Research on supply chain data privacy protection and anomaly detection empowered by federated learning
papers.abstract: In the context of digital transformation, sensitive data flowing through various links of the supply chain faces severe privacy leakage risks. Traditional centralized data sharing models struggle to balance data utilization and privacy protection, and the cross-organizational collaborative needs for supply chain anomaly detection urgently need to be met. This research aims to construct a supply chain data privacy protection and anomaly detection system based on federated learning, addressing core issues such as distributed storage of supply chain data, stringent privacy protection requirements, and high accuracy requirements for anomaly detection. The research designs a multi-level anomaly detection algorithm integrating variational autoencoders and gradient boosting decision trees through a compliant supply chain data collection and preprocessing process; constructs a federated learning framework including participant models and data collaborative processing mechanisms, and combines homomorphic encryption, differential privacy, and de-identification strategies to achieve data privacy protection; and compares the performance of different machine learning methods, designing a multidimensional evaluation index system. Experimental results show that the proposed federated learning method achieves an anomaly detection accuracy of 89.2% and a recall of 85.1%, which are 1.7% and 2.8% higher than traditional centralized learning, respectively. Furthermore, it significantly improves privacy protection and reduces model training time by 15.6%. This research provides a feasible technical solution for anomaly detection and data privacy protection in crossorganizational supply chain collaboration, and has significant theoretical and practical value for promoting the digital transformation of the supply chain and improving the overall risk management capabilities of the industry.
papers.venue: International Conference on Wireless, Optical Communication, and Information Engineering (WOCIE)

papers.title: RelayFL: A firefly optimization-based relay federated learning framework for heterogeneous clients
papers.venue: Journal of Network and Computer Applications

papers.title: An Adaptive Federated Learning Model for Fault Detection and Node Reuse Using Deep Learning Mechanism in Wireless Sensor Networks
papers.abstract: The growing complexity of Wireless Sensor Networks (WSNs) within Internet of Things (IoT) enabled applications presents significant challenges related to fault detection, energy efficiency, and network resilience. Node failures can cause severe disruptions, leading to increased energy consumption, data loss, and reduced network lifespan. Conventional fault detection methods lack flexibility when dealing with node relocations, while machine learning-based techniques often overlook energy efficiency considerations. This research proposes the Adaptive Federated Learning for Fault Detection and Node Reuse (AFL-FDNR) framework, which combines federated learning with Deep Q-Network (DQN) to provide an adaptive, energy-efficient solution for fault detection and node recovery. Federated learning ensures scalable, privacy-preserving model training across sensor nodes, while DQN optimizes node recovery decisions based on real-time network conditions. Simulation results demonstrate that AFL-FDNR achieves 96.01% fault detection accuracy, reduces energy consumption to 1910 J, and extends network lifetime to 11,452 hours. These metrics demonstrate the framework’s ability to enhance the reliability, efficiency, and sustainability of large-scale WSNs, making it a robust solution for modern IoT applications.
papers.venue: International Research Journal of Computer Science

papers.title: Machine Learning for Predictive Maintenance of Industrial Systems: A Review of Methods, Benchmarks, Challenges and Future Directions
papers.abstract: Aims: To critically review how machine learning is applied to predictive maintenance of industrial assets, to compare the main method families and benchmark practices, and to identify the barriers that limit industrial adoption and the priorities for future research. Study Design: Narrative (non-systematic) review. Methodology: Peer-reviewed journal articles, conference papers and established review studies published between 2006 and 2026 were identified from major scientific databases and publisher platforms using combinations of the terms predictive maintenance, condition monitoring, fault diagnosis, prognostics, remaining useful life and machine learning. Seminal and highly cited works, benchmark-dataset papers and recent advances were prioritised. The evidence was synthesised by maintenance task, method family, dataset, evaluation metric and deployment issue. Results: Machine learning in predictive maintenance has progressed from feature-engineered shallow classifiers to deep convolutional, recurrent and attention-based networks that learn directly from raw sensor signals, and, more recently, to transfer learning, federated learning, physics-informed hybrid models and large foundation models. Deep models report strong accuracy on public benchmarks for bearing fault diagnosis and turbofan remaining-useful-life estimation, and hybrid physics and deep-learning models have extended prognostic horizons while requiring less training data. However, most evidence comes from a small number of laboratory or simulated datasets; performance under domain shift, scarce failure data, uncertainty quantification, interpretability and the link between prediction and maintenance decisions remain weakly addressed. Conclusion: Machine learning is a mature enabler of predictive maintenance, but industrial value depends less on marginal benchmark gains than on robust, explainable, uncertainty-aware and decision-oriented models validated on field data. Standardised evaluation protocols, open industrial datasets, hybrid knowledge-and-data models and cost-benefit evidence are the main priorities for future work.
papers.venue: Journal of Engineering Research and Reports

papers.title: Federated learning-driven quantum models for EEG-based neurological disorder classifications
papers.abstract: Electroencephalography (EEG) enables non-invasive detection of neurological disorders with Deep Learning (DL). However, traditional methodologies for the training of DL models raises privacy concerns due to its centralized training. Federated learning (FL) mitigates these issues by training models in decentralized manner while keeping data on-device. Most peer studies rely on centralized data, and it remains unclear whether emerging quantum classifiers and circuits can match or surpass DL models under FL settings. This study, therefore, presents FL framework for EEG classification using DL models and quantum models while preserving the data locality. Five clients trained locally on 80/20 splits and shared only local model weights for aggregation of the global model. DL models included EEGNetv1, EEGNetv4, EEGITNet, and EEGInception. Quantum models included Quantum Support Vector Machine (QSVM), Variational Quantum Classifier (VQC), and Quantum Convolutional Neural Network (QCNN). Two public datasets e.g., OpenNeuro and TUH EEG Corpus have been utilized. Results show that on the OpenNeuro dataset QSVM global model outperformed with a classification accuracy of 93.57%, and among DL models EEGNetv1 outperformed with an accuracy of 96.92%. Whereas, for the TUH dataset the QCNN model outperformed with an accuracy of 94.52% and EEGInception outperformed among DL models with an accuracy of 92.38%, respectively. This framework demonstrates decentralized training under FL settings and shows that quantum models are comparable to tailored EEG DL models for multiclass classification problem. The results demonstrate the feasibility of integrating FL with quantum models for decentralized EEG based diagnosis, highlighting the practical approach for healthcare industry.

papers.title: Hybrid Chunking and Blockchain-Oriented Secure Deduplication with Federated Authentication for ScalableIIoT–Cloud Ecosystem
Interpretable Federated Learning for Pneumonia Detection: A Data Locality Baseline
papers.abstract: Deep learning in medical imaging is often hinderedby strict data privacy regulations. Federated Learning (FL)provides a decentralized solution, allowing medical centers tocollaboratively train models without transmitting raw data. Thismanuscript evaluates a simulated federated baseline architecturefor pneumonia detection from chest X-rays. We analyze dataheterogeneity, local model drift, and aggregation algorithms, comparing Federated Averaging (FedAvg) with proximal regularizedFedProx. To simulate clinical disparities, we partition a publicdataset into discrete clients with defined label and quantity skews,creating nonindependent and identically distributed (non-IID)environments. We also integrate Gradient weighted Class Activation Mapping (Grad-CAM) for qualitative visual feedback onmodel predictions. Results show federated training significantlyoutperforms isolated local training, approximating centralizedmodel accuracy. We frame this architecture as a data localitybaseline, not a cryptographically secure system, and note thatvisualizations require independent clinical validation. The fullprototype and configurations are open sourced for methodologicaltransparency.
papers.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

papers.title: Decentralized Federated Learning for Multi-Class Predictive Maintenance in Industrial IoT Systems
papers.abstract: Predictive maintenance (PdM) is a key enabler of reliability and cost reduction in Industrial Internet of Things (IIoT) systems. However, conventional centralized learning approaches require raw data aggregation, raising serious concerns regarding data privacy, communication overhead, and single points of failure. Federated Learning (FL) addresses part of this challenge by enabling distributed model training, yet centralized FL architectures still rely on a central aggregator. This paper proposes a decentralized federated learning (DFL) framework based on a ring topology for multi-class predictive maintenance in IIoT environments. The proposed approach enables collaborative model training among distributed edge nodes without relying on a central server, thereby enhancing system robustness, scalability, and data privacy. A lightweight deep neural network (DNN) is employed to classify five machine operating states using multi-sensor data, including vibration, temperature, and current measurements. Extensive experiments are conducted using a real-world sensor dataset collected from three-phase AC motors under multiple fault conditions. The performance of the proposed DFL approach is systematically compared against a non-federated baseline and a centralized FL (CFL) scheme. Experimental results demonstrate that the decentralized framework achieves clas-sification performance comparable to centralized FL, with an accuracy of up to 99.83%, while eliminating the dependency on a central coordinator. The findings confirm the feasibility of decentralized federated learning for predictive maintenance applica-tions, particularly in distributed industrial settings where data privacy, fault tolerance, and communication efficiency are critical.
papers.venue: International Journal of Mechatronics Robotics and Artificial Intelligence

papers.title: Lightweight and Poisoning-Resilient Federated AI Framework for Secure 5G Edge Communications
papers.abstract: With the rapid popularization of 5G edge communication systems, their decentralized architecture and the ultra-large attack surface brought by massive access devices have created severe network security challenges. Although current artificial intelligence-based intrusion detection systems and conventional federated learning schemes can achieve high intrusion detection accuracy, they universally suffer from two major limitations: excessive computational overhead and vulnerability to poisoning attacks, which make them unable to adapt to resource-constrained edge deployment environments. To address this issue, this paper proposes a lightweight anti-poisoning federated learning framework for low-latency secure 5G edge communications, with two core design elements: First, it integrates lightweight GRU/CNN models and a trust-aware aggregation mechanism to weaken the negative impact of malicious model updates; second, it introduces a deviation-based poisoning detection strategy to identify and filter adversarial updates during the federated learning process. We used the public CICIDS2017 dataset to complete tests in a simulated 5G edge environment equipped with 100 to 1000 edge devices, covering multiple scenarios including DDoS, MITM, and poisoning attacks. The results show that compared with existing similar schemes, the proposed framework reaches a maximum detection accuracy of 98.3\%, reduces communication latency by 30-35\%, cuts computational overhead by 40-60\%, and sees only a negligible drop in accuracy under poisoning attacks. It can support a wide range of real-time 5G edge applications such as intelligent transportation, smart cities, and the industrial Internet of Things.
