papers.title: CAMRA: Cross-Architecture Multimodal Reinforcement Learning with Federated Adaptation for IoT Malware Detection and Classification
papers.abstract: Abstract The domain of Internet of Things (IoT) has been rapidly developing, consequently expanding the attack surface for malware that exploits vulnerabilities across various hardware architectures and evades conventional static detection techniques. Past frameworks for IoT malware detection and classification often rely on a single data modality or are designed for a specific device architecture, which limits their ability to detect and classify malware in heterogeneous environments. This paper proposes CAMRA, a cross-architecture malware detection and classification framework that combines multimodal data, Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL), and Federated Learning (FL). Using the CIC-YNU-IoT-MAL-26 dataset, CAMRA fuses network-level (PCAP), hardware-level (SAR), and system-level (STRACE) data streams through cross-modal attention across the ARM, MIPS, MIPSEL, and x86 architectures. A DRL controller adapts the per-class loss weights during training to address class imbalance, and federated learning adapts the centrally trained model across architecture-specific clients while keeping their raw data local. Over ten random seeds, CAMRA achieves a Macro-F1 of $$0.752 \pm 0.012$$ (accuracy $$98.4\%$$ ), and the federated model achieves $$0.741 \pm 0.008$$ (accuracy $$98.6\%$$ ), outperforming every single-modality model and standard baseline. Ablation and paired statistical tests show that the frequency-based class weights and the loss function are the main drivers of performance, with the DRL controller performing on par with fixed class weighting. In holdout experiments, malware from unseen architectures and from an unseen malware family is detected as malicious, while an unseen ARM architecture leads to false alarms on benign data.
papers.venue: International Journal of Computational Intelligence Systems

papers.title: Editorial: Data-driven brain imaging and signal analysis: methods from acquisition to clinical insight
papers.abstract: Introduction -There has been rapid advancement in the fields of neuroimaging, electrophysiology, and computational methods, which has greatly increased our capacity to investigate the human brain. Methods including electroencephalography (EEG), intracranial EEG (iEEG), magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), diffusion imaging, and positron emission tomography (PET) offer detailed insights into the structure, function, dynamics, and molecular processes of the brain, while machine learning (ML), deep learning, multimodal analysis, and distributed computing allow for a more detailed analysis of these data sets. Yet the use of complex technologies does not ensure that the results obtained are reliable or have clinical significance. The reliability of data-driven neuroscience relies on the whole research process, from accurate data collection and suitable preprocessing through to robust analysis and a meaningful biological and clinical interpretation. It is therefore necessary to ensure reliability at every stage if complex brain data are to be turned into useful scientific and clinical insights.The research topic entitled 'Data-Driven Brain Imaging and Signal Analysis: Methods from Acquisition to Clinical Insight' combines methodological and applied research involving brain data acquisition, quality assessment, the analysis of MRI and PET-MR data, EEG and iEEG, functional connectivity, biomarkers, AI, multimodal learning, federated learning, and immersive experimental methods [1 -13]. Together, these studies show a translational pathway from reliable acquisition of brain data and its meaningful representation to a more advanced analysis and to insights that are relevant in a clinical context. This editorial presents the main contributions and points out the common methodological themes as well as the future directions.Reliable acquisition and data quality -First of all, reliable data acquisition is a fundamental basis of data-driven neuroscience. The data from brain imaging and neural recordings can be influenced by features of the participants, the acquisition protocols, the equipment used, the practices of the operators, movements of the participants, physiological changes, and clinical conditions. Such factors can have an impact on the reproducibility and generalizability of computational models. Study [1] provides a retrospective motion-related quality estimate using a 3D CNN trained on synthetically motion-corrupted structural MRI. Incorporating this estimate into cortical morphometric analyses improved statistical model fit in several datasets. This study highlights that acquisition quality must be regarded as an essential component of quantitative neuroimaging. Likewise, Study [13] emphasizes that reproducible clinical neuroimaging requires more than standardized acquisition parameters: it depends on coordinated workflows that accommodate participants' clinical needs while maintaining consistent acquisition and qualitycontrol practices. By linking participant preparation, staff training, and timely quality assessment, the framework treats data quality as a responsibility throughout the acquisition workflow rather than a problem addressed only during preprocessing.Together, these studies highlight complementary roles for prospective acquisition procedures [13] and retrospective motion estimates [1] in supporting reproducibility. It is therefore essential to have clear protocols, carry out consistent quality checks, and provide proper documentation if reliable data is to be obtained and if meaningful downstream analysis is to be supported.Complex measurements to meaningful representations -Secondly, it is paramount to represent complex brain measurements in such a way that biologically and clinically relevant information is retained. Since brain activity is dynamic and spread out over different spatial and temporal scales, it is essential to use appropriate methods of data representation if meaningful analysis is to result. Study [2] looks at multi-frequency dynamic functional connectivity in schizophrenia by means of constrained tensor decomposition and shows that brain connectivity changes both over time and frequency. The temporal organisation of brain activity is also examined in [3] by means of frequency-specific EEG microstates during ciprofol-induced changes in consciousness. Study [4] looks at the stage-specific ERP responses that occur during audiovisual facial emotion processing and their association with depressive tendencies.Together, these studies show that temporal and frequency-specific neural patterns can offer insights into brain function and behaviour.Study [5] constructs an age-references normative quantitative EEG space and uses Mahalanobis distances to quantify individual deviations in SNAREopathies, linking these deviations to distinct dimensions of clinical severity. Study [6] uses diffusion kurtosis imaging to identify widespread reductions in radial kurtosis in obstructive sleep apnea, with regional associations with lowest oxygen saturation and cognitive performance. These remain as indirect measures of tissue microstructure. Study [7] relates intravoxel incoherent motion (IVIM)-derived diffusion and perfusion measures to PET-measured amyloid and tau burden, reporting associations rather than direct evidence of glymphatic clearance. These studies highlight the value of individual normative comparisons [5] and the importance of distinguishing imaging associations [6,7] from evidence of specific biological mechanisms.Together, these contributions demonstrate that the aim is not merely to obtain a greater number of brain measurements, but rather to create meaningful representations which link neural signals and imaging findings with biological processes and clinical outcomes.Artificial intelligence beyond conventional classification -Artificial intelligence (AI) has now become a significant component of modern neuroscience and medical imaging. The studies included in this research area indicate that the value of AI should be judged not just on its accuracy but also on its reliability and practical usefulness. Study [8] introduces CPRSCA-ResNet for the purpose of detecting seizures based on EEG data and tests it in both patient-dependent and patientindependent scenarios. The patient-independent approach is especially significant when it comes to evaluating the method's ability to be applied to new patients. Study [9] applies feature-based optimization in the classification of brain tumours from MRI scans, emphasizing the ongoing importance of good feature selection and representation, particularly in cases where data size, efficiency, and interpretability are key factors. Study [10] identifies resting state functional connectivity as the strongest modality for distinguishing patients from controls and predicting symptom severity in binge-type eating disorders. Multimodal fusion did not improve diagnostic classification beyond the best single modality, although it improved prediction of selected symptom-related outcomes. These findings highlight that the added value of multimodal integration depends on the prediction target and should be demonstrated rather than assumed. At the same time, study [11] introduces FLightcase, an open-source federated learning toolbox, and demonstrates its real-world deployment across three international centers to predict cognitive performance in multiple sclerosis from T1-weighted MRI using transfer learning from a brain-age model. Beyond enabling collaborative training without sharing patient data, the study highlights the challenges posed by inter-center differences in imaging and clinical measures, underscoring the importance of harmonization and site-specific performance assessment.These studies together show that in order for AI to be effective in the field of neuroscience it is necessary to have more than just high accuracy; robustness, generalizability, interpretability, reproducibility, privacy, and clinical relevance are just as important if the results are to be meaningfully translated into practice.Multimodal and ecologically relevant approaches -This area also shows the advantages of using more natural experimental situations. The study referred to in [12] offers a framework that integrates intracranial EEG with immersive virtual reality, enabling high-resolution neural activity to be examined during experiences that are controlled yet more realistic. These kinds of approaches are capable of helping to fill the gap between the highly controlled conditions of laboratory experiments and the complexity of real-world behaviour.In total, the topic collection combines imaging, electrophysiology, behavioural information, clinical data, and computational methods. Such integration is essential for precision neuroscience since an increasing understanding of brain function requires information from different spatial, temporal, and biological levels.Key themes and future directions -Several common themes and future directions can be identified in the collection. First, data quality and reproducibility should continue to be at the heart of the research pipeline. Even with the use of advanced algorithms, it is not possible to compensate for poor data acquisition, motion-related artefacts, incomplete metadata, or inconsistent protocols. Second, the issue of generalizability is still a major one. Good performance on one dataset does not mean that this performance will carry over to other institutions, different scanners, various populations, or different clinical settings. External validation, multi-site studies, data harmonization, and privacy-preserving methods such as federated learning will therefore become increasingly important. Third, when integrating multiple modalities it is necessary to do so on the basis of biological meaning. The various modalities differ in their spatial and temporal resolution, measurement uncertainty, and biological interpretation. Merely combining datasets does not ensure that meaningful results will be obtained. Finally, clinical translation presupposes more than just high computational performance. The models should also be reliable, interpretable, feasible, and able to provide information that can assist in making actual clinical decisions. Attaining this goal will depend on ongoing collaboration between clinicians, neuroscientists, engineers, computer scientists, statisticians, and data scientists.Editorial process -The editorial process involved the evaluation of the contributions to this research topic by means of peer review and editorial assessment within the respective Frontiers journals and specialty sections. This collection includes methodological and applied studies covering neuroimaging, neural signal analysis, AI, and clinical neuroscience. Instead of concentrating on one particular technique, the research topic shows that significant advances require complementary improvements in data acquisition, quality control, representation, computation, integration, and interpretation.The research topic demonstrates how quickly the field of neuroscience has developed and how diverse it has become. It covers a wide range of areas, including neuroimaging acquisition and the assessment of motion, functional connectivity, EEG analysis, diffusion imaging, PET-MR, AI, multimodal learning, federated learning, and immersive neural recording, thereby demonstrating the close relationship between advances in methodology and clinical objectives. One of the key points is that valuable clinical insights hinge on the reliability of the whole research process. Reliable data is made possible by high-quality acquisition, robust analysis is achieved through appropriate representations, and well-validated computational methods can help to lead to a biological understanding and clinical translation.More powerful algorithms alone will not be enough to achieve future progress. Data-driven neuroscience also needs to become more reproducible, interpretable, generalizable, privacy-aware, and clinically useful. We hope that this research topic will help to achieve that aim and promote further integration of acquisition, signal and image analysis, computational intelligence, and clinical neuroscience.

papers.title: How Robust Are Robust Aggregators? Model Poisoning in Federated Learning under Data Heterogeneity
papers.abstract: Federated learning trains a shared model acrossmany clients without collecting their data, but a few maliciousclients can sabotage training by sending falsified updates. Robustaggregation rules are designed to resist such attacks, yet theyare often evaluated on homogeneous data, whereas real clientshold heterogeneous data. We study how data heterogeneity affectsfive aggregation rules (FedAvg, coordinate-wise median, trimmedmean, Krum and norm clipping) under four poisoning attacks,in 585 experiments on Fashion-MNIST with Dirichlet-partitionedclients. We find that heterogeneity strongly amplifies the attacks:under sign flipping with 20% malicious clients, the robust ruleslose less than 2 points of accuracy with nearly IID data, but 8 to12 points with highly heterogeneous data. In this setting, Krumis 39 points less accurate than FedAvg even without attackers,while norm clipping, which bounds each client’s influence withoutdiscarding updates, is the most resilient. These results suggestthat robust aggregation rules should be evaluated under realisticnon-IID conditions.
papers.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

papers.title: Reproducible Implementation of an Attention-Enhanced Meta-Learning Network for Personalized Federated Learning with Heterogeneous Client Data
papers.abstract: This protocol describes the implementation and evaluation of attention-enhanced meta-learning personalized federated learning (AEML-PFL) for heterogeneous image-classification clients. The custom PyTorch simulation uses 50 clients, synchronous aggregation, and five independent random-seed runs. It evaluates Fashion-MNIST, Federated Extended MNIST (FEMNIST), and the Canadian Institute for Advanced Research datasets CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100. Client data are not independent and identically distributed (non-IID). FEMNIST uses the same 50-writer cohort of 18,642 images across all five seeds; the other datasets use Dirichlet-based label partitions. Personalized test accuracies are 93.6%, 86.0%, 74.3%, and 47.1%, respectively, after checkpoint selection by validation accuracy. On CIFAR-10, the mean accuracy of the five worst-performing clients is 62.7%, and the across-client standard deviation is 6.2 percentage points. The number of rounds to 95% of each method's own peak validation accuracy is 166 for AEML-PFL and 214 for federated averaging. The protocol provides a workflow for examining personalized performance under label and sample-count heterogeneity.

papers.title: BC-MFAIGC: The Blockchain-Enabled Mobile Federated Artificial Intelligence Generated Content
papers.abstract: With the rapid advancement of artificial intelligence, AI-generated content (AIGC) applications are becoming increasingly prevalent. However, it remains challenging to deliver high-quality AIGC services in edge scenarios that have real-time requirements and limited resources. In this paper, we propose BC-MFAIGC, a blockchain-enabled framework for mobile federated AIGC. The proposed BC-MFAIGC architecture coordinates edge computing, federated learning, and blockchain. Edge computing brings selected services closer to terminals, federated learning supports collaborative training without transferring raw user data, and blockchain provides transaction authentication, traceable update records, and governance functions. We evaluate the implemented denoising diffusion probabilistic model (DDPM) federated-training workflow under malicious updates using single-machine simulations. Under a medium-strength Gaussian weight-perturbation condition, the observed Fréchet Inception Distance (FID) increase is approximately 2.5% for BC-MFAIGC-Soft and 9.3% for NOBC-MFAIGC-Soft, compared with about 22% for FedAvg in the three-seed evaluation, while the worker-layer detection rate in the near-threshold regime is 9.03–14.29%, reflecting the difficulty of distinguishing malicious from benign updates when their score distributions overlap. Under the current attack condition, the mean FID across five seeds is 307.62 for BC-MFAIGC-Soft and 285.86 for NOBC-MFAIGC-Soft compared with 372.55 for FedAvg. The paired mean difference between BC-MFAIGC-Soft and FedAvg is −64.93 with an unadjusted 95% bootstrap CI ranging from −96.64 to −29.53. The corresponding difference between NOBC-MFAIGC-Soft and FedAvg is −86.69 with an unadjusted 95% bootstrap CI ranging from −120.75 to −50.80. Both comparisons have Holm-adjusted p=0.25. Separate protocol tests cover transaction authentication, block-integrity checking, and replay handling, and the simulated ledger configuration increases round wall-clock time by 8.6%.

papers.title: Energy Allocation Between Computation and Wi-Fi Transmission in TinyML Federated Learning on IoT Devices: A Measured Crossover
papers.abstract: Abstract Energy models for federated learning (FL) on battery-powered Internet of Things (IoT) devices often assume that radio transmission costs far more than on-device computation. We test this assumption on a Wi-Fi microcontroller: an ESP32-S3 trains the output head of a keyword-spotting model and exchanges its updates over 2.4 GHz Wi-Fi, while an independent power monitor and hardware phase markers separate the energy of computation from that of communication. Across 105 runs, computation costs 1.00 mJ per local epoch with no detectable fixed overhead, and communication costs 7.4 to 9.7 mJ per client turn in two sessions, regardless of the number of epochs. The two are therefore equal at 7.4 to 9.7 local epochs. Training started immediately after a radio burst absorbs about 0.5 mJ of tail energy, which a short pause removes. Shannon-capacity and switching-energy models underestimate the measured energies by 95% to 99% at their nominal parameters, because they omit protocol overhead and memory activity, and neither contains the power drawn while the device is awake. We show that sleeping between rounds moves the crossover toward the ratio of exchange time to epoch time, which yields 11 to 19 epochs with sleep powers measured on the same board. In deep sleep the board draws 17.2 mW, but each wake-up, dominated by Wi-Fi re-association, costs 0.68 J, 35 times the marginal energy of a ten-epoch turn. From these results, we derive a measurement-calibrated procedure for selecting the number of local epochs and design guidelines for energy-constrained IoT clients.

papers.title: Artificial Intelligence-Based Intrusion Detection Systems for Smart University Ecosystems: A Survey of IoT Security, Cloud Learning Platforms, and Connected Campus Services
papers.abstract: Smart Universities increasingly rely on connected learning platforms, smart classrooms, Internet of Things (IoT) devices, cloud services, and digital administrative systems. This integration expands the attack surface and creates security requirements involving educational data, heterogeneous infrastructure, and the continuous availability of academic services. This survey examines AI-based intrusion detection through three complementary perspectives: campus-specific threats and architectural layers, detection approaches and their deployment trade-offs, and operational evaluation and governance requirements. It reviews machine learning, deep learning, ensemble and hybrid models, lightweight detection, federated learning, and explainable AI, relating their capabilities and limitations to device, edge, network, cloud, and application layers. The analysis highlights gaps between benchmark performance and evidence of suitability for operational university environments, including limited campus-specific validation, incomplete reporting of latency and resource requirements, and insufficient assessment of privacy safeguards and explanation usefulness. Conventional detection metrics remain necessary but should be complemented by false-alert workload, end-to-end latency, temporal robustness, communication costs, and analyst-centered evaluation. The survey provides a campus-oriented synthesis, an operational evaluation matrix, and a staged research and deployment roadmap prioritizing documented datasets, accountable data governance, baseline assessment, and monitored pilots before broader federation or automated response. AI-based intrusion detection offers promising capabilities for Smart Universities, but its practical value requires validation under representative campus conditions and alignment with institutional resources, privacy obligations, and incident-response processes.

papers.title: Blockchain-Federated Learning using advanced Bayesian LSTM-FAN for Real Option Valuation prediction
papers.abstract: Real Option Valuation (ROV) forecasting is an estimate of the value of flexible investment opportunities in the presence of uncertainty treating them as financial options. Unlike conventional valuation techniques, ROV considers the acknowledgment of strategic choices that can be decided by managers, like waiting, growing, or shelving a project depending on evolving market conditions. Forecasting methodologies tend to employ simulations and complex models, such as Deep Learning (DL), to predict uncertain variables affecting option value. This strategy delivers a more realistic and flexible evaluation, enabling organizations to make more informed decisions in the context of uncertainty. This work aims to design a hybrid DL model for ROV prediction. The key objective is to design a blockchain-Federated Learning (FL) model integrated with DL for ROV prediction. FL constructs a global model by aggregating locally trained models on the blockchain so that the collaboratively trained global model can give improved and more accurate predictions. The local model learns with the proposed Bayesian Long Short-Term Network-Fourier Analysis Networks (BayesianLSTM-FAN), a fusion of Bayesian Long Short-Term Network (BayesianLSTM) and Fourier Analysis Networks (FAN). The data is preprocessed first by data cleaning and scaling (StandardScaler) and then by statistical feature extraction (Rolling window), and prediction is done using the proposed BayesianLSTM-FAN. Lastly, the model also enables simultaneous training of a global model with the use of blockchain technology as well as FL. Experimental results show that the proposed approach obtained an MSE value of 0.001, an MAE of 0.024, and an R-squared value of 0.965.
papers.venue: International Journal of Wavelets Multiresolution and Information Processing

papers.title: Multi-Agent Agentic AI and Federated Learning for Attack Detection in Sustainable IoT
papers.abstract: The Internet of Things (IoT) comprises a vast number of digitally networked devices. Machine learning (ML), deep learning (DL), and federated learning (FL), all subfields of artificial intelligence (AI), have recently been investigated as cybersecurity solutions for protecting these networked devices from intrusions and cyberattacks. However, existing ML and DL techniques for Sustainable IoT data carry significant privacy implications. Because of its inherent suitability for IoT settings, AI-based cybersecurity, and FL in particular, has become critical, yet traditional FL-based approaches themselves fall short in several respects. We need a framework that prioritizes privacy while enabling effective FL on edge-generated data. This research aims to address three persistent problems in traditional FL-based systems: class imbalance, unequal data distribution across devices, and computational complexity. To this end, we propose a novel Multi-Agentic AI framework in which each device decomposes its local workload across three cooperating: Agent 2 performs data preprocessing, including WGAN-based oversampling to correct class imbalance; Agent 1 performs data distribution, applying a vertical federated learning (VFL) partitioning scheme to address the unequal data distribution that typically affects FL-based IoT systems; and Agent 3 performs classification, training a deep autoencoder and an MLP on the resulting features while keeping the computational load on each device manageable. Experiments on the Modbus ICS network and ToN-IoT datasets show that our framework improves on the performance of comparable ML models while overcoming the limitations of existing FL-based techniques. Our VFL approach delivers consistent data distribution and higher attack detection accuracy, reaching 99.56% and 99.62% on the two datasets, respectively. Overall, this multi-agent agentic AI methodology offers a practical way to address the core challenges of FL and meaningfully improve AI effectiveness in privacy-sensitive sustainable IoT domains.

papers.title: Audit-weighted annotator reliability in federated learning on neonatal EEG: a pre-specified negative result (protocol, code and run records)
papers.abstract: Frozen protocol, code, raw run records and analysis for a pre-specified test of whether temporal, audit-based annotator-reliability weighting improves federated seizure detection on neonatal EEG (Helsinki dataset, recordings eeg1 to eeg20; three expert scorers; simulated annotator failures). The primary criterion (S1) and the temporal-smoothing criterion (S3) were not met. Audit-based weighting recovered most of the oracle gain when one source was inverted, but temporal smoothing added nothing beyond a memoryless audit weighting. Limitations: the annotator failures are simulated; the 15 fold-by-seed evaluation units are not independent, so p-values are descriptive; the reference is a three-scorer consensus, not clinical truth; some audit infants were seizure-free, so some audit observations carry specificity-only information. Licensing by component: the record is CC BY 4.0; hinn_rnn.py keeps its original MIT licence (Mohammad Behdad Jamshidi); eeg20.npz is derived from the CC BY 4.0 Helsinki dataset (Stevenson et al., Scientific Data 2019, doi:10.5281/zenodo.4940267). See README.md in the archive.

FedIDS-IIoT: Federated Intrusion Detection Under Non-IID and Temporal Distribution Shift Using the CICAPT-IIoT Dataset
papers.abstract: The increasing interconnection of industrial devices, programmable logic controllers, edge platforms, and networked control systems has expanded the attack surface of Industrial Internet of Things (IIoT) environments. Machine-learning-based intrusion detection can improve the identification of malicious activities, but centralized training requires the collection of distributed industrial data and may provide an unrealistic estimate of detector performance when evaluation relies on randomly partitioned traffic. Federated learning offers a data-local alternative; however, its effectiveness can be affected by non-independent and identically distributed (non-IID) client data and temporal changes in attack and network behavior. This study presents FedIDS-IIoT, a federated intrusion detection framework evaluated using the CICAPT-IIoT dataset, with particular emphasis on non-IID attack distributions and temporal distribution shift. Sample-size-weighted federated averaging (FedAvg) is evaluated across controlled client configurations in which attack observations are progressively concentrated among five simulated clients. A training-only feature-selection procedure is used to derive a compact 20-feature representation, while model selection and operating-threshold determination are completed before evaluation on a chronologically later and previously untouched traffic block. The federated detector is evaluated against a centralized XGBoost reference and two matched federated optimizers, FedProx and FedAdam, under the same development protocol and feature representation. In the matched federated comparison, FedAvg achieves the highest F1-score in the mild and moderate development partitions, whereas FedProx is marginally higher in the severe partition (0.9643 vs. 0.9633). This result is interpreted as an optimizer-dependent operating trade-off rather than evidence of universal FedAvg superiority. Under the frozen operating threshold, FedAvg also produces substantially fewer false positives on the temporal test set. The non-IID experiments indicate that moderate differences in attack distribution have limited impact, whereas severe concentration of attack evidence can reduce detection performance. A paired McNemar test confirms that the difference in temporal error behavior between the two detectors is statistically significant, and a cost analysis shows that the federated detector needs only a few thousand parameters and a few megabytes of communication over the entire training run. The MADQN component is treated as a secondary exploratory simulation and is not presented as real-life network-response validation. These findings demonstrate the importance of evaluating federated IIoT intrusion detection under both client-level distribution heterogeneity and temporal distribution shift rather than relying solely on conventional random train–test evaluation.

papers.title: Vehicular Federated Learning: A Survey on Architectures, Challenges, and Future Directions
papers.abstract: Connected and Autonomous Vehicles (CAVs) enhance the driving experience and passenger comfort through various safety and entertainment applications, many of which are based on machine learning. Given the need to use personal data to improve these technologies, federated learning emerges as an alternative for training machine learning models with privacy guarantees. However, in a dynamic, highly mobile environment, Vehicular Federated Learning (VFL) presents challenges beyond those inherent to traditional FL. We contextualize the basic execution and relevance of VFL, introduce its architecture, and detail strategies to overcome latency and mobility challenges in vehicular scenarios. Furthermore, the paper discusses the network infrastructure required for VFL, analyzing the data plane and the control plane in model transmission and task orchestration. Finally, we discuss open issues and future research directions.

papers.title: AI Architectures for Audience Personalization and Strategic Content Production
papers.abstract: The convergence of massive foundational models and sequential recommendation engines redefines digital personalization by merging content generation and curation into a continuous adaptive cycle. The chapter traces the transition from collaborative filters to multimodal transformers, illustrates with cases from Netflix, Spotify, and e-commerce, and shows that hyper-personalization increases engagement and value. However, it identifies risks of bias, opacity and high energy consumption, proposing green metrics, federated learning and narrative explainability to mitigate externalities. It is argued that governance based on distributed ledgers and ethical audits strengthens data sovereignty and regulatory trust. In short, the emerging competitive advantage will depend on orchestrating responsible recommender ecosystems that balance utility, justice and sustainability throughout their life cycle. Integrates comprehensive meta-analytic approach and
papers.venue: Advances in computational intelligence and robotics book series

papers.title: The Energy-Data Dilemma: When Self-interest meets Federated Learning
papers.abstract: We study a federated learning (FL) system in which a central server coordinates a group of self-interested clients, each holding a local dataset. Each client, seeking to maximise accuracy per unit energy, strategically decides whether to join the federation or train in isolation and, if joining, how much local data to contribute. Modelling this as a non-cooperative game, we provide a complete characterisation of pure Nash equilibria under empirically motivated assumptions on the accuracy-to-training-cost ratio: initially convex when data is scarce and strictly concave beyond a threshold. We establish that any interior pure Nash equilibrium is symmetric, lies strictly in the concave region, and that for any given federation size and participation cost within an explicitly characterised feasible window, a unique such equilibrium exists. As the number of active contributors grows, per-player contributions vanish, aggregate provision saturates at a finite limit, and the stability margin against free-riding decays quadratically, yet individual welfare rises monotonically. Increasing the participation cost raises aggregate provision but erodes individual contribution incentives. Comparing Nash outcomes to a fair cooperative benchmark, in which all clients participate with equal energy expenditure, reveals systematic under-provision; the resulting inefficiency grows with federation size but remains bounded above by a parameter-free constant. Numerical experiments on CIFAR-10 confirm the theoretical predictions and indicate that moderate federation sizes paired with sufficiently high participation costs best balance welfare gains against equilibrium robustness.

papers.title: Relative-Error Composite Federated Optimization with One Server-Side Proximal Step per Round
papers.abstract: We consider deterministic composite federated optimization, in which distributed smooth client objectives are combined with a shared, possibly nonsmooth, regularizer. We propose Relative-Error Composite FedDyn (REC-FedDyn), an inexact method that supports partial participation, with one server-side proximal evaluation per communication round. REC-FedDyn employs a directly testable relative-error criterion that allows each client to independently control the accuracy of its local subproblem, without a server-side acceptance test. We establish almost-sure iterate convergence for strongly convex and convex problems, almost-sure asymptotic stationarity for nonconvex problems, and communication and parallel gradient-evaluation complexity bounds, all under partial participation and without assuming bounded data heterogeneity. Experiments on image inpainting, fMRI prediction, and neural-network classification with structured regularization demonstrate efficiency and robustness across levels of data heterogeneity and client participation.

papers.title: FedCGR: Federated Cross-Domain Generative Recommendation
papers.abstract: Cross-domain recommendation (CDR) transfers preference knowledge across related domains, but federated deployment makes cross-domain alignment difficult because the behavioral anchors that align item spaces, such as overlapping users and shared interaction signals, are often sparse, unavailable, or privacy-sensitive across clients. To address this tension, we revisit federated CDR as generation over a stable semantic item language. By representing items as discrete semantic ID (SID) sequences derived from public item-side metadata, cross-domain item alignment is induced by a shared vocabulary rather than by exchanging private interactions or aligning domain-specific embeddings. Directly federating SID-based generators, however, introduces two design constraints: the SID tokenizer must remain fixed to preserve cross-client token consistency, which creates a semantic-only bottleneck because local collaborative filtering (CF) signals cannot be globally shared or aligned; meanwhile, standard federated averaging can cause negative transfer under domain heterogeneity. To overcome these constraints, we propose FedCGR, a federated generative CDR framework that keeps the item language stable and makes adaptation explicit. FedCGR injects local CF evidence through a reliability-aware semantic interface and trains a prototype-personalized generator that selectively aggregates shared parameters according to domain relatedness while keeping domain-specific quantities local. Experiments on six Amazon cross-domain scenarios show that FedCGR consistently outperforms federated generative baselines and achieves competitive performance against strong sequential and federated CDR methods under both full-ranking and sampled evaluation protocols. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/ZhuodLiu/FedCGR.

papers.title: Backdoor Poisoning Mitigation for Federated LoRA via Structural Adaptive Control
papers.abstract: Large pre-trained models are increasingly adapted on user devices, but direct fine-tuning in federated settings is constrained by computation, memory, and communication limits. These constraints have motivated the use of parameter-efficient fine-tuning methods, among which LoRA is widely adopted by concentrating adaptation in low-rank parameters. While this design improves efficiency, it also changes the security setting. In federated LoRA, backdoor behavior can exploit the low-rank adaptation structure and persist across communication rounds, making defenses designed for full-model updates less reliable. To address this gap, we propose StrAP, a server-side defense tailored to federated LoRA fine-tuning. StrAP combines reliability control before aggregation with structure-aware regulation after aggregation. Before aggregation, client updates are softly weighted based on their alignment with a clean validation gradient and tracked across rounds using a stateful trust mechanism, which suppresses persistent anomalies while allowing benign recovery. After aggregation, StrAP analyzes the LoRA parameter structure to identify suspicious rank channels using robust cross-client statistics and applies utility-calibrated structural actions guided by clean validation loss. Extensive experiments show that StrAP consistently reduces backdoor attack success rates with minimal impact on clean accuracy. Our code is available at https://github.com/HwhCN-ui/StrAP.

papers.title: FedICL-KVc: Federated In-Context Learning via KV Cache
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly constrained by the scarcity of high-quality public data, making private data essential for further improvement. However, private data is typically distributed across resource-constrained devices and cannot be shared due to strict privacy requirements, rendering conventional federated fine-tuning of LLMs impractical under limited computation and communication budgets. To address these challenges, we propose Federated In-Context Learning via KV Cache (FedICL-KVc), a novel framework that enables effective utilization of private data without parameter updates. Instead of transmitting raw demonstrations, clients upload only the corresponding key--value (KV) caches generated during auto-regressive inference, which are compact, smaller than full-model parameter payloads, and subject to an empirical reconstruction-risk evaluation under a restricted attack model. To further enhance efficiency and effectiveness, we introduce a confidence-based demonstration selection strategy to identify informative client samples, and a server-side KV cache compression method guided by a proxy dataset to reduce inference cost and suppress irrelevant information. Experiments on multiple tasks demonstrate that FedICL-KVc achieves competitive performance without client-side parameter updates or full-model parameter transmission while avoiding direct raw-data transmission.

papers.title: Federated Lightweight Transformer for Network-Layer Cyberattack Detection in O-RAN
papers.abstract: Open Radio Access Network (O-RAN) improves radio access network flexibility through disaggregation, open interfaces, and programmable RAN Intelligent Controllers (RICs). However, the same openness and distribution increase the attack surface and make centralized intrusion detection difficult to scale across heterogeneous RAN sites. This paper presents a federated lightweight Transformer framework for privacy-preserving network-layer cyberattack detection in O-RAN. Each participating site trains a compact Transformer locally on temporally ordered network-flow records, while only model parameters are shared with a federated coordinator. To model realistic site heterogeneity, the client datasets are partitioned according to a Dirichlet distribution, resulting in non-independent and identically distributed (non-IID) local data. The local detector uses feature projection, positional encoding, multi-head self-attention, feed-forward layers, and temporal pooling to classify five network-layer attack categories: ICMP, Slowloris, SYN, TCP-ACK, and UDP. Experiments on the NetsLab 5G O-RAN intrusion-detection dataset show an overall accuracy of 94.89 % and a macro-F1 score of 81.09 %.

papers.title: A geospatial approach to measuring economic activity
papers.abstract: Abstract We introduce a methodology to detect and measure economic activity using geospatial data and apply it to steel production, a major industrial pollution source worldwide. Combining plant output data with geospatial data, such as ambient air pollutants, nighttime lights, and temperature, we train machine learning models to predict plant locations and output. We identify about 88% (94%) of plants missing from the training sample within a 1 km (5 km) radius and achieve R 2 above 0.8 for output prediction at a 1 km grid and at the plant level, as well as both regional and time series validations. We use the model trained on Chinese steel data to reliably detect the location and measure the total annual output of steel plants in South Korea and Iran. Our approach can be adapted to other industries and regions, and used by policymakers and researchers to track and measure industrial activity in near real time.

papers.title: Visual LLM-guided consensus spatial domain detection with L-STAR
papers.abstract: Abstract Spatial transcriptomics measures gene activity while preserving the locations of cells within tissue. A key analysis step is to divide the tissue into spatial domains, but the performance of computational methods varies considerably across datasets, and no single method consistently performs best. Here we show that a large language model can compare spatial domain maps and identify the better-performing methods. We developed L-STAR, which visually compares and ranks candidate methods, then builds a consensus map from the highest-ranked results. Across datasets representing different tissues, species, and technologies, L-STAR matched expert annotations more closely than individual methods or consensus analysis using a fixed set of methods. Its rankings were reproducible and generally stable when image colors or presentation order changed. L-STAR also provided rationales for its comparisons and assigned biologically meaningful names to the detected domains. These findings show that large language models can make spatial transcriptomics analysis more adaptive, robust, and interpretable.

papers.title: GATA transcription factors coordinate developmental progression in the arabidopsis root
papers.abstract: Proper organ development requires the coordination of cell type-specific differentiation programs with general maturation processes through precise spatiotemporal gene regulation. In plants, where RNA polymerase pausing is not well established, alternative mechanisms must ensure this coordination. Here, using single-cell resolution transcriptomic and chromatin accessibility data, we reconstruct developmental trajectories of the Arabidopsis root ground tissue to investigate these mechanisms. We describe phased transcriptional landscapes governing the transition from stem cell to early differentiation, in which chromatin accessibility marks the activation of key developmental regulators. A major transcriptional switch in the late meristematic zone, underpinned by extensive chromatin remodeling, drives the transition from cell division to differentiation. Leveraging machine learning to examine integrated transcriptomic and chromatin accessibility trajectories, we identify GATA transcription factors (TFs) as central coordinators of this switch; a role we validate experimentally. We show that the GATA TFs sit at the tipping point of a feedback-driven bistable system that integrates inputs from auxin and cytokinin to balance proliferation and differentiation, ensuring temporal precision in root development at both the tissue and organ scales.

papers.title: Spatial protein interactomics in solid primary human tissue
papers.abstract: Protein-protein interactions (PPIs) in diseased tissues represent a promising class of potential drug targets. However, PPIs are typically identified in live cells, lysate, and genetically engineered model organisms, limiting their translational value to human disease. Here we describe MAP-IT, an optimized photocatalytic carbene-based proximity labeling method for direct PPI mapping in primary human tissue sections, which bypasses the need for model organisms in the initial discovery step. We use MAP-IT to profile PPIs in situ for cell surface and nuclear target proteins, identify and orthogonally validate new interactors of EGFR in colon cancer, and couple light-powered MAP-IT labeling with spatially patterned visible light irradiation guided by neural network image segmentation to map location-specific protein interactomes. Protein-protein interactions (PPIs) represent a promising class of drug targets. Here, the authors describe MAP-IT, a photocatalytic carbene-based proximity labeling method for direct PPI mapping in primary human tissue sections.

papers.title: Will AI grant reviews make science more conservative?
FedReady: Bounded Agents for Federation Formation
papers.abstract: Federated learning (FL) runtimes standardize aggregation and deployment, but each new study still requires federation formation: selecting task-eligible sites and preparing their local data and task code for federated training or analysis. This preparation recurs when the target changes, while raw records and site-private mappings are excluded from cross-site FL messages. We present FedReady, a system that performs federation formation with bounded LLM agents. Agents propose shared contracts, local adapters, and task code; the runtime owns workflow state and accepts artifacts only after checks tied to their digests. Candidate site discovery prioritizes recall; local eligibility verification checks task support before site admission. Once participating sites and artifacts are fixed, conventional federated training or analysis proceeds without readiness agents. Across 39 simulated retinal sites and four tasks, discovery reaches recall 1.00 at precision 0.65; local eligibility verification removes all 17 false positives without losing an eligible site-task pair. The participating sites supply 45,575 task-record instances and complete four 100-round jobs, including one with a runtime-generated contract. Across ten patient cohorts, preparation supports seven patient populations and holds endpoints at three sources as unsupported. Comparison with manually prepared reference populations and analysis (the manual reference) gives a maximum survival-curve difference of 0.001133. We also analyze 19 development failures, targeted classification ablations, and standalone and heterogeneous agent configurations. These results establish the feasibility of task-specific data preparation before ordinary FL training or analysis.

papers.title: Pod-wise Multimodal Federated Learning for Heterogeneous IoT
papers.abstract: Federated learning (FL) is well suited to Internet of Things (IoT) sensing. However, devices carry different sensors and come online in periodic patterns, and as such, the sensors among the participants change from round to round. Under naive averaging, devices without a sensor overwrite its parameters, and a single-sensor device never learns how its sensor relates to the others. Existing methods either redesign local training for mismatched sensors (assuming always-available devices) or select clients without regard to their sensors. We propose Tier-aware Intra-pod Decoupled Encoders (TIDE). Specifically, each sensor has its own encoder and auxiliary head, whose parameters are merged only within the "pod" (i.e., the devices that hold the sensor), while the fusion layer and the task head remain shared by all devices. On three multimodal activity recognition datasets against eight baselines, TIDE reaches 78.06% on ActionSense, 7.63 points above the next method, is the most accurate on all three datasets at half its own communication, and at equal communication leads on ActionSense and is ahead within seed variation on the other two.

papers.title: DisC: Incentive Design for Green, Robust, and Fair Client Self-Participation in OTA Federated Learning
papers.abstract: Over-the-Air Federated Learning (OTA-FL) improves communication efficiency by exploiting waveform superposition over wireless Multiple-Access Channels (MAC). However, client heterogeneity, fading, energy constraints, and participation imbalance can degrade both fairness and aggregation accuracy. Existing Pareto-oriented fair OTA-FL schemes may still suffer from large aggregation distortion when highly weighted clients experience poor channel conditions. This paper proposes DisC, a game-theoretic distributed client selection framework for fairness-aware, channel-aware, and energy-efficient OTA-FL. Each client selects its participation level by maximizing a utility that captures Pareto fairness importance, learning relevance, OTA distortion, energy consumption, and delay. We show that DisC admits a Nash equilibrium and can be formulated as an exact potential game, where stable equilibria correspond to locally optimal OTA-FL operating points. DisC therefore offers a distributed, incentive-compatible alternative to centralized client selection under wireless and resource constraints.

papers.title: Comparative study of global pooling for pre-departure ship fuel consumption prediction: Advantages over per-ship and adaptation-based approaches
papers.abstract: Most fuel oil consumption (FOC) models for voyage planning are per-ship models and thus generalize poorly beyond each vessel's records. Transfer and federated learning have been reported to perform better, but under different protocols that often use inputs unavailable before departure or random data splits. It therefore remains unclear which approach performs best. In this study, we compare 11 per-ship, adaptation-based, and global methods on 21 vessels. To prevent leakage, all methods receive identical inputs known or forecast before departure, excluding engine RPM and shaft power, and are tested on intact voyage legs after all training records of each vessel. Global pooling, in which one model describes each vessel by its ship identity and seven ship specifications, performs best overall in every setting examined. For in-fleet vessels, Global LightGBM reaches an overall MAPE of 8.92%, against 11.14% for Per-Ship LightGBM, and outperforms every per-ship and adaptation-based model. Global models of five architectures, including a Transformer, all outperform the per-ship and federated models. Fine-tuning a global model for each vessel, even by low-rank adaptation of the Transformer, adds no accuracy. Without any records of a vessel, the global model reaches a median MAPE of 11.20% and outperforms a per-ship model trained on that vessel's records for 14 of 21 vessels. Adding its first records to the pooled data is as accurate as vessel-specific adaptation. Ship identity and specifications are largely interchangeable for in-fleet vessels, but only the specifications support zero-shot prediction. Its error grows as a vessel's specifications differ from the fleet's. Per-ship models and vessel-specific adaptation are therefore unnecessary under fair comparison. One global model can serve a whole fleet, including newly delivered vessels with similar specifications.

papers.title: MultiMental-IAS: A Multimodal Driver Mental State Analysis Dataset for Context-Aware Non-IID Evaluation
papers.abstract: Robust driver-state modelling requires synchronized physiological, behavioural, and contextual signals, yet existing open resources typically target a single cognitive state, omit continuous vehicle context, or do not define evaluation protocols that expose inter-subject heterogeneity. We present Multimental-IAS, a multimodal driver mental-state dataset collected in a cockpit-in-the-loop simulation built on CARLA. It contains vehicle telemetry with scenario-context channels, four-channel EEG and three-channel PPG from a Muse 2 headband, and cabin-facing video from 23 participants, recorded in 148 trials (11.6 hours) under six induced states: Normal, Distracted, Alerted, Stressed, Relaxed, and Drowsy. We document the acquisition pipeline in detail and provide a benchmark with one protocol for all models: chronological within-subject splits, participant-disjoint cross-subject folds, validation-based model selection, and ablations over modalities, scenario-context channels, and signal normalization. Multimodal fusion reaches a macro-F1 of 0.94 for drivers seen during training. For unseen drivers, fusing driving dynamics with per-window normalized EEG/PPG raises macro-F1 from 0.408 (telemetry alone) to 0.485, consistently across all five folds, while the gap between the two protocols quantifies the inter-driver heterogeneity that personalized models must address. Multimental-IAS thus provides a concrete testbed for non-IID generalization, personalization, and federated learning in driver monitoring.

papers.title: A Novel Federated Learning Framework for Defending Against Gradient Inversion Attacks
papers.abstract: Federated Learning (FL) offers a paradigm for collaborative machine learning model training among clients, preserving data privacy by avoiding direct data sharing. However, the gradient information exchanged in FL has been shown to be vulnerable to Gradient Inversion Attacks (GIA), which can reconstruct sensitive user data. To counter these threats, various privacy-enhancing technologies like Secure Multi-party Computing (SMC), Homomorphic Encryption (HE), and Differential Privacy (DP) have been integrated into FL. While effective, these methods often introduce significant trade-offs between privacy and model utility. By revisiting the key to privacy exposure in FL under GIA, which lies in the frequent sharing of model gradients that contain private data, we take a new perspective by designing a novel privacy-preserving FL framework that effectively ``breaks the direct connection'' between the shared parameters and the local private data to defend against GIA. Our proposed framework, HyperFL++, leverages hypernetworks to generate local model parameters, where only the hypernetwork parameters are aggregated by the server. To ensure practicality, HyperFL++ incorporates a Row-wise Kronecker Decomposition (RKD) to mitigate the memory and communication overhead from the hypernetwork. Comprehensive theoretical analysis and extensive experiments validate our method's effectiveness in protecting data privacy while maintaining high model utility. Our code is available at https://github.com/Pengxin-Guo/HyperFL/tree/hyperfl%2B%2B.

papers.title: A federated many-to-one Hopfield model for associative neural networks
papers.abstract: Federated learning (FL) enables collaborative training without centralizing raw data, but remains notoriously challenged by severe client heterogeneity and catastrophic forgetting under streaming distribution shifts. We propose a federated many-to-one (M2O) associative-memory framework designed for the unsupervised recovery of shared archetypes in continual, non-i.i.d. regimes. Departing from standard gradient-exchange methods, each client compresses its local experience into a low-rank Hebbian correlation operator. A central server then aggregates and factorizes these operators into global archetypes via an L-layer Associative Memory (LAM) architecture, strictly preserving raw-data locality. We rigorously cast the server-side aggregation as a low-rank-plus-noise spectral inference problem, utilizing random matrix theory to derive BBP phase transitions for archetype detectability and retrieval robustness: exact at initialization and, in the feedback-driven continual phase, extended through a conditional decomposition of the aggregated operator that leaves the detection threshold unchanged up to an explicit, server-observable inflation factor. To manage the distributed stability-plasticity dilemma, we introduce a local, label-free entropy controller that adaptively modulates client updates. Finally, we show that our adaptive framework, extended to federated Boolean-Gaussian Restricted Boltzmann Machines (RBMs), significantly outperforms standard FedAvg on structured non-IID datasets, validating the spectral mechanism of federated consolidation.

papers.title: Hybrid one-shot and vertical federated learning framework for privacy-preserving brain tumor classification and segmentation using the BRISC2025 dataset
papers.abstract: Introduction From MRI images, diagnosis of brain tumors may have limitations due to restriction over patient privacy and lack of annotated datasets so that models cannot be trained across multiple institutions. Methods HOS-VFL: A Hybrid One-Shot and Vertical Federated Learning framework with a two-round protocol that jointly enjoys the advantages of prototype-based one-shot aggregation and encrypted vertical feature space augmentation. Tested on BRISC2025 MRimages of glioma, meningioma, pituitary and non-tumor, with T1-weighted images, expert-annotated, at five simulated institutions, with simulated IID and Dirichlet setups. Results HOS-VFL obtained values of 98.73% on accuracy and 35–50 for conventional federated learning, with a 94.3% reduction compared to the best baseline valued. HOS-VFL performed 98.73% accuracy and 35–50 for the conventional federated learning with an improvement of 94.3% when compared with its best baseline accuracy. The mean Dice and IoU of Segmentation was 0.9147, 0.8423 respectively. Performance did not wane differently in terms of competitive levels and number of institutions, and was able to withstand gradient inference attacks. Discussion HOS-VFL philosophy is centralised performance with minimum communication with retention of raw data local. The method needs to be validated on larger real multi-center datasets before their clinical use.

papers.title: Artificial Intelligence and Digital Twins in Advanced Manufacturing: A Pathway Toward Intelligent and Sustainable Industry 4.0
papers.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Digital Twin (DT) technologies are transforming advanced manufacturing by enabling intelligent, data-driven, and sustainable production systems. This study presents a comprehensive analysis of the synergistic integration of AI algorithms with cyber-physical Digital Twin frameworks across key manufacturing domains, including additive manufacturing, microwave hybrid heating, robotic machining, and metal cladding. AI-driven models facilitate real-time defect detection, predictive maintenance, adaptive process control, and parameter optimization, while Digital Twins provide high-fidelity virtual replicas for simulation, synchronization, and closed-loop decision-making. The convergence of these technologies enables predictive and prescriptive manufacturing strategies, reducing waste, improving energy efficiency, and enhancing product quality. Furthermore, the study examines system-level integration architectures, cloud–edge computing infrastructure, and emerging approaches such as physics-informed neural networks and federated learning. The transition toward Industry 5.0 is discussed, emphasizing human-centricity, sustainability, and ethical AI deployment. The findings highlight AI–DT integration as a foundational pillar for intelligent, resilient, and environmentally responsible manufacturing ecosystems.

papers.title: Deep Looking in Digital Pathology: An Explainable Federated Learning Framework for Lung Cancer Classification
papers.abstract: Background/Objectives: Lung cancer is the leading cause of cancer death worldwide, and growing slide volumes add to pathologists’ cognitive load. Deep learning can assist histopathological diagnosis, but two obstacles limit its clinical use: privacy regulations keep patient images in institutional “data silos”, and the “black-box” behavior of neural networks undermines clinical trust. Inspired by Topol’s Deep Medicine, we aimed to build a diagnostic platform that preserves privacy and explains its decisions. Methods: We developed the Lung Cancer Analysis System (LCAS), which combines federated learning (FL), explainable artificial intelligence (XAI), and a locally deployed medical large language model (LLM). Three public H&E datasets (LC25000, HistoSet-5×14, and CLID; 18,000 images; adenocarcinoma, squamous cell carcinoma, benign tissue) acted as three hospital nodes with source-induced non-independent and identically distributed (non-IID) data. DenseNet121, EfficientNet-B3, and MobileNetV3-Small were trained centrally and with FedAvg/FedProx for 20 rounds. Grad-CAM produced visual evidence, and MedGemma 1.5, served offline through LM Studio, converted predictions and heatmap descriptors into structured reports. Results: Centralized training reached 99.50% ± 0.21% accuracy with DenseNet121. Under non-IID federated training with FedProx, DenseNet121 and EfficientNet-B3 achieved 96.97% and 97.49% accuracy on an independent external blind test set of 958 images, whereas MobileNetV3-Small reached 91.23%. Accuracy remained 99.78% under Gaussian blur. t-SNE showed that global features clustered by tissue class rather than by hospital, and Grad-CAM highlighted glandular and tumor-nest regions consistent with histopathological criteria. Conclusions: FL, XAI, and on-premise LLM reporting can be integrated into a single workflow that keeps raw images within each institution while giving pathologists numerical, visual, and textual explanations, providing a practical path toward trustworthy cross-institutional computational pathology.

papers.title: Sustainable Federated Continual Learning for environmental monitoring: a systematic review
papers.abstract: Introduction The use of distributed sensing infrastructures is increasingly becoming a key approach to environmental monitoring that is required to be mobile, flexible and adaptable to non-stationary conditions, preserve data privacy and consume as few resources as possible. The decentralized training paradigm provided by Federated Learning together with the ability of adapting sequentially over time without forgetting from Continual Learning has resulted in a concept of Federated Continual Learning (FCL) which offers a promising approach for privacy preserving environmental sensing systems that are capable of learning over time without forgetting. This systematic review provides an in-depth synthesis of the latest research, progress, environmental applications, sustainability, trustworthiness and future directions of Federated Continual Learning (FCL) for environmental monitoring. Methods A total of 90 peer-reviewed publications were identified by conducting a systematic literature search using pre-defined inclusion/exclusion criteria, quality assessment, bibliometric analysis and qualitative evidence synthesis with the framework of PRISMA 2020. Results The synthesized evidence suggests that Federated Learning has come of age in terms of optimization, communication complexity, robustness, and personalization, but Federated Continual Learning is still in its infancy with few applications in the real world. Typically, sustainability, trustworthiness, privacy, fairness, personalization and explainability are explored separately and not in parallel. Although most applications have been single-shot Federated Learning systems, without genuine continual adaptation, isolated examples include some applications from air quality to water quality, agriculture to disaster monitoring and remote sensing. Seven cross-cutting research gaps are identified: disjointed integration of research directions, few deployments in the real world, absence of standardized evaluation, unsolved multi-objective optimization, poor scaling in the long term, weak sustainability-trustworthiness coupling, and poor cross-domain generalization. Discussion It is not just about the evolution of single algorithmic breakthroughs anymore, but actual realization of Federated Continual Learning systems that can effectively assist in continual adaptation while ensuring communication efficiency, sustainability, trustworthiness, scalability and long-term deployment under real environmental conditions.

papers.title: Radiomics- based biomarkers for immunotherapy in non-small cell lung cancer: advances, challenges, and future perspectives in biological interpretation and clinical translation
papers.abstract: Immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) have improved outcomes in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), yet treatment benefit remains heterogeneous and resistance is common. Genomic alterations, tumor microenvironment (TME) remodeling, and metabolic reprogramming across spatial and temporal scales that are incompletely captured by single-site tissue sampling. Radiomics extracts quantitative features from routine images and offers a framework for investigating macroscopic correlates of these processes. This narrative review critically examines computed tomography (CT) and fluorine-18 fluorodeoxyglucose positron emission tomography/CT (¹ 8 F-FDG PET/CT) radiomics in relation to oncogenic alterations, immune and stromal phenotypes, programmed death-ligand 1 (PD-L1) expression, tumor mutational burden, and metabolic–immune interactions in NSCLC. It should be highlighted that such observed statistical links only generate plausible biological hypotheses and do not constitute experimental proof of true mechanistic relationships. Rather than merely summarizing predictive model performance, we emphasize evidence boundaries and interpretive caveats for radiomic-TME associations. We further elaborate on key translational bottlenecks including limited reproducibility, technical standardization deficits, and retrospective-model overfitting. We discuss ongoing efforts toward cross-scale multi-omics integration, alongside the promises and inherent limitations of explainable artificial intelligence and federated learning for clinical translation. To move beyond purely predictive tools toward mechanism-aware decision-support systems, future radiomic research requires prospective multicenter validation, rigorous data harmonization, and combined analyses integrating spatial transcriptomics, digital pathology, and circulating biomarkers for precision immuno-oncology.

papers.title: The 2026 IEEE IoT Theory and Practice Seasonal School - Federated Learning and IoT: Fundamentals
Machine Learning Approaches for Detecting Encrypted and Compressed Malicious Files: A Review
papers.abstract: The advancement of cyber threats has intensified with the rise of encrypted and compressed malicious files, posing significant challenges to traditional signature-based detection methods. Machine learning (ML) has emerged as a promising solution, capable of uncovering hidden patterns without relying on known malware signatures. This review explores recent developments in applying ML techniques such as deep learning, transfer learning, ensemble methods, and anomaly detection to identify encrypted malicious files. Studies have demonstrated that ML models can effectively analyse structural, statistical, and behavioural features, offering improved adaptability and detection accuracy. Despite these advancements, significant challenges persist, including encryption evasion, polymorphic malware, data imbalance, scalability issues, and adversarial attacks. Innovative strategies like explainable AI, federated learning, scalable architectures, and continuous learning are being investigated to enhance robustness and transparency. The dynamic evolution of cyber threats underscores the urgency of developing intelligent, adaptable, and privacy-conscious detection systems. Ultimately, this review highlights the critical role of ML in strengthening cybersecurity defences against increasingly sophisticated encrypted malicious files, emphasizing the need for continued research to address ongoing challenges and ensure resilient, scalable protection across diverse digital environments.
