papers.title: The 2026 IEEE IoT Theory and Practice Seasonal School - Lab/Demonstration: Federated Learning and DNN Partitioning-Based Federated Learning
Dynamic Digital Twins for trustworthy healthcare: Fusing multimodal EEG and endoscopic data for explainable clinical decision support
papers.abstract: Background: Translating data-driven AI innovations into clinically meaningful solutions requires addressing biomedical data complexity and the need for explainable models. We introduce a novel approach to personalized medicine by leveraging Dynamic Digital Twins (DDT) to represent real-time patient states. Methods: This study proposes an explainable, multimodal architecture combining 1D physiological signals (EEG arrays for cognitive state) and 2D medical imaging (wireless capsule endoscopy). Utilizing a Graph Attention Network (GAT) integrated with a federated learning framework, the system processes cross-modal features while preserving data privacy across distributed clinical nodes. Results: In rigorous clinical validation protocols, the multimodal DDT model achieved a diagnostic accuracy of 94.8% (95% CI: 93.1%–96.4%), representing a 14.2% improvement over unimodal baselines. Processing latency was reduced by 31%, and clinician-assessed trustworthiness improved significantly, with SHAP-based interpretability scores reaching 0.89/1.0. Conclusion: By successfully synthesizing cognitive biomarkers and localized imaging into a unified digital twin, this framework provides a highly accurate, transparent, and privacy-preserving tool ready for real-world clinical implementation.

papers.title: An explainable data-local federated learning framework for intrusion detection in connected healthcare systems
papers.abstract: Introduction Connected healthcare networks link medical sensors, gateways, electronic health record systems and cloud services, which enlarges their exposure to cyberattacks. Centralized intrusion detection systems (IDSs) require traffic from all sites to be pooled in one repository, which conflicts with data-residency constraints and creates a single high-value target, and their alerts are often not interpretable. Methods This paper proposes an explainable, privacy-aware federated learning (FL) framework for intrusion detection in which privacy is limited to data locality: clients exchange trained models and summary statistics instead of raw records, but model updates are not encrypted, securely aggregated or differentially private. The framework combines (i) federated training, (ii) client-side SHAP-guided feature ranking reconciled at the server into a common global feature set, and (iii) SHAP and LIME explanations of the aggregated model that are evaluated quantitatively. The framework was evaluated on the WUSTL-EHMS-2020 healthcare dataset, which combines network-flow and patient biometric features, partitioned into five simulated clients under IID and non-IID settings, using a leakage-controlled protocol in which host identifiers and record indices were excluded and all preprocessing was fitted on training data only. Results Under non-IID partitioning, the federated gradient-boosting model reached an accuracy of 0.935 ± 0.009, a Matthews correlation coefficient (MCC) of 0.673 ± 0.045 and a ROC-AUC of 0.895 ± 0.020, compared with an MCC of 0.700 ± 0.013 for centralized training and 0.540 ± 0.036 for local-only training. All data-alteration attacks were detected, whereas most spoofing attacks were missed. SHAP-guided feature selection and reliability-weighted aggregation did not improve detection and are therefore presented as design options; LIME explanations had low local fidelity ( R² = 0.332), and the usefulness of the explanations for security analysts was not evaluated. Discussion All results come from a single laboratory dataset partitioned into simulated clients; they demonstrate experimental feasibility only and do not establish generalizability to other healthcare networks or readiness for clinical deployment.

papers.title: Artificial Intelligence-Driven Quality by Design in Pharmaceutical Formulation Development: Applications, Challenges, and Future Perspectives
papers.abstract: The development of pharmaceutical formulations is changing. It is moving away from trial-anderror ways. Now modern approaches rely on science and data. Quality by Design or QbD offers a structured way to develop medicines. It starts with defining the Quality Target Product Profile or QTPP. Then it identifies Critical Quality Attributes or CQAs. It also looks at Critical Material Attributes or CMAs and Critical Process Parameters or CPPs. Design of Experiments or DoE helps in planning studies. This leads to the creation of a design space and a control strategy. Traditional QbD methods may not work well when variables are complex. They may not handle effects or strong interactions between factors. Artificial intelligence machine learning and predictive models can help. These tools can find patterns in data from experiments, formulations and manufacturing. This review looks at how AI fits into every stage of formulation development. It covers preformulation excipient selection, compatibility prediction, formulation optimization and predicting CQAs. It also includes identifying CMAs and CPPs. AI helps with process monitoring, Process Analytical Technology or PAT design space development and control strategy design. Applications are shown in solid dosage forms, modified-release systems, nanoparticulate and lipid-based formulations, continuous manufacturing, personalized medicines and 3D-printed medicines. Some challenges exist. These include data, overfitting models, models that are hard to understand lack of validation difficulties in scaling up regulatory issues and the need for diverse expertise. New ideas, like twins, continuous process verification, hybrid models that combine mechanics and AI generative AI and federated learning may push the field forward. In the end AI should support science not replace it. Experimental verification and mechanistic understanding are still essential.
papers.venue: Journal of Pharmacy Practice and Community Medicine

papers.title: Artificial Intelligence in Cybersecurity: A Comprehensive Review of AI-Powered Threat Detection, Cyberattack Prevention, and Information Security
papers.abstract: The rapid expansion of digital technologies, cloud computing, interconnected networks, and online services has significantly increased the complexity of modern cybersecurity challenges. Organizations increasingly face sophisticated cyber threats, including malware infections, ransomware, phishing campaigns, unauthorized network intrusions, insider threats, and advanced persistent threats (APTs). Traditional cybersecurity mechanisms, which primarily depend on predefined rules, signature-based detection, and manual security monitoring, often struggle to identify previously unknown attacks and respond effectively to rapidly evolving threats. Artificial intelligence (AI), particularly machine learning (ML), deep learning (DL), natural language processing (NLP), and behavioral analytics, has emerged as a promising approach for strengthening cybersecurity capabilities.This review examines the application of AI-driven technologies in modern cybersecurity, emphasizing intelligent threat detection, cyberattack prevention, and information security. It explores the role of machine learning and deep learning in network intrusion detection, malware classification, phishing identification, anomaly detection, behavioral threat analysis, and automated incident response. Furthermore, the review investigates emerging developments in explainable artificial intelligence (XAI), adversarial machine learning, federated learning, and generative AI, highlighting their implications for developing more adaptive and resilient security infrastructures. Recent academic research published in 2024 and 2025 is considered to evaluate technological developments, practical applications, and emerging limitations.The review identifies several important challenges affecting the practical adoption of AI-based cybersecurity systems, including data quality, model interpretability, false-positive detection, privacy concerns, adversarial manipulation, computational requirements, and the limited generalizability of models across different network environments. The analysis suggests that AI should complement, rather than completely replace, conventional security controls and human cybersecurity expertise. A layered cybersecurity architecture integrating AI-based detection, explainable decision support, continuous model monitoring, and human-supervised incident response may provide a more reliable approach to protecting modern digital environments. Finally, the paper identifies research opportunities related to adversarial robust AI, privacy-preserving collaborative learning, trustworthy generative AI, and autonomous cyber defense.

papers.title: Artificial intelligence in pediatric head and neck tumor imaging: a mini review of current applications and future directions
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is creating new opportunities to enhance medical imaging in pediatric oncology through quantitative image analysis and clinical decision support. This mini review examines the emerging role of AI in pediatric head and neck tumor imaging, including applications in lesion detection and characterization, tumor segmentation and volumetric analysis, treatment planning, longitudinal surveillance, prognostication, and precision medicine. Particular attention is given to the challenges of translating these approaches to pediatric populations, where rare and heterogeneous tumors, limited datasets, variable imaging protocols, and insufficient multicenter validation remain important barriers. We also discuss emerging strategies that may facilitate clinical translation, including federated learning, multimodal data integration, explainable AI, and integration with existing radiology workflows. Although pediatric-specific evidence remains limited, continued multicenter collaboration and prospective validation may enable AI-based tools to provide more reproducible quantitative imaging assessment and increasingly personalized clinical decision support. Ultimately, the clinical value of these technologies will depend on their ability to augment radiologist expertise and improve patient care through responsible integration into routine practice.

papers.title: Trustworthy Federated Clinical Intelligence with Homomorphic Encryption and Explainable AI
papers.abstract: Cross-institutional clinical artificial intelligence is constrained by fragmented patient data, non-identically distributed (non-IID) populations, leakage from shared model updates, and limited interpretability. Federated learning (FL) preserves data locality, but ordinary FL neither makes model updates confidential nor guarantees stable optimization under heterogeneous clients. This paper proposes a defense-in-depth framework that coordinates Federated Proximal (FedProx) optimization, record-level differential privacy (DP), Cheon–Kim–Kim–Song (CKKS) approximate homomorphic encryption, and explainable artificial intelligence (XAI). FedProx limits local model drift; DP-SGD bounds the influence of an individual training record; and CKKS permits weighted aggregation while client updates remain encrypted. A key-separated design keeps the aggregation server from being provisioned with the secret key used to reveal individual contributions; only the aggregate is released for global-model construction. Grad-CAM and SHAP/LIME provide clinician-facing explanations, while an audit dashboard reports convergence, privacy-accounting inputs, encryption status, and systems overhead. We formalize the learning objective, privacy mechanism, encrypted aggregation, threat model, numerical approximation error, communication footprint, and an evaluation protocol spanning IID and controlled non-IID partitions. The contribution is a reproducible system-level co-design and evaluation framework rather than a new cryptographic primitive or optimization algorithm.
papers.venue: International Journal on Advanced Computer Engineering and Communication Technology

papers.title: VFCI: A Federated Framework for Vertical Causal Inference
papers.abstract: Causal inference is crucial for understanding the relationship between cause and effect and is widely applied in fields such as medicine and policy decision-making. When the input data is distributed over multiple participants, most causal inference models require data to be centrally aggregated. However, participants are often prohibited or reluctant to share sensitive data due to data protection regulations and privacy concerns. To address this, federated learning has been proposed to perform data analysis in a privacy-preserving manner. Specifically, vertical federated learning is a subcategory where participants possess the same set of instances but different feature spaces. When causal inference meets vertical federated learning, a new topic arises: how to perform causal inference from multi-source vertically distributed data while protecting data privacy? In this paper, we propose a general framework, termed VFCI , for vertical federated causal inference. We design a general workflow that leverages a three-phase split mechanism to train traditional causal inference models securely. Based on this general workflow, we then show how to instantiate more complex causal inference models, such as two-stage approaches. Further, we conduct a comprehensive analysis regarding the security of our framework. Extensive experimental results verify the effectiveness and efficiency of VFCI over different workloads.

papers.title: Trimmed-mean federated chain for robust aggregation against poisoning attacks in federated learning
papers.abstract: Federated learning enables collaborative model training across decentralised devices while preserving data privacy. However, its distributed nature makes it vulnerable to poisoning attacks, including Byzantine attacks, backdoor attacks, and Coordinated Model Poisoning (CMP) attacks. Recent studies have highlighted increasing concerns regarding coordinated and adaptive poisoning attacks, where malicious clients collaboratively manipulate model updates to evade conventional robust aggregation mechanisms. Although existing approaches such as the Krum Federated Chain (KFC) provide robustness against traditional adversarial settings, their effectiveness may degrade under increasingly complex datasets and coordinated attack scenarios. To address these limitations, this paper proposes the Trimmed-Mean Federated Chain (TFC), a blockchain-based robust aggregation framework that integrates global norm stabilisation, directional filtering, and trimmed-mean aggregation within a federated chain architecture. The proposed framework suppresses abnormal client updates with excessively large magnitudes and applies layerwise cosine similarity filtering to identify directionally inconsistent updates before aggregation. Extensive experiments are conducted on benchmark image classification datasets, including EMNIST, Fashion-MNIST, and CIFAR-10, under Byzantine, backdoor, and CMP attack settings. Experimental results demonstrate that TFC generally achieves stronger robustness performance than KFC under Byzantine and backdoor attacks while maintaining competitive performance under more challenging CMP scenarios. These findings indicate that the integration of stabilisation, directional filtering, and trimmed-mean aggregation improves empirical robustness under the evaluated adversarial settings, although the present study does not establish formal Byzantine fault-tolerance or convergence guarantees.

papers.title: "Smart home IoT Traffic"
papers.abstract: "The growing deployment of Internet of Things (IoT) devices expands the attack surface of smart environments and challenges centralized intrusion detection approaches, which may incur communication overhead, scalability limitations, and privacy risks. This thesis proposes a distributed, multi-agent intrusion detection system designed to support efficient and privacy-aware IoT security. Lightweight agents monitor local network behavior and build device-specific traffic profiles, while mobile detection agents support distributed analysis. Federated learning enables collaborative model improvement without requiring raw local traffic to be centrally shared, and a permissioned blockchain provides a trusted mechanism for recording and coordinating relevant security information. Experimental evaluation reports 97.8% accuracy, an F1-score of 0.97, and a 2.1% false-positive rate, alongside approximately 64% lower monitoring traffic and 38% computational overhead. The work also characterizes real-world smart-home traffic through a dataset containing over 30 million packets, supporting statistical analysis and future evaluation under realistic IoT communication conditions during everyday operation."

papers.title: The 2026 IEEE IoT Theory and Practice Seasonal School - DNN Partitioning-Based Federated Learning for IoT Devices
Secure Federated Learning with FBFT Consensus for 6G-Enabled IoMT Systems
papers.abstract: The development of sixth-generation (6G) communications networks will enable the delivery of ultra-reliable and low-latency communications, which are necessary to support intelligent healthcare services in Internet of Medical Things (IoMT) environments. The ongoing creation of information by distributed medical devices necessitates collaborative learning paradigms that safeguard patients’ 109 privacy without compromising model accuracy and the reliability of coordination. The idea of federated learning allows training numerous hospitals in a decentralized model without sharing the raw medical information; however, the authenticity of the local updates should be credible to prevent the introduction of inaccurate models. Federated Byzantine Fault Tolerance (FBFT) consensus integration into a permissioned blockchain system ensures the secure and fault-tolerant coordination of federated updates. Secure aggregation further protects model parameters during transmission. Experimental evaluation demonstrates steady accuracy improvement, consistent reduction in training and testing loss, bounded consensus latency, and stable throughput. These results indicate that the integrated 6G-FL-FBFT architecture provides scalable, privacy-aware, and reliable distributed intelligence for next-generation healthcare ecosystems.

papers.title: A systematic critical review on AI-driven cyber-resilient communication frameworks and architectural standards for DC microgrids
Communication-Efficient Federated Learning for IoT Edge Computing with LION-Based Optimization
papers.abstract: Abstract Training a shared model on Internet of Things (IoT) data presents two practical difficulties: devices have limited computing resources, and repeated exchanges with a remote server consume time and bandwidth. Federated learning keeps the training data on the devices, but it does not remove these costs. We propose HELA-FL, a hierarchical framework that places edge servers between IoT clients and a central server. Clients learn from their local datasets, edge servers coordinate intermediate updates and aggregation, and the central server combines the resulting edge models. The framework uses the LION optimizer to support model optimization within this hierarchy. Its purpose is to make use of the greater computing capacity available at the edge while reducing the frequency of global communication. We implemented the framework in Python and evaluated it on MNIST with a non-independent and identically distributed (non-IID) allocation of data. The simulation used five edge servers, each serving twenty clients. We compared HELA-FL with FedAvg, FedBuff, AdamW, FedCMFL, FedEdge, FedNova, FedScalar, and FedProx over twenty training rounds. The reported final accuracy was approximately 94%, with latency of about 12 to 12.5 seconds and a combined cost of approximately 220 units under the study's cost definition. Some baselines reached higher accuracy. The value of the proposed approach therefore lies in the balance between accuracy, latency, and cost in this experiment. These results support further investigation of hierarchical aggregation with LION for IoT edge systems; evaluation on a physical testbed remains future work.

papers.title: Navigating the Future
papers.abstract: Smart geospatial technologies are changing the way governments, industries, and societies collect, analyze, and use spatial data to solve complex global challenges. This comprehensive chapter explores the evolution, current state, challenges, emerging trends, real-world applications, and future directions of intelligent geospatial systems, highlighting the transformative impact of integrating artificial intelligence (AI), blockchain, the Internet of Things (IoT), unmanned aerial vehicles, light detection and ranging (LiDAR), global navigation satellite systems (GNSS) real-time kinematic (RTK) positioning, and cloud computing technologies into spatial intelligence workflows. New trends such as AI-driven spatial classification, predictive modeling, and automation are signaling a paradigm shift in geospatial intelligence. The geospatial intelligence market, with annual growth rates of over 25% and a projected value exceeding $60 billion, is poised for wide deployment across multiple sectors. Innovations in explainable artificial intelligence, generative AI-based models, and federated learning promise to increase trust, transparency, and privacy in spatial data analytics ( Google Research, 2025) . Additional technological advances include the integration of blockchain to provide decentralized spatial data, quantum and edge computing for ultrafast analytics, the combination of digital twins with building information modeling (BIM) for dynamic urban simulations, and the use of augmented and virtual reality to create interactive geospatial experiences. This chapter highlights these advances through a rich series of real-world case studies. Singapore’s digital twin initiative combines the IoT, BIM, and 3D/4D GIS to optimize resource use, achieving an estimated US$7.5 million in water savings per year while improving air quality monitoring. California’s 2024 wildfire response used AI-driven satellite classification and drone LiDAR maps to reduce emergency response times by 30%. In the Netherlands, precision agriculture projects using drone multispectral imagery with IoT soil sensors increased yields by 10% and reduced fertilizer use by 20%. European infrastructure monitoring demonstrated cost-effective safety improvements through autonomous drone inspection and BIM-GIS integration. In autonomous transportation, Waymo demonstrated a 40% reduction in accident rates by combining GNSS RTK with LiDAR and SLAM technologies. Other applications include monitoring Arctic sea ice for climate modeling, analyzing COVID-19 spatial data to optimize public health interventions in India, and Amsterdam’s smart transportation network, which reduced passenger travel times by 25% and https://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"> CO 2 emissions by 15%. By synthesizing these insights, this chapter presents a holistic framework for researchers, policymakers, urban planners, engineers, data scientists, and industry professionals to understand the changing landscape of smart geospatial technologies. It highlights the importance of responsible adoption, continuous innovation, and strategic collaboration to unleash the transformative potential of spatial intelligence for a smart, safe, and sustainable future.

papers.title: Adaptive Federated Edge Transformer with Multi-Level Knowledge Distillation and Hybrid GA–SQP Optimization for Privacy-Preserving Zero-Day Attack Detection in Heterogeneous IoT Network
papers.abstract: The increasing availability of diverse internet of things devices has made possible an increase in zero-day attacks, but at the same time, it has brought up several issues related to data privacy, overhead communications, and computation scalability for central intrusion detection systems. Federated learning provides an effective decentralized approach for cooperative cyber threat intelligence; however, its efficiency is hindered by non-independent and identically distributed data, unstable client contribution, restricted resources of edge devices, and ineffective model aggregation. In order to overcome the aforementioned problems, this paper presents an Adaptive Trust-Aware Federated Edge Transformer (AFET) with multi-level knowledge distillation (MLKD) and hybrid Genetic Algorithm–Sequential Quadratic Programming (GA–SQP) optimization for privacy-preserving zero-day attack detection in diverse IoT environments. The AFET architecture implements an adaptive trust-aware model aggregation process that adjusts the aggregation weights based on the clients’ reliability and data quality, whereas the MLKD module implements knowledge transfer from a global teacher network to edge transformers through multi-level information sharing. In addition, the hybrid GA–SQP optimizer optimizes the parameters of both the transformer and federated learning algorithms. The experimental results performed on benchmark intrusion detection datasets prove that the proposed framework attains detection accuracy of 99.18%, precision of 98.07%, recall of 97.91%, F1-score of 98.03%, and AUC of 0.998. This is an alternative tool for privacy-preserving zero-day attack detection in heterogeneous IoT networks.

papers.title: Hybrid Federated Learning for Multimodal Fusion under Missing Modalities and Site Heterogeneity
papers.abstract: Multimodal fusion is studied under hybrid federation, where data are partitioned across samples and feature blocks. The proposed two-dimensional federated smooth multiple-kernel large-margin learning method (2D-FedSMKL) integrates availability-corrected modality scores, group-kernel regularization, and smooth worst-site risk aggregation. For fixed maps and propensities, the objective is convex and smooth. Curvature bounds and exact synchronous block-gradient equivalence are established for binary and multiclass scores, giving a conditional accelerated rate. An oracle-propensity binary risk bound and a propensity-perturbation result are also derived. Simulations and two public activity-recognition benchmarks assess site heterogeneity and modality absence. Worst-site aggregation improves worst-site performance under heterogeneity, including reversed and size-balanced designs. On the benchmarks, validation selects the correction; the selected model is not significantly worse than the strongest reference at the worst site, and group-regularization benefits vary by dataset.

papers.title: FedCap-Priv: Geometry-Aware Privacy and Bandwidth-Efficient Routing for Federated Capsule Learning
papers.abstract: Capsule networks explicitly encode pose and part–whole structure, making them attractive for heterogeneous visual and speech data but creating structured messages and substantial communication costs in federated learning. We present FedCap-Priv, a federated capsule framework that jointly addresses transcript privacy, predictive utility, and uplink cost through three capsule-specific procedures. Secure Routing by Agreement (SeRBA) retains dynamic routing on each client and replaces direct vote exchange with compact directional and low-rank agreement sketches. Pose-Sensitive Differential Privacy (PS-DP) clips each layer sketch and applies anisotropic Gaussian perturbation aligned with pose variability. Our client-level Rényi-DP analysis accounts for data-dependent means and covariances, visible selection indices, layer composition, client participation, and temporal composition. Sparsity-Guided Partial Aggregation (SGPA) selects salient parent blocks after perturbation and uses error feedback to reduce communication. Across MNIST, Fashion-MNIST, CIFAR-10, and Speech Commands, FedCap-Priv improves accuracy over isotropic FedDP and lowers reconstruction scores under DLG, iDLG, and cosine-TV attacks. On CIFAR-10, it reaches 73.9% accuracy versus 68.9% for isotropic FedDP while reducing the mean participating-client uplink from 220 KB to 22.1 KB per round, a 9.95-fold reduction. The sketch interface supports vector- and matrix-pose capsules and can be combined with secure aggregation.

papers.title: AI, Machine Learning, and Cybersecurity for Digital Transformation
papers.abstract: Digital transformation has become a fundamental driver of innovation across industries, public institutions, financial services, healthcare, manufacturing, education, and digital commerce. The increasing adoption of cloud computing, the Internet of Things (IoT), big data analytics, mobile applications, and interconnected digital platforms has created significant opportunities for organizational efficiency and service innovation. However, these developments have also expanded the cyberattack surface, increasing exposure to malware, ransomware, identity theft, financial fraud, data breaches, and sophisticated network intrusions. Traditional cybersecurity mechanisms, which frequently depend on predefined rules and known attack signatures, may struggle to identify previously unseen threats and respond to rapidly changing attack patterns. Artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) offer promising capabilities for strengthening digital security through automated threat detection, behavioral analytics, anomaly identification, fraud prevention, and intelligent incident response. This paper presents a comprehensive review of the relationship between AI, ML, cybersecurity, and digital transformation. It examines major learning paradigms, cybersecurity applications, intelligent threat detection techniques, explainable AI, federated learning, graph-based analytics, and ensemble learning. It also discusses the limitations associated with adversarial manipulation, biased training data, privacy, computational overhead, model drift, regulatory compliance, and the shortage of cybersecurity expertise. A conceptual framework is proposed to integrate data collection, intelligent analytics, risk assessment, automated response, human supervision, and continuous improvement into a unified security architecture. The discussion further considers resource-constrained organizations, sustainable digital transformation, cybersecurity governance, and the economic and societal consequences of cyber incidents. The paper concludes that effective AI-enabled cybersecurity requires a balanced combination of reliable data, robust machine learning models, transparent decision-making, defense-in-depth controls, and accountable governance. Rather than replacing conventional security mechanisms or human experts, AI should complement them within an adaptive, risk-based, and continuously evaluated cybersecurity strategy.
papers.venue: International Journal of Advance Scientific Research

papers.title: PQD-FL: A Privacy preserving decentralized federated learning on post-quantum secure scalable blockchain
papers.abstract: This presentation introduces PQD-FL, a research proposal for a privacy-preserving and decentralized Federated Learning (FL) platform secured by a scalable, post-quantum blockchain architecture. The project addresses critical limitations of conventional centralized machine learning, including data privacy risks, fragmented data ownership, computational overhead, and the lack of transparent mechanisms for rewarding participants. By enabling collaborative model training across distributed datasets without requiring the exchange of raw data, PQD-FL explores a more secure and equitable approach to decentralized intelligence. At its core, the proposed framework integrates post-quantum cryptographic security, blockchain-based coordination, and cooperative game theory to establish trust among distributed participants. A Shapley value-based incentive mechanism, managed through smart contracts, is designed to evaluate individual contributions and facilitate fair reward distribution. The framework further explores mechanisms for discouraging malicious participation and maintaining transparent, tamper-resistant records of model aggregation and contribution rewards. By bringing together privacy-preserving machine learning, quantum-resistant security, and incentive-aware collaboration, PQD-FL aims to establish a foundation for trustworthy, scalable, and economically sustainable federated learning ecosystems.
papers.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

papers.title: Abstract 19023: Federated Learning for Multi-Site ECG Modeling: External Validation and Comparison with Pooled Training
papers.abstract: Background: Multi-site ECG machine learning may improve external validity, but direct waveform pooling is constrained by data-governance requirements. Whether federated training can preserve ECG-age estimation and clinically meaningful delta-age signals relative to centralized pooled training remains uncertain. Hypothesis: We tested whether a four-client federated ECG-age model would achieve external performance and outcome associations comparable with an identical centrally pooled model, without waveform pooling. Methods: Using uniform preprocessing, a convolutional neural network (CNN-BiLSTM) model was trained to estimate chronological age from 12-lead ECGs in a simulated federated framework with four independent clients (CODE-15%, n=345,779; MIMIC-IV, n=800,000; Georgia, n=10,344; and PTB-XL, n=21,799 ECG datasets). The pooled model used the same architecture and input pipeline. External testing was performed in an independent cohort of 1,202,162 ECGs. Delta-age was defined as predicted minus chronological age and standardized within each model. Adjusted logistic regression tested associations between delta-age and atrial fibrillation (AF), heart failure (HF), coronary artery disease (CAD), chronic kidney disease (CKD), and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). Mortality discrimination was assessed by area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC), and time-to-event associations by Cox regression. Models adjusted for chronological age, sex, and race. Results: Internally, centralized pooled training showed slightly better age-estimation performance than federated training (MAE 7.61 vs 7.87 years; R 2 0.650 vs 0.626). In external validation, however, federated training generalized more favorably, with lower error, higher explained variance, and stronger correlation with chronological age than pooled training (MAE 7.74 vs 8.04 years; R 2 0.647 vs 0.611; r=0.818 vs 0.798). Per 1-SD higher delta-age, adjusted odds ratios (federated vs pooled) were 1.70 vs 1.78 for atrial fibrillation, 1.69 vs 1.63 for heart failure, 1.45 vs 1.40 for coronary artery disease, 1.43 vs 1.36 for chronic kidney disease and 1.41 vs 1.36 for chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. Mortality discrimination was similar between approaches, with a small numerical advantage for federated learning (AUROC 0.7301 vs 0.7286; p<0.001). In Cox models, the federated delta-age association with mortality was stronger than the pooled association (Δβ=0.053; p<0.001). Conclusions: In a large external validation cohort, federated ECG-age training preserved clinical delta-age associations and modestly improved external age-estimation performance versus centralized pooled training. These findings support federated ECG modeling as a practical strategy for multi-institutional model development when direct waveform pooling is not feasible.

papers.title: Federated Affine Variational Inequalities: Exact Averaging and Complexity Limits
papers.abstract: We study the classical Local Stochastic Extragradient method (Local SEG) for monotone variational inequalities under intermittent communication, where devices perform several local oracle calls between synchronization rounds. For affine monotone mean operators, including nonsymmetric bilinear saddle systems, we prove that equal device averaging commutes pathwise with both stages of the stochastic extragradient update. Local trajectories may therefore drift apart while their mean follows a centralized stochastic-extragradient recursion driven by averaged noise. The identity remains valid when individual oracle realizations are nonlinear and query dependent. Under conditionally centered oracle errors that are conditionally independent across devices within each stage, the reduction yields a restricted weak-gap rate that uses the local sequential depth for deterministic progress and the aggregate oracle budget across devices for variance reduction. When every device makes at least two local oracle calls per communication round, the bound contains no additional mixed client-drift term and is also attained by a terminal-only aggregation schedule. An affine Gaussian lower bound matches the depth and sample dependences before statistical saturation for distributed zero-respecting algorithms; its statistical component applies to arbitrary randomized algorithms. A complementary lower bound for feasible distributed zero-respecting methods shows that bounded geometry and query-dependent noise can create an additional communication-locality obstruction. These results delineate the exact-averaging regime of unconstrained affine Local SEG and a complexity boundary that arises under active feasibility constraints.

papers.title: Genome-anchored foundation model embeddings improve molecular prediction from histology images
papers.abstract: Precision oncology requires accurate molecular insights, yet obtaining these directly from genomics is costly and time-consuming for broad clinical use. Predicting complex molecular features and patient prognosis directly from routine whole-slide images (WSIs) remains a major challenge for current deep learning methods. Here we introduce PathLUPI, which uses transcriptomic privileged information during training to extract genome-anchored histological embeddings, enabling effective molecular prediction using only WSIs at inference. Through extensive evaluation across 49 molecular oncology tasks using 11,361 cases from 20 cohorts, PathLUPI demonstrates superior performance compared to conventional methods trained solely on WSIs. Crucially, it achieves an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of at least 0.80 across 18 biomarker prediction and molecular subtyping tasks, and a concordance index of at least 0.70 across survival cohorts spanning five major cancer types. Moreover, PathLUPI embeddings reveal distinct cellular morphological signatures associated with specific genotypes, whose spatial fidelity is substantiated in representative high-resolution spatial transcriptomics samples. By effectively encoding molecular context to refine WSI representations, PathLUPI offers a strategy to bridge molecular insights with routine pathology workflows for wider clinical application. Obtaining accurate molecular insights for precision oncology remains costly and time consuming. Here, the authors develop PathLUPI, a deep learning method to enable effective molecular prediction in cancer using only routine whole-slide images, with evaluation across 49 molecular oncology tasks in 20 different cohorts.

papers.title: Reconstructing the single-cell spatiotemporal dynamics of glioblastoma invasion
papers.abstract: Glioblastoma invasion into healthy brain tissue remains a major barrier to effective treatment, but the dynamic single-cell behaviors underlying this process remain difficult to measure across patient models. Here, we introduce GlioTrace, an ex vivo imaging and computational framework for real-time tracking of glioblastoma invasion in patient-derived xenograft brain slices. Combining whole-specimen confocal microscopy with machine learning-based morphology classification and probabilistic modeling of state transitions, GlioTrace reconstructs how tumor cells switch between invasion phenotypes and how these dynamics are shaped by local tissue context and therapy. Across six patient-derived models, GlioTrace reveals that invasion plasticity is patient-specific, spatially organized, and modulated by vascular proximity and microglial interaction. Targeted therapies selectively alter phenotype composition and transition probabilities, whereas standard-of-care treatment enriches a highly motile, transition-connected branching state consistent with a treatment-tolerant invasive phenotype. Thus, GlioTrace makes glioblastoma invasion a measurable dynamic process for comparing patient-specific treatment responses in living brain tissue.

papers.title: Fairness in infectious disease modeling
papers.abstract: Abstract The concept of fairness has been extensively examined within the domains of Machine Learning and Artificial Intelligence more broadly. It remains, however, largely underexplored in the field of Computational Epidemiology. Considering the substantial influence that epidemic models exert on public health policy, particularly in the context of outbreak preparedness and response, this shortcoming is of great relevance. Here, we propose a mathematical framework, grounded in core principles from Social Epidemiology, for evaluating the fairness of computational epidemic models. We begin by applying our framework to a range of epidemic modeling approaches and simulation scenarios, such as the initial spread of COVID-19 in London, New York, and Santiago de Chile, as well as the 2016 Zika virus outbreak in Colombia, demonstrating its consistent capacity to assess model fairness across diverse disease dynamics. Subsequently, we illustrate how our definition of fairness can be incorporated into the design of immunization strategies as a way to enhance health equity while simultaneously improving the overall effectiveness of such interventions. Overall, our results offer a new systematic methodology for quantifying fairness in computational epidemiology.

papers.title: AI needs meaningful versioning
When Is Personalized Federated Learning Worth Its Deployment Cost?
papers.abstract: Personalized federated learning (PFL) may improve client-level performance, but deeper personalization increases deployment cost. We formulate personalization-depth selection as a utility-based empirical decision problem in which client utility equals Macro-F1 minus a cost-sensitivity weight times deployment cost, over six personalization depths labeled P0 through P5. We compare fixed policies with an offline per-client Oracle reference and report allocation maps over Dirichlet data heterogeneity and cost sensitivity. Although evaluated on this hierarchy, the formulation can accommodate any finite candidate set. On CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and a PTB-XL subset, personalization shows empirical, setting-dependent decision regimes rather than a universal benefit: higher cost sensitivity shifts Oracle mass toward the global-only depth P0; low cost sensitivity can favor deeper actions. Patterns are grid observations (three seeds per cell), not theoretical boundaries. Best-uniform is competitive with Oracle assignment (6.5 percent plus or minus 7.8 percent relative regret; 95 percent confidence interval 5.9 to 7.1), whereas random and personalize-all incur much larger regret (189.3 percent plus or minus 367.1 percent and 409.0 percent plus or minus 803.2 percent). Under the same utility, Ditto full-model personalization is substantially suboptimal once cost is counted. The contribution is an offline characterization of when personalization depth is worth its cost, not a new PFL optimizer or deployment-time scheduler.

papers.title: Rethinking Model Aggregation for Federated Learning with Domain Skew: A Knowledge-Preserving Perspective
papers.abstract: Domain skew challenges federated learning by requiring a shared model to accommodate distinct visual distributions. Domain-specific experts can capture these distributions separately, creating an opportunity to integrate their representations in a unified predictor. We propose Federated Knowledge-Preserving Learning (FKPL), a two-stage framework that combines domain-oriented expert training with prototype-based classifier calibration. First, a one-shot subspace-based clustering procedure groups clients for intra-cluster training. The resulting expert encoders are concatenated and frozen, preserving each learned feature mapping during global integration. Second, clients interpolate their concatenated features with class-matched domain prototypes and upload the resulting virtual features. The server trains a global linear classifier on these features, concentrating classifier optimization at the server after a single feature upload. FKPL achieves average accuracies of 73.01\%, 67.00\%, and 64.51\% on Office-Caltech-10, PACS, and a four-domain subset of DomainNet, respectively. On DomainNet, its cross-domain standard deviation is 7.50 percentage points, the lowest among the evaluated methods. With the same concatenated extractor, prototype-based calibration improves average accuracy over federated classifier training by 9.99 and 14.94 percentage points on Office-Caltech-10 and PACS. These results identify classifier calibration as an effective way to combine preserved domain representations into a global predictor.

papers.title: Privacy-Preserving ECG-HRV Emotion Classification for Mood Swing Detection using Federated Learning on Constrained Edge Devices
papers.abstract: This paper presents a privacy-preserving mood monitoring framework that classifies emotional states from ECG-derived heart rate variability (HRV) features. The framework is evaluated on three public datasets comprising 74 participants and further validated using a wearable device in a pilot study. Leave-One-Participant-Out cross-validation (LOPO-CV) is used to assess generalization to unseen individuals. A series of experiments investigates the impact of temporal windowing, HRV feature selection, and class balancing on both four-class valence-arousal and binary valence classification. Results show that class balancing substantially improves minority-class recall, while Logistic Regression consistently outperforms five alternative classifiers and achieves competitive performance against HRV-based baselines. Pilot validation using a Polar H10 wearable achieves 75% binary valence accuracy on an unseen individual without calibration, demonstrating the feasibility of real-world deployment. To preserve privacy, the framework is also implemented using federated learning on a six-node Raspberry Pi cluster. Federated Logistic Regression achieves performance comparable to centralized training without sharing raw physiological data. These results demonstrate the potential of interpretable and privacy-preserving mood monitoring for continuous mental health assessment in clinical and community settings.

papers.title: Domain-Aware Hierarchical Federated Learning for UAV Swarms Across Heterogeneous Environments
papers.abstract: Hierarchical federated learning (HFL) enables communication-efficient training in unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) swarms, but performance degrades under changing and heterogeneous environments. This paper proposes domain-aware HFL (DA-HFL), integrating mobility-informed clustering, cluster-level aggregation, cloud-based Fisher-weighted merging, a domain-adversarial shared backbone, environment-specific heads, and gated inference with local adaptation. A mission-weighted optimization formulation incorporates energy, latency, and cluster-head eligibility constraints. Theoretical analysis establishes resource feasibility, a conditional backbone-stationarity bound, the quadratic optimality of Fisher-weighted merging, and communication and computation complexity bounds. Simulations across four heterogeneous environments demonstrate faster convergence, improved accuracy during environmental transitions, and more stable, purer clusters than the evaluated baselines, with modest energy overhead over resource-aware HFL. Ablation studies validate the contributions of the proposed components.

papers.title: Does the Trust Boundary Hold over Time? A Long-Horizon Benchmark for Receiver-Directed Federated Learning
papers.abstract: In receiver-directed federated learning, each site draws a trust boundary. For every source and model component it judges, on its own data, whether the transfer helps (admit), harms (reject) or cannot yet be told (abstain). We ask whether this boundary holds over hundreds of rounds. Our benchmark has a federation of thirteen semi-synthetic sites, an exact oracle for every evaluated transfer, paired seeds, an attack protocol, fourteen methods over 600 rounds and Qwen3-1.7B LoRA sites over 500. The answer depends on which boundary is measured. Across 20 paired CPU seeds, a gate judging against a fixed reference better identified transfers useful relative to the site's starting model. Yet it admitted 29% of transfers harmful to the model the site now has. A gate judging against the current model admitted 2% of harmful transfers on that target in the CPU tier, but missed many transfers useful to the starting model. Two short propositions explain these distinct failures. We also evaluate a held out audit that leaves gate verdicts intact. After training, it decides whether each final model is deployed or the site falls back to local training, and reports admissions that have gone stale. With independent audit data its guarantees hold after any training history. At 600 rounds the audit deployed 65 to 72% of models, none with negative benefit on its target, and kept 98% of the gain. No stale report had the wrong sign in our runs. With 20,000 audit observations, a variance-adaptive bound found 99% of stale transfers that cost at least 0.01 in log loss. A common-target Qwen3 comparison on 60 selected transfers shows the same tension over 100 rounds. With 38% adversarial sites, FedFomo and CS-Gate were the only evaluated methods with positive mean gain in every honest group.

papers.title: A federated relational-graph multi-agent reinforcement learning framework for privacy-compatible electric vehicle scheduling in coupled multi-park microgrids
papers.abstract: This study investigates collaborative electric vehicle scheduling in regional multi-park microgrids, where operational information is retained within individual parks while scheduling decisions remain physically coupled through a shared transformer (TR). This creates a fundamental challenge: decentralized park controllers must coordinate a common regional safety constraint without centralizing detailed local operating trajectories, while heterogeneous operating patterns further limit direct policy sharing. To address this problem, this paper proposes a federated relational-graph multi-agent reinforcement learning framework, termed FedRG-MARL. The shared TR constraint is transformed into privacy-compatible aggregate and park-specific coordination feedback and incorporated with heterogeneous local resources into a relational decision representation with explicit physical semantics. Pre-correction local and regional constraint costs further guide each decentralized policy to adapt its requested actions to both local operating limits and shared-TR pressure. The shared–private relational policy simultaneously separates common relation-level interaction knowledge from park-specific decision components, allowing transferable relation parameters to be selectively exchanged and personalized according to the target park’s own reward–constraint evaluation while raw trajectories remain local. In this manner, regional physical coordination, constraint-aware local adaptation, and cross-park knowledge transfer form an interconnected learning process without centralized collection of detailed park-level operating data. Simulation results over 150 common stochastic test scenarios show that, while maintaining constraint-compatible execution, FedRG-MARL improves mean daily system profit by 76.3% relative to the constrained graph-based GNN-CSAC baseline, while users’ net charging expenditure remains within a comparable range to the learning-based baselines.
papers.venue: Journal of King Saud University - Computer and Information Sciences

papers.title: An integrative review of hybrid deep learning approaches for malware detection: Recent advances, challenges, and future directions
papers.abstract: Malware is evolving, and signature-based detection systems are struggling to keep up with the new features of malware, such as obfuscation, polymorphism, metamorphism and zero-day attack capabilities. To overcome these challenges, AI and deep learning methods have become promising approaches to create adaptive and intelligent malware detection systems. In this review, we systematically analysed 77 peer-reviewed papers published from 2025 to 2026, which are related to the latest developments in deep learning and hybrid deep learning techniques for malware detection. The selected studies were reviewed using a PRISMA methodology, which included different aspects including malware detection techniques, feature representation techniques, deep learning architectures, explainability mechanisms, adversarial robustness, and new cybersecurity paradigms. The analysis shows that there is a strong trend towards the use of hybrid models that combine Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), Long Short-Term Memory networks (LSTMs), Graph Neural Networks (GNNs), Transformers, multimodal feature fusion, and ensemble learning strategies. Moreover, Explainable Artificial Intelligence, Federated Learning, and Large Language Models have garnered more focus to enhance transparency, privacy protection, and intelligent threat analysis. Comparative results indicate that hybrid and multimodal architectures are always better than traditional architectures, since they can capture the spatial, temporal, structural and behavioural features of malware and are more resistant to new cyber threats. This review suggests an Integrative Hybrid Deep Learning Framework that integrates multimodal feature fusion, graph-based learning, transformer-based contextual analysis, explainability, and strong classification capabilities, addressing the identified research gaps. The findings provide valuable insights and a research direction for developing scalable, reliable, and robust malware detection systems to address the increasing threats in the cybersecurity landscape.

SPeCTRA: Stealthy PPO-enhanced coordinated trigger attack against Robust Federated Aggregation
papers.abstract: Reference implementation of SPeCTRA, a PPO-driven backdoor attack on federated learning. A reinforcement-learning agent adapts a frequency-domain phase trigger in the YCbCr chrominance channels under Hermitian symmetry, evading eight Byzantine-robust and backdoor-specific aggregation defenses across SVHN, CIFAR-10, and Fashion-MNIST.

papers.title: AI DRIVEN DIGITAL TWINS FOR DRUG REPURPOSING: CURRENT EVIDENCES, APPLICATIONS, TRANSLATIONAL CHALLENGES AND FUTURE DIRECTIONS
authors: Ch. Usha Priyadarsini1, G. Devi Bramarambha1*, G. Mounica1, U. Sireesha Devi1, V. Sandeep1, A. Durga Pallavi2, Dr. Y. B. Manjulatha3, Dr. V. Bhaskara Raju4
papers.abstract: Conventional drug discovery and development is associated with substantial financial costs, lengthy development timelines, and high attrition rates during preclinical and clinical evaluation. Drug repurposing provides an alternative strategy by identifying new therapeutic applications for existing drugs with previously characterized pharmacological and safety profiles. Recent advances in artificial intelligence, multimodal biomedical data integration, mechanistic modelling, and digital twin technology have created new opportunities to improve computational drug repurposing and patient-specific treatment prediction. This review examines the emerging integration of AI-driven digital twins with drug repurposing, focusing on digital twin architectures, artificial intelligence methodologies multi modal data integration, drug target prediction, pharmacokinetic or pharmacodynamic modelling, treatment-response simulation, and personalized therapeutic decision-making. The review also discusses applications across cancer, neurodegenerative, cardiovascular, infectious, metabolic, and rare diseases. Particular emphasis is placed on the development of patient-specific digital twins, integration of multi-omics and clinical data, virtual treatment simulation, and validation through computational, experimental, and clinical approaches. Major challenges include data heterogeneity, interoperability, model reliability, uncertainty quantification, interpretability, algorithmic bias, cybersecurity, privacy, clinical workflow integration, and regulatory acceptance. Emerging approaches, including causal AI, federated learning, multimodal foundation models, virtual clinical trials, and real-time adaptive digital twins, may further enhance the translational potential of AI-enabled drug repurposing. However, prospective clinical validation and standardized regulatory frameworks remain necessary before widespread clinical implementation.

papers.title: Personalised Construction Site Safety Management Using Machine Learning: A Bibliometric Review
papers.abstract: Purpose: Construction sites have high accident rates, emphasising the need for better safety management. This study examines the current research on personalised machine learning (ML) safety management in construction through a bibliometric review. Design/Methodology/Approach: A critical realist approach was used within the historical context. Scopus served as the source for bibliographic data extraction, focusing on publications from 2014 to 2024 and using specific search phrases. Data analysis involved co-citation, citation, and keyword analyses with VOSviewer software. Research Limitation: This study examines a specific timeframe and may overlook recent developments. Relying solely on published literature may not capture all current research efforts. Findings: The review identified 90 publications, showing increasing interest in personalised ML-based safety management. The United States, China, and South Korea lead the research efforts, with notable contributions from Turkey and India. The findings highlight the potential of ML algorithms such as random forest, text mining, and deep learning for personalised safety interventions. Practical implications: This study provides valuable insights for researchers and practitioners on the current research landscape and promising opportunities to utilise ML in construction safety management. Construction professionals can leverage federated learning and edge computing for distributed and localised data processing in personalised safety systems. Social implications: This study provides insights into the development of personalised safety solutions to improve worker safety and well-being in the construction industry. Originality/Value: This study enhances the understanding of personalised ML in construction safety by showcasing potential algorithms and their ethical implications. It provides practical guidance for researchers and practitioners to support further development.

papers.title: Artificial intelligence for sustainable power systems applications challenges and future directions
papers.abstract: Abstract Stretching the integration of renewable energy, energy storage, electric vehicles (EVs) and smart-grid technologies at an unprecedented rate will produce increasingly complex and dynamic power systems that defy conventional optimization and control methods. This paper offers a systematic engineering review of the state of the art and future potential for the application of artificial intelligence (AI) in sustainable and resilient electric power systems, which includes machine learning, deep learning, reinforcement learning (RL), hybrid AI, explainable artificial intelligence, federated learning (FL), and digital twins (DTs). The review covers their use in renewable energy and load forecasting, energy management, predictive maintenance, demand response, adaptive control, energy storage, smart grid and EV/Vehicle-to-Grid coordination. A single framework based on the grid is presented that integrates predictive intelligence, optimization, adaptive control, cyber-physical systems, explainability, cyber-security, and sustainability in a closed-loop system. The analysis underscores the transformative possibilities of AI in enhancing the use of renewable energy, its efficiency, resilience of the grid and smart decision making. But, deployment needs to address the uncertainties, data quality, computational costs, latency, Cybersecurity, interoperability, scalability, model drift, and regulatory needs. The review also highlights Green AI to tackle the energy and carbon footprint of increasingly large AI models. Lastly, physics-informed and uncertainty-aware AI, safe RL, DT-assisted validation, edge intelligence, FL and real-world benchmarking are identified as key directions for next-generation power systems to remain trustworthy and sustainable.

papers.title: Privacy-Preserving Federated Learning with Causal Multiscale Decomposition for Regional Short-Term Load Forecasting in Smart Grids
papers.abstract: Accurate regional short-term load forecasting is essential to the reliable operation and efficient energy scheduling of smart grids. However, the data needed for collaborative model training are often distributed across regional utilities and grid operators, creating data silos that limit cross-regional learning. To address these challenges, we propose a hybrid regional load forecasting model, EMA-GRU-N-HiTS, and further extend it into a privacy-preserving federated learning framework, FL-EMA-GRU-N-HiTS. Specifically, a causal additive exponential moving average (EMA) filter bank decomposes each historical load window into low- and high-frequency component groups without using future observations. The low-frequency components are modeled by a gated recurrent unit (GRU), whereas the high-frequency components are learned by an adapted neural hierarchical interpolation for time-series forecasting (N-HiTS) network. In the federated setting, aggregation weights jointly reflect the client sample size, local training error, and update similarity. Paillier encryption enables fixed-point parameter aggregation while protecting individual uploads from an honest-but-curious cloud server under a trusted, non-colluding third party (TTP). Experiments on regional load data from the New York Independent System Operator (NYISO) show that both methods achieve the lowest test errors among the evaluated baselines across the four forecasting horizons. Under sample imbalance, contribution-aware aggregation mitigates prediction degradation caused by the evaluated label-scaling and model-update attacks. Encrypted aggregation incurs substantial computational and communication overhead, while small-scale CPU parallelism reduces the cryptographic stage time.

papers.title: The lightweight multi-task federated learning collaborative training framework based on power network edge computation scenario
papers.abstract: Power load forecasting, fault detection, and other scenarios are driving increasing demand for computing platforms. However, the traditional Federated Learning (FL) framework has several problems, including limited computing power and storage resources of Edge Computing (EC) nodes and redundant parameters. The FL framework is prone to negative migration, which leads to the decline of model accuracy. Besides, the power edge node test illustrates that the computing power is difficult to bear the node threshold after deployment. In response to these problems, this study constructs a Lightweight Multi-Task Federated Learning (LMTFL) collaborative training framework. Combined with the needs of power edge scenarios, it builds a deployment adaptation model, which innovatively realizes the dual optimization of lightweight and multi-task collaboration. Thus, the limitations of single optimization in the existing technologies are solved. In the quantitative aspect, the redundancy of model parameters is reduced by more than 77% by PP, the negative migration is controlled within 5% by TAC, and the transmission delay is reduced to less than 80 ms by HA. Furthermore, through the experiment, it is shown that the comprehensive performance of the framework is 0.892, which is 23.7% higher than that of PP and 25.9% higher than that of KD + FL. The robustness value is 0.913, and the performance fluctuation is only 4.3%, which is much better than that of KD + HA (0.802). Besides, the practicability reaches 0.906. The deployment cost is reduced by 24.6% compared to PP + KD. The parameter redundancy is only 22.7%, and the computing power occupancy rate is controlled within 44.8%. The proposed framework is primarily applicable to small- and medium-scale edge clusters (≤ 50 nodes) where the computing power disparity among nodes does not exceed a factor of 7. For ultra-large-scale node deployments or highly dynamic wireless edge environments, the aggregation latency and cold-start performance still require further optimization. Lastly, the lightweight and scenario-based implementation of FL technology in the power field are promoted, which shows an important engineering application value and a technical reference significance.
papers.venue: Journal of King Saud University - Computer and Information Sciences

papers.title: Securing next-generation edge intelligence: A survey from federated learning to autonomous agents in cyber–physical systems
papers.abstract: The integration of Large Language Models (LLMs) and Small Language Models (SLMs) as autonomous agents at the network edge marks a shift in cyber–physical systems and the Internet of Things (IoT). Deploying these non-deterministic reasoning engines in resource-constrained environments, however, disrupts traditional security paradigms. This survey reviews the threats to autonomous edge agents and their defenses. Through a layered taxonomy spanning the Perception, Cognition, Actuation, and Collaboration layers, we categorize the emerging cyber–physical threats, among them sensor-borne prompt injection, context-sequential injection, tool hijacking, and Sybil-based poisoning of the federated substrate. Several have been demonstrated on physical platforms, most starkly the jailbreaking of a deployed commercial robot, whereas the surveyed multi-agent attacks run only in simulation and software; attacks on quantized vision models further show that the aggressive quantization that edge hardware demands can open evasion vectors of its own. Evaluating the prevailing defenses, we expose the latency cost of inference-heavy semantic guardrails and the sequential blindness of stateless pre-execution firewalls, and we map their coverage against the taxonomy, separating experimental from inferred mappings. We flag stateful behavioral tracking as a largely unrefereed direction against the reasoning-to-action gap, not as a settled defense family. The survey’s principal output is a coverage map isolating three edge-induced threats that no edge-deployable runtime mechanism surveyed addresses: energy-targeted resource exhaustion, quantization-specific evasion, and model provenance against supply-chain weight poisoning. For the second, every surveyed hardening strategy that preserves adversarial robustness through quantization has been evaluated only on vision classifiers.

papers.title: Digital twin-driven collaborative task offloading method for vehicular edge computing
papers.abstract: Vehicular edge computing (VEC) has emerged as a critical paradigm for meeting the demands of computation-intensive and delay-sensitive vehicular applications by pushing computational capabilities to the network edge. However, in highly dynamic traffic environments, vehicle mobility, fluctuating wireless channels, limited resources, and stochastic task arrivals make offloading decisions vulnerable to insufficient state awareness, unbalanced resource allocation, and degraded service continuity. To address these issues, this paper proposes a digital twin (DT) driven collaborative dynamic task offloading framework for VEC. Leveraging DT technology to construct a real-time virtual mapping of the physical VEC network, the proposed framework facilitates the collaborative allocation of computing resources between edge servers (ESs) and opportunistic edge servers (OESs) through global state monitoring and prediction. Specifically, it fully exploits the collaborative computational capabilities of roadside units (RSUs) and opportunistic vehicles, leveraging idle resources of opportunistic vehicles to construct a vehicular ad-hoc cloud to alleviate the load pressure on ESs. Based on this architecture, a task execution model including local computing, V2R offloading, and V2V offloading is formulated. Transmission delay, computing delay, energy consumption, resource capacity, and task completion constraints are jointly considered to minimize system delay and energy consumption while improving the task completion rate. To solve the multi-vehicle continuous offloading and resource allocation problem, a federated learning-assisted multi-agent deep deterministic policy gradient (FL-MADDPG) algorithm is developed. MADDPG enables cooperative decision-making among vehicles, while FL aggregates vehicle-side model parameters to reduce local training bias, preserve data privacy, and enhance policy generalization. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed algorithm can balance system load more effectively and outperform mainstream baseline algorithms in terms of convergence performance, average system latency, and task completion rate.
papers.venue: Journal of King Saud University - Computer and Information Sciences

papers.title: Evaluating reinforcement learning approaches for leaderless UAV swarms in obstacle-laden environment
papers.abstract: Unmanned Aerial Vehicle (UAV) swarms provide huge potential for complex missions, yet coordinating large-scale collectives in obstacle-laden environments without a single global leader remains a significant challenge. While Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL) has become a dominant paradigm for such coordination, systematic comparisons of how different training architectures perform within hierarchical manager-worker swarm topologies that deliberately eliminate the top-level aggregator remain absent from the literature. This study compares centralized (CTDE), decentralized (DTDE), and federated (FTDE) training approaches, all with decentralized execution, for a leaderless hierarchical UAV swarm of 18 agents organized into three manager-worker clusters. All paradigms are implemented using Asynchronous Proximal Policy Optimization (APPO) and evaluated over a fixed ten-session training budget. Centralized learning achieves the highest final reward, while federated learning attains the highest cumulative reward over the training budget by avoiding a mid-training performance drop observed in the centralized approach. Federated learning is also the only approach whose reward stays within a stability band through the end of the training budget, reaches a final collision rate comparable to that of centralized learning, and reduces inter-cluster training communication by approximately 80% relative to centralized learning. Under simulated manager failure, decentralized and federated learning each retain over 94% of nominal performance, compared to 63.9% for centralized learning. A theoretical analysis shows that the inter-cluster communication cost of the federated approach is independent of the number of workers per cluster when the number of manager clusters is fixed, although it grows with the number of clusters. Validation with an alternative algorithm (MAPPO) preserves the ordering of the three approaches on both final and cumulative reward, and an obstacle-density study preserves the final-reward ordering. These results indicate that peer-to-peer federated learning provides a balanced trade-off between learning performance, communication overhead, fault tolerance, and scalability for hierarchical UAV swarms.

papers.title: Federated Learning Beyond Training: Optimization, Personalization, Security, and Unlearning
papers.abstract: Federated learning (FL) leaves training records with participating clients, but restrictions on the visibility and retention of model updates can limit later verification, robustness checks, and deletion. This review examines these dependencies across distributed optimization, personalization, parameter-efficient foundation-model adaptation, privacy, Byzantine robustness, and federated unlearning. For a specified actor and authorized observation, an exact downstream operation is obstructed when two admissible states produce identical observations but require different outputs. Aggregate-sum and merged low-rank examples establish this information limit, while a two-round example shows why replaying historical updates need not reproduce retraining without a deleted client. A conditional screening procedure examines information access, common assumptions, and declared resource budgets. A specified cross-silo case separates demonstrated obstructions, alternatives that change the available operation, and claims not established for complete protocols. This review distinguishes component-level proofs and experiments from evidence for joint implementations and identifies evaluation requirements under changing client distributions, correlated participation, adaptive attacks, and sequential deletion. Its conclusions are limited to a selected narrative literature and analytical examples; no general joint security or unlearning guarantee is claimed.

papers.title: Medical data protection: Advanced Bayesian tactical unit framework for encryption and auditing
A novel federated unlearning framework with feature-heterogeneity-aware aggregation for privacy-preserving UAV anomaly detection
Understanding Client Heterogeneity and Update Usefulness in Federated Residential Energy Forecasting
papers.abstract: Federated learning is a distributed learning framework for forecasting residential electricity consumption without centralizing raw client data. Thirty complete households were selected as simulated FL clients from the real-world dataset, after quality controlled preprocessing and hourly aggregation of the data. Next-hour electricity consumption is predicted using a GRU model with a 24-hour lookback and a chronological train–validation–test protocol. Centralized GRU, FedAvg, a drift-aware reliability-weighted prototype, and diagnostic conflict-aware aggregation are evaluated. FedAvg achieves a test MAE of 0.205108 kWh/hour, RMSE of 0.377878, and R² of 0.606950, while the drift-aware prototype achieves MAE of 0.208843, RMSE of 0.380713, and R² of 0.601030. Client-level analysis shows there is no significant predictive power of the static measure of heterogeneity on the forecasting MAE but update-alignment and conflict measures are associated with post-update validation error. Conflict-aware weighting does not give evidence of improvement and actually causes a 0.000170 increase in MAE compared to FedAvg.

papers.title: Wearable IoT Patient Monitoring with On-Device Fall Detection: A Review of Edge-AI Methods, Embedded Deployment, and Open Challenges
papers.abstract: Falls are a leading cause of injury in older adults and in patients recovering from illness or surgery, and wearable monitors that recognize a fall at the point of sensing are an active research area. This review examines wearable Internet of Things (IoT) patient monitors that combine physiological sensing with on-device fall detection, using 40 peer-reviewed and preprint studies published between 2024 and 2026. The literature is organized around the architecture of edge-AI wearables, fall-detection and activity-recognition algorithms, embedded deployment via tiny machine learning (TinyML), physiological sensing, and the connectivity, privacy, and evaluation practices that surround them. Threshold, classical machine-learning, and deep-learning detectors report high offline accuracy, often above 95%, yet performance degrades in real-time use, under integer quantization, and during subject-independent validation. A smartwatch CNN-LSTM, for example, dropped from an F1-score of 87.6% offline to 70.2% in live tests. Few studies report latency, memory, energy, and false alarms per hour together, and most live validation involves young volunteers performing simulated falls. Low-cost optical sensors estimate pulse rate and oxygen saturation with small errors in controlled tests, although motion, skin tone, and sensor placement remain unresolved, and privacy-preserving designs such as lightweight encryption and federated learning are rarely tested on microcontrollers. The evidence is summarised in seven tables and seven figures, six research gaps are identified, and a five-level validation roadmap is proposed that moves from public datasets to long-term daily wear. The review provides a structured basis for researchers designing low-power, privacy-aware wearable monitors and for clinicians evaluating them.
