Federated learning over industrial data spaces: an end-to-end operational pipeline framework for predictive maintenance
papers.abstract: Current Industrial predictive maintenance depends on Data-Driven Artificial Intelligence. However, operational datasets are isolated due to privacy, sovereignty and regulation concerns. Data heterogeneity among manufacturers and the lack of a framework that enables data sharing introduce additional obstacles. To address these issues, this paper proposes an operational pipeline based on a generic sovereign and distributed manufacturing architecture through Federated Learning workflows within an Industrial Data Space utilizing standardized Digital Twins. The operational validation of the framework is addressed through a cyber-physical manufacturing use case involving distributed machining spindle heads, which provides a first demonstration of collaborative diagnostics under data sovereignty constraints. At the semantic and interoperability level, the Asset Administration Shell standard is instantiated via Eclipse BaSyx. On the one hand, to translate heterogeneous edge vibration signals into uniform digital representations and on the other, to enable collaborative FL model and parameter sharing using the IDTA 02060-1-0 AI Submodel Nameplate specification. In addition, Eclipse Dataspace Components connectors orchestrate the policycompliant and auditable exchange of model parameters, so that every training round is bound to negotiated usage contracts. • Keywords: Federated learning, Data standardization, IDTA Digital Twin, Asset Administration Shell, Predictive maintenance, Data Spaces

papers.title: Artificial Intelligence in Neurology: A Critical Narrative Review of Clinical Evidence, Translation, and Responsible Implementation
papers.abstract: PURPOSE: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly applied to neuroimaging, electrophysiology, clinical text, and digitally measured behavior, but reported performance often exceeds the maturity of clinical evidence. METHOD: We conducted a structured narrative review, informed by SANRA principles, of English-language human studies, reviews, and regulatory sources identified in PubMed/MEDLINE and IEEE Xplore from January 2022 through July 2026; older landmark studies were retained when necessary for historical or methodological context. We applied a common translational-evidence framework across six prespecified neurological domains to distinguish technical performance from external validation, prospective clinical evaluation, implementation, and demonstrated patient benefit. Evidence was appraised according to cohort representativeness, patient-level data separation, external and prospective validation, calibration, clinical comparators, regulatory status, workflow integration, and patient-level benefit. FINDING: Across stroke, dementia, Parkinson disease, epilepsy, multiple sclerosis, and neuro-oncology, the strongest evidence concerns narrowly defined imaging and signal-processing tasks. A cluster-randomized stroke study demonstrated shorter thrombectomy workflow time, and several externally validated models show improved portability. In contrast, many high-accuracy classification and segmentation studies remain retrospective, single-dataset, internally validated, and uncalibrated. Multimodal learning, foundation models, federated learning, and large language models broaden capability but introduce additional risks related to dataset shift, bias, opacity, privacy, and automation. CONCLUSION: Neuro-AI should be judged by its intended clinical task and evidence maturity rather than headline accuracy. Multicenter external validation, prospective workflow evaluation, calibration, subgroup reporting, human-factors testing, and post-deployment surveillance are prerequisites for safe and equitable clinical use.

papers.title: FairChoice: A Device Selection Approach for Fair and Robust Federated Learning under Non-IID Data
papers.abstract: The rapid integration of machine learning (ML) and artificial intelligence (AI) into distributed environments, such as smart cities, has heightened the need for privacy-preserving and equitable data-driven systems. Centralizing citizen data is often impractical or undesirable due to privacy, security, and regulatory constraints, making Federated Learning (FL) a natural alternative. However, ensuring fairness in FL remains a critical yet underexplored challenge, particularly when data across devices is not independent and identically distributed (non-IID). Two major forms of non-IID data- protected attribute skew , where demographic groups are unevenly represented across devices, and label skew , where class distributions differ among devices-can significantly distort both model performance and fairness. To address this, we propose FairChoice , a novel FL algorithm that jointly optimizes group fairness and model accuracy through dynamic device selection. FairChoice evaluates device contributions using both loss and the Average Odds (AO) fairness metric, with a fairness budget parameter ( β ) that flexibly regulates the trade-off. It requires neither group-level statistics nor a server-side validation set with protected attributes, sharing only model updates and per-device loss and AO values. Experiments on real-world datasets demonstrate that FairChoice improves group fairness by up to 82% under protected attribute skew and 38% under label skew (relative improvement) compared to FedAvg, while maintaining high accuracy-making it a promising step toward ethical, reliable, and privacy-conscious AI in smart communities.

papers.title: Standardising ocular surface photography for artificial intelligence: current limitations and a proposed roadmap
papers.abstract: Slit-lamp colour photography remains a cornerstone of anterior segment documentation and longitudinal monitoring. However, conventional slit-lamp photography has seen relatively limited technological advancement compared with the rapid development of quantitative anterior-segment modalities such as AS-OCT, Scheimpflug tomography and confocal microscopy. Despite the wide diffusion of digital cameras, smartphones, and high-end slit-lamp systems, ocular surface photography (OSP) remains hampered by the absence of standardised acquisition and processing protocols. The convex, aspheric geometry of the ocular surface, off-axis illumination, peripheral defocus, automatic colour correction, and pupil-driven exposure variation in retroillumination limit reproducibility, inter-device comparability, and clinical utility. In this review we critically appraise current OSP applications across major ocular surface conditions (dry eye disease, conjunctival hyperaemia, infectious keratitis, ocular surface burns, and ocular surface neoplasia), mapping the hardware, software, and reproducibility limitations that constrain clinical practice. We then examine how these limitations propagate into artificial intelligence (AI) development, where the absence of large, well-annotated, demographically diverse OSP datasets, together with the lack of reproducible quantitative phenotypes and reliable labels, is now the principal bottleneck to clinically deployable models; we discuss patient-level data partitioning and external validation, and outline how deep learning, federated learning and foundation models can both utilise and improve OSP. Finally, we propose a minimum acquisition and dataset specification, tiered by clinical setting from research to community screening, and a staged roadmap that combines hardware standardisation (focus-stacked, illumination-controlled, colour-calibrated acquisition), interoperable metadata-rich storage (DICOM where infrastructure permits), quantitative phenotype definition, and diverse international dataset collaborations, so that the ocular surface can benefit from quantitative imaging and AI as other areas of ophthalmology have begun to.

papers.title: DecFedFreq: Frequency‐Guided Cluster‐Restricted Encoder Residual Aggregation for Decoupled Personalized Federated Learning at the Edge
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Heterogeneous edge‐intelligence systems require federated models that preserve useful shared representations while adapting to persistent client differences. Existing decoupled personalized federated learning methods separate a shared encoder from private prediction heads and coordinate encoder information across clients. This paper proposes DecFedFreq, a framework that makes encoder residual aggregation adaptive. The method uses a low‐frequency discrete cosine transform descriptor as a deterministic, compressed summary of encoder‐update residuals for similarity estimation, applies affinity‐based grouping to infer dynamic client clusters, and restricts complete encoder‐residual aggregation to those clusters while prediction heads remain local. Across 10 matched random seeds under severe heterogeneous partitions with full participation, DecFedFreq obtains final‐round accuracies of on Fashion‐MNIST, on CIFAR‐10, and on CIFAR‐100. Relative to FedRep, the corresponding paired gains are 1.33, 2.96, and 5.13 percentage points, respectively, with all two‐sided paired ‐tests yielding . Additional five‐seed Fashion‐MNIST analyses of heterogeneous availability, unequal local‐computation budgets, representation alternatives, and a single‐global‐cluster control indicate that the main measured gain arises from similarity‐based grouping and cluster‐restricted aggregation. Discrete Cosine Transform is therefore positioned as the deterministic, empirically stable default similarity representation in the tested setting, with competitive accuracy and an eightfold reduction in similarity‐input dimension relative to the complete raw residual, rather than as an independently optimal accuracy component; server‐only profiling quantifies the added computation and memory over 25–100 active clients.

VeilFL: Two-Stage Accountability for Anonymous Federated Learning
papers.abstract: Anonymous credentials can hide which registered client participates in federated learning, but their unlinkability also makes repeated misconduct difficult to associate. We present VeilFL, a two-aggregator protocol that adds staged accountability to PINE (USENIX Security '24). Each submission binds two private PINE messages, a round-specific pseudonym, and a tracing pair to the same hidden credential secret. This design enables detection of duplicate submissions within a round without introducing a persistent identifier for normal participation. VeilFL implements accountability in two stages. After a confirmed duplicate or joint PINE rejection, a threshold tracing committee reveals a stable handle that links faults associated with the same credential. The client's registered identity is recoverable only after the public log records the requisite number of linked faults and a separate threshold committee authorizes identification. Accepted and unopened submissions remain unlinkable under the stated assumptions. This work establishes submission binding and duplicate detection, anonymity, fault non-frameability, controlled two-stage opening, and preservation of PINE's privacy and validity guarantees. In the prototype implementation, creating a submission requires a median of 2.11 ms, while verification requires 3.01 ms. Batch verification reduces the cost to 1.86 ms per submission for a batch of 1,000. The public part of each submission is 608 bytes, with 1,248 bytes of additional VeilFL protocol data across the two aggregator submissions. Each opening stage completes within 4.3 ms for the different committee configurations.

papers.title: ParaBlock++: Communication-Computation Parallel Blockwise Hierarchical Federated Learning
papers.abstract: In the emerging 6G paradigm, where AI-driven services operate over decentralized and resource-constrained infrastructures, the convergence of distributed learning algorithms remains a significant challenge. This paper introduces $\mathrm{ParaBlock}$++, a low Earth orbit (LEO) satellite-assisted hierarchical federated learning (HFL) framework, enabling resource-limited terrestrial clients to collaboratively engage in federated learning (FL) via ground-satellite links (GSLs) supported by LEO satellite megaconstellations. Within this architecture, LEO satellites serve multiple roles: as edge servers aggregating and broadcasting models, as clients accelerating training, and as high-throughput relays managing inter-satellite routing through inter-satellite links (ISLs). Departing from conventional synchronous Jacobian-type updates, $\mathrm{ParaBlock}$++ employs asynchronous BCD-type updates to enhance convergence speed. We provide theoretical convergence guarantees for convex, strongly convex, and non-convex objectives, and formulate optimization problems to determine optimal cluster resource allocation and model partitioning for minimizing global training latency. Experimental evaluations demonstrate that $\mathrm{ParaBlock}$++ achieves faster initial convergence and comparable final performance for deep neural networks (DNNs) such as ResNet-18, offering promising directions for federated learning across geographically remote areas enabled by 6G technologies, but much less global rounds and communication cost.

papers.title: Hierarchical Asynchronous Federated Learning over Space-Air-Ground Integrated Networks
papers.abstract: With the emerging 6G paradigm where AI services operate over decentralized and resource-constrained edge infrastructure, performance of distributed learning algorithms remains a significant challenge. This paper proposes HAFL, a Low Earth Orbit (LEO) satellite-assisted hierarchical asynchronous Federated Learning (FL) framework, enabling resource-limited terrestrial clients to collaborate via Ground-Satellite Links (GSLs). Within this framework, LEO satellites serve multiple roles: as edge servers aggregating and broadcasting models, as clients accelerating training, and as high-throughput relays managing inter-satellite routing through Inter-Satellite Links (ISLs). Unlike conventional synchronous Jacobian-type updates, HAFL employs asynchronous Gauss-Seidel-type updates to enhance convergence speed. We provide theoretical convergences for convex, strongly convex, and nonconvex objectives, respectively, and formulate optimization problems to jointly determine optimal hyperparameters to minimize global training latency. Evaluations demonstrate that HAFL achieves faster initial convergence and comparable final performance for benchmark DNNs and datasets, offering promising FL systems across remote areas with 6G technologies, but much less global rounds and communication cost.

papers.title: Cyber-physical security and resilience in microgrids: a comprehensive review of attack scenarios, detection methods, and defense mechanisms
papers.abstract: The rapid transition toward renewable-dominated energy systems has transformed microgrids (MGs) into highly interconnected cyber-physical systems (CPSs), where advanced communication, intelligent control, and inverter-based resources enhance operational flexibility while introducing unprecedented security vulnerabilities. This paper presents a comprehensive review of cyber-physical security and resilience enhancement strategies for MGs by establishing a unified framework that integrates attack scenarios, detection methodologies, and defense mechanisms. The evolving threat landscape is systematically analyzed, including false data injection, denial-of-service, spoofing, replay, and coordinated hybrid attacks targeting communication infrastructures, control layers, and physical power dynamics. Furthermore, existing detection approaches are critically reviewed and categorized into model-based, statistical, artificial intelligence and machine learning-based, physics-informed, and digital twin-enabled frameworks. Particular attention is given to emerging techniques such as deep learning, reinforcement learning, graph neural networks, federated learning, and physics-informed neural networks, highlighting their potential and limitations under nonlinear and uncertain inverter-dominated operating conditions. Defense and resilience strategies are investigated through secure communication, adaptive control, redundancy, attack mitigation, self-healing operation, and recovery-oriented approaches. The review further emphasizes the importance of real-time validation platforms and digital twins for predictive risk assessment and autonomous cyber-physical resilience management. Finally, key research challenges are identified, including scalability, explainability of intelligent security models, realistic hardware-in-the-loop validation, standardized resilience metrics, and the development of integrated physics–AI frameworks for future secure and adaptive MGs.

papers.title: Generation of synthetic clinical text: a systematic review
papers.abstract: Generating medical synthetic text represents an effective solution for clinical NLP issues like sparsity and privacy. This paper conducts a systematic review on synthetic clinical text generation by formulating quantitative analysis to three research questions concerning the generation’s purpose, generation techniques, and the evaluation methods. We searched four databases including PubMed, Scopus, ScienceDirect and Web of Science for publications associated with the topic and identified 87 relevant articles out of 1148. Results showed that the generation purposes were dedicated to Trustworthy, Medical Assistance, and Language Resource themes. Prompting LLMs was the main source of synthetic text (40 articles). GPTs were the main predominant technique used to generate the text (63 articles), especially ChatGPT (47 articles). Additionally, there were four main aspects of evaluation, including similarity, privacy, structure, and utility, where utility was the prevailing method for assessment (52 articles). The synthetic medical text empowered data augmentation and clinical documentation. Using text alteration, controlling real text portions, and federated learning, generative models can produce privacy-preserving medical text. This accelerates the development of new digital health applications.

Precision Agriculture Using AI for Crop Yield Prediction and Disease Detection: A Comprehensive Review of Machine Learning and Deep Learning Approaches for Sustainable, Data-Driven Farming
papers.abstract: Abstract Precision agriculture amalgamates artificial intelligence (AI) with field-level sensors to enhance agricultural yield while reducing resource use. This article offers an extensive examination of the application of machine learning (ML) and deep learning (DL) methodologies to two essential functions: forecasting crop production based on environmental and soil information, and identifying plant diseases using leaf images. We investigate the historical evolution of the discipline, outline prevalent data sources and preprocessing methodologies, evaluate the reported efficacy of prominent model families across various benchmark analyses, showcase representative case-study workflows, and assess the resource and economic implications of AI-assisted agriculture. We provide a deeper examination of regional deployment trends, delineate the practical and technological obstacles hindering large-scale implementation, and suggest prospective research avenues such as federated learning, edge deployment, and interpretable AI. The evaluation aims to function as a comprehensive resource for scholars and professionals exploring this swiftly advancing domain.

papers.title: FedHAD: Enhancing federated learning under Non-IID data distributions
papers.abstract: In federated learning, Non-IID client data biases local updates away from the global objective. FedHAD is a client-side policy for cross-silo federations with full participation: each client computes a normalized coefficient-of-variation score from its local label counts and uses it to set its number of local epochs and its learning rate, plus a fixed proximal term, leaving aggregation unchanged. It is evaluated on MNIST, FashionMNIST and CIFAR-10 under Dirichlet partitioning and on a ten-writer FEMNIST federation, against FedAvg, FedAvgM, FedProx, FedNova and SCAFFOLD over 30 paired seeds, with the baselines at a default of five local epochs and a learning rate of 1 0 − 2 . Relative to these defaults, FedHAD records 10 to 35% fewer training FLOPs; on CIFAR-10 it attains the highest mean accuracy under extreme skew and is within 0.2 points of the best baseline other than SCAFFOLD under moderate skew. SCAFFOLD is more accurate where stable but, at the configuration evaluated, collapses in 18 of 90 extreme-skew runs. In controls from a common initial checkpoint, a uniform learning rate preserving the aggregate first-order step of FedHAD is 1.13 points more accurate under extreme skew, so client-specific rates are not needed for the accuracy effect. A FedProx tuned on separate validation seeds is practically equivalent under extreme skew with about 62% of FedHAD’s updates, and FedHAD is non-inferior to it at the tested margin under high skew, where the tuned configuration uses about 85%. The contribution is automatic client-local configuration, without additional validation search in the evaluated experiments.

Implementation and Evaluation of a Blockchain and Decentralized Identity-Based Federated Learning Prototype for GPT-2 Fine-Tuning
papers.abstract: Large language model development depends on large-scale training data, yet centralized collection raises privacy risks and concentrates control among a few organizations. Federated learning addresses part of this problem but retains a central aggregator, cannot readily verify contributions, and lacks sustained incentives. Blockchain integration resolves coordination and transparency, yet participant identity remains exposed to sybil attacks. This study designs, implements, and evaluates a prototype platform combining these three technologies. The prototype uses GPT-2 Small with 10,000 Alpaca samples partitioned Non-IID across five clients, the FederatedHub contract on Ethereum, and IPFS as off-chain storage. Evaluation covers 5 rounds across 3 seeds, 9 attack variants, a sybil attack using 10 identities, and two-attacker collusion. The delta-based scoring function yields scores from 27.3 to 73.0 correlating 0.920 to 0.991 with data volume, perplexity falls from 24.6722 to 7.7798, and ROUGE-L rises by 106.6%. The gate catches 8 of 9 variants, yet one variant that positions itself inside the acceptance range passes every trial while capturing 95.2% of legitimate client rewards. All sybil identities are admitted, and gas cost limits the system to 15 or 16 participants. The weakness lies in the identity and incentive layers, not in model quality.

papers.title: Federated Learning for Official Statistics: A Systematic Review of Privacy‐Preserving Architectures and the Path Toward GSBPM Integration
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT National Statistical Offices (NSOs) face an escalating “privacy‐utility” impasse, where the demand for high‐granularity data must compete with the near zero risk tolerance of legal frameworks like the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR). Traditional centralized collection creates “honeypots” for breaches, exposing a nation's entire digital census or tax records. This paper provides a systematic review of Federated Learning (FL) as a decentralized framework that eliminates raw microdata consolidation. Drawing on 77 peer‐reviewed. Studies and technical reports published between 2020 and 2026, the study evaluates Horizontal and Vertical FL architectures alongside Privacy‐Enhancing Technologies (PETs). The analysis reveals that while PETs introduce a “utility gap,” Under controlled experimental settings and standardized non‐IID configurations, the evaluated architectures frequently achieve utility bounds exceeding 90% of their centralized equivalents, though this outcome varies based on the assigned privacy budget () and data distribution. Crucially, the study demonstrates that the mathematical noise required for Differential Privacy (DP) can threaten strict accuracy thresholds; for example, an aggressive privacy budget can cause census distributions to shift more than 77% from the true mean, rendering indicators like Gross Domestic Product (GDP) or unemployment rates statistically meaningless. Beyond these accuracy trade‐offs, the paper addresses the Non‐Independent and Identically Distributed (Non‐IID) nature of government datasets and identifies research gaps in standardized audit trails. The paper proposes a novel roadmap for integrating FL into the Generic Statistical Business Process Model (GSBPM), offering NSOs and international statistical bodies a technically grounded and legally coherent pathway toward next generation data infrastructure.
papers.venue: Concurrency and Computation Practice and Experience

papers.title: Trust-Driven Pre-Aggregation Federated Learning with Agentic Orchestration and Blockchain-Based Auditing for Secure Healthcare Systems
papers.abstract: Federated Learning (FL) reduces direct exposure of sensitive clinical data, but decentralized healthcare deployments remain vulnerable to Byzantine and data-poisoning attacks and are complicated by non-independent and identically distributed (non-IID) data across institutions. Existing defenses typically address these problems in isolation: robustness mechanisms add computational overhead without provenance guarantees, blockchain-only integrations improve auditability at the cost of scalability, and agentic-AI orchestration approaches are rarely reconciled with healthcare interoperability standards such as FHIR and HL7. This paper proposes the Tri-Layer Agentic Federated Blockchain Architecture (TAFBA), a system-design framework that integrates privacy-preserving FL, agentic trust orchestration, and permissioned blockchain auditing in a single closed-loop pipeline. The central methodological contribution is a pre-aggregation validation pipeline (local training, differential-privacy injection, agentic trust scoring, anomaly-based rejection, and trust-weighted, cluster-aware aggregation) that departs from the aggregate-then-filter paradigm used in most federated systems. TAFBA is developed through a theoretical and system-design methodology: we formalize the threat model and an explicit adversarial-fraction assumption, derive a composite, temporally smoothed trust score, and give an analytical argument, with an asymptotic complexity analysis, showing how pre-aggregation filtering and trust weighting bound the influence of adversarial nodes. We also specify an architecture-level mapping to FHIR resources and HL7 interaction points and a reproducible protocol for future empirical validation against Byzantine-robust baselines such as Krum, Multi-Krum, and FLTrust. TAFBA does not report empirical performance figures; it provides a mathematically grounded foundation for regulatory-aware, adversary-resilient decentralized learning in clinical settings, together with a defined pathway toward empirical validation.
papers.venue: Journal of Computers Mechanical and Management

papers.title: A federated learning framework for anomaly detection in electric vehicle charging networks
papers.abstract: Charging networks for electric vehicles (EVs) are also coming under attack from cyber threats such as Denial-of-Service (DoS) attacks, unauthorized access, load balancing the network, and sudden charging network disruptions. The traditional centralized anomaly-detection and authentication schemes are not suitable for large-scale, geographically distributed and privacy-focused charging infrastructure, as they include SPOF, high communication overhead and limited adaptability to the changing threats. This paper proposes a federated-learning (FL) framework, which is composed of (i) a dual-layer authentication architecture, namely a Global Authentication Protocol (GAP) using TLS with a fallback Local Authentication Protocol (LAP), and (ii) a heterogeneous pipeline of anomaly detections, such as supervised models (Random Forest, Decision Trees), unsupervised models (Autoencoders, Principal Component Analysis), and regression-based normal-behavior forecasters (Linear Regression, Support Vector Regression), with BERT-based log preprocessing. To ensure the parameters of the neural-network part of the model can be meaningfully aggregated, only the Autoencoder and the BERT-based log encoder are being aggregated using Federated Averaging. To achieve this aggregation for the other models, either the tree-based model or the PCA model are replaced by the global model after each round, which is referred to as a model-replacement strategy. A combined real-world dataset (ACN (Caltech and JPL sites) and ElaadNL (snapshot) was used together with a simulated dataset of 500 K events generated using ACN-Sim. DoS, unauthorized-access, load-balancing and abrupt-charging-disruption events were synthesized using a formal threat model and attack-injection procedure. To compare the baselines, all baselines (Hybrid IDS, System used in and a protocol-compliance reference implementation of ISO 15118) were re-implemented and tested using the same data splits, preprocessing and hardware. Across five repeated runs, the proposed framework achieved a mean detection accuracy of 95.4% (95% CI: 94.6–96.2%) on ACN, 92.1% (91.2–93.0%) on ElaadNL, and 90.3% (89.2–91.4%) on the simulated set, with mean latency of 205 ms (ACN), 223 ms (ElaadNL), and 248 ms (simulated). The framework has been tested to support an average of 1,500 concurrent charging sessions and achieved a measured 28.7% decrease in communication costs from a centralized baseline. We further study the framework’s ability to resist model-poisoning attacks through a secure aggregation mechanism (coordinate-wise median, with a fallback to a trimmed-mean algorithm). We also discuss the question of compatibility of the framework with Distributed Ledger Technologies (DLTs) for auditable federated updates. There are clear specifications and open discussion regarding the limitations of dataset diversity, real-time live-network validation, and lack of differential privacy.

papers.title: A Quality-Gated, Event-Triggered Edge–Cloud Framework for Collaborative Predictive Maintenance of Three-Phase Induction Motors
papers.abstract: Three-phase induction motors are widely used in industrial pumps, fans, compressors, conveyors, and production machinery. Their failures can interrupt processes, increase maintenance costs, and create secondary equipment damage. Machine-learning studies have reported promising results for vibration-based classification and sensorbased monitoring, while recent work has explored self-supervised and federated learning for noisy, distributed motor data. However, these contributions address different tasks and do not by themselves establish the performance of a single deployable Edge–Cloud system.

papers.title: THE EL-RAKHAWI FRAMEWORK FOR SELF-HEALING DECENTRALIZED NEURAL NETWORKS A Predictive Packet Switching Protocol Based on Federated Learning and Game Theory for DDoS Resilience and Dynamic Congestion Management
papers.abstract: "The El-Rakhawi Framework for Self-Healing Decentralized Neural Networks" revolutionizes internet architecture by transforming passive packet-switching into an active, self-immune system. It addresses critical vulnerabilities like DDoS attacks, dynamic congestion, and centralized failure points through three synergistic pillars. First, Federated Congestion Prediction uses Temporal Convolutional Networks (TCNs) to forecast network bottlenecks 5-10 seconds in advance, sharing only model updates to preserve absolute privacy. Second, Game-Theoretic Autonomous Routing operates at the flow level, enabling data streams to negotiate optimal paths via Nash equilibrium, dynamically evading congestion and trapping malicious traffic in topological dead-ends. Third, Lightweight DAG-Based Blockchain Verification replaces centralized DNS, cryptographically preventing IP spoofing and cache poisoning. System performance is quantified by the Neural Network Resilience Index (NNRI), a strictly bounded metric (0.0-1.0) evaluating prediction accuracy, detection latency, throughput, and decentralization. This framework provides a scalable, privacy-preserving, and robust pathway for the future of IoT and global digital infrastructure. Author: Dr. Mohamed Kamal Arafa El-Rakhawi. DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23843112.

Unsupervised federated autoencoders for IoT botnet detection under non-IID and contaminated training data
papers.abstract: Federated learning (FL) has been proposed for privacy-preserving intrusion detection in internet of things (IoT) networks, yet most studies assumed labeled traffic and identically distributed client data. This study benchmarked unsupervised federated autoencoders for IoT botnet detection under non-IID heterogeneity and training-data contamination. N-BaIoT and Edge-IIoTset were partitioned into clients using IID, natural per-device, and Dirichlet partitions with concentration parameters of 1.0, 0.5, and 0.1, and botnet traffic was injected into the benign training data of 30% of the clients at rates of 0% – 20%. Lightweight autoencoders were trained on unlabeled traffic and aggregated with FedAvg and FedProx, with local-only and centralized training as references, in 264 runs over five random seeds. FedAvg did not outperform local-only training in any of the ten dataset–partition settings (mean AUC-PR difference of 0.058, Holm-adjusted p = 0.014) and, on N-BaIoT, declined by up to 0.087 after an early peak. FedProx prevented this decline on N-BaIoT (AUC-PR up to 0.999) but gave no gain on Edge-IIoTset. Under heterogeneity, a single global threshold raised the false positive rate from about 1% to 22.2%, whereas client-level thresholds kept it at or below 1.0%. Contamination of 20% reduced the worst-client F1-score by 0.33 for FedAvg and 0.47 for FedProx, and client-level thresholds did not recover this loss. These findings indicated that standard aggregation and a single global threshold were insufficient for unsupervised federated botnet detection and motivated label-free, heterogeneity-aware aggregation with client-level threshold calibration.

papers.title: Privacy-preserving AI-driven healthcare analytics in post-quantum clouds
papers.abstract: Healthcare analytics leverages Artificial Intelligence and Cloud Computing in disease prediction, Clinical Decisions Making, Personalized Treatment and Remote Monitoring.However, having all of the information in a single place increases the risk of medical information being breached, misused, accessed and new threats in the quantum era.This study aims at designing an AI-powered healthcare analytics system with privacy in postquantum cloud computing era.Incorporates Federated learning, Differential privacy, Secure aggregation, Post quantum key encapsulation, Quantum resistant digital signature, Role based access control and Explainable Artificial Intelligence.Patients' data is kept locally and a global model is trained collaboratively by healthcare institutions.Differential privacy preserves the contribution of the individual, secure aggregation presents the institutional update in an obscure manner and post quantum mechanisms secure authentication and communication.An evaluation based on a diabetes dataset demonstrates the framework's ability to classify with 92.94% accuracy with a reduction in membership-inference and gradient-reconstruction risks while using simulation.The latency, memory consumption and communications overhead of security mechanisms are high, but they are kept under control.

papers.title: The Privacy Paradox of Smart Environments: Reconciling Continuous Sensing with Privacy-Preserving Digital Intelligence
papers.abstract: Smart environments increasingly rely on continuous sensing and artificial intelligence to interpret human activity, anticipate needs, and automate decisions across homes, healthcare facilities, workplaces, and public infrastructure. Although these capabilities can improve safety, responsiveness, and efficiency, persistent data collection also enables behavioral profiling, sensitive inference, secondary data use, and surveillance of individuals who may have limited control over monitoring. This narrative review critically examines the privacy intelligence tension by integrating technical, empirical, behavioral, and governance perspectives. It considers risks arising across the data lifecycle and evaluates the capabilities and limitations of data minimization, edge computing, federated learning, differential privacy, and cryptographic safeguards. The analysis highlights three recurring challenges: privacy guarantees that address isolated threats rather than cumulative inference, inconsistent measures of privacy and system utility, and insufficient attention to institutional power and the circumstances of affected individuals. It argues that privacy protection and intelligent functionality are not inherently incompatible, but their reconciliation depends on proportional sensing, clearly defined purposes, realistic threat models, and accountable deployment. To integrate these requirements, the review proposes a Context-Adaptive Privacy–Intelligence Assurance Framework linking necessity assessment, purpose-limited sensing, protected inference, context-sensitive action, and continuous oversight. The framework offers an agenda for future empirical evaluation rather than a validated solution, emphasizing longitudinal testing, bystander protection, and meaningful user control across diverse settings and changing technological and institutional conditions.

papers.title: Integrating Machine Learning, Deep Learning and Robotics for Intelligent Information Management and Decision Support
papers.abstract: Machine Learning, Deep Learning, and Robotics are revolutionizing the landscape of intelligent information management and decision support, connecting data processing, predictive analysis, and autonomous action. This review discusses the conceptual background, technological architectures, and application areas of integrated intelligent systems. It brings together the latest advances in machine learning, deep learning, robotic perception, autonomous control, reinforcement learning, digital twins, edge AI, federated learning and human-in-the-loop decision support. The review also compares the machine learning, deep learning, robotics, and integrated approaches in terms of accuracy, scalability, adaptability, computational efficiency, explainability, and real-time decision making. These technologies are increasingly becoming relevant in the healthcare sector, in manufacturing, in supply chains, in the finance sector, in cybersecurity, in smart cities, in agriculture, and in environmental monitoring. While significant strides have been made, there are still numerous challenges to address, such as data quality, privacy, security, interoperability, computational complexity, transparency, and trust. Multimodal intelligence, foundation models, Distributed learning, and Self-learning robotics are expected to become increasingly common in future intelligent systems. In summary, learning, reasoning, and robotic execution, when integrated, provide a strong basis for trustworthy, adaptive, explainable and human-centric decision support in real-world complex environments and retain the effectiveness of human involvement in the decision process and the responsibility of system governance.

papers.title: Healthcare Data Governance in The AI Era: A Review of Privacy, Quality, Security, And Regulatory Compliance
papers.abstract: The significance of healthcare data governance has grown in tandem with the widespread use of AI and ML inside healthcare systems. Healthcare data management at its best involves following best practices to safeguard patient information, keep data accurate, keep it secure, and meet all applicable regulations. The trustworthiness of AI-powered healthcare apps, however, is susceptible to threats including data fragmentation, lack of interoperability, missing or inaccurate medical information, algorithmic bias, and privacy concerns. With an eye on healthcare data sources, data management techniques, governance frameworks, and new technology, this analysis delves into the essentials of healthcare data governance in the age of artificial intelligence. Topics covered include artificial intelligence's function in healthcare decision assistance, data purification, quality improvement, and information extraction. Additionally, methods that safeguard sensitive patient data while processing data and developing collaborative models are investigated. These methods include federated learning, secure multi-party computing, homomorphic encryption, and differential privacy. The assessment also discusses the ethical and regulatory concerns with AI deployment and how blockchain helps with data integrity and auditability. In order to ensure that AI-enabled healthcare systems are accountable, safe, and trustworthy, it is necessary to have well-coordinated policies, dependable data management, strong security measures, and stakeholder participation.
papers.venue: International Research Journal of Medical Sciences and Health Care

papers.title: Secure Multi-Disease Detection using Federated Learning and Optimized Graph-Based Deep Feature Attention with Blockchain Support
papers.abstract: The rise of digital healthcare systems has generated large, fragmented medical data for enhanced illness prediction. However, modern centralized machine learning algorithms distribute sensitive patient data, raising privacy, security, and legal concerns. Federated learning allows collaborative model training while protecting raw healthcare records, but heterogeneous medical data distributions, limited feature representation, and insufficient secure and reliable model-sharing mechanisms among healthcare institutions often present challenges. This study proposes a Blockchain-Enabled Federated Learning (BCFL) framework for privacy-preserving multi-disease prediction by integrating several complementary optimization and deep learning techniques. The framework employs the Humboldt Squid Optimization Algorithm (HSOA) for optimal feature selection, the Geometric Algebra Transformer (GATr) for enhanced feature representation, the Federated Graph Multilayer Edge Attention Network (FGMEAN) for graph-aware federated disease prediction, and the Great Wall Construction Algorithm (GWCA) for adaptive hyperparameter optimization. Blockchain technology is incorporated to strengthen security and data integrity within the federated learning environment, thereby supporting secure and privacy-preserving multi-disease prediction. The proposed framework is evaluated using the Heart Disease, Diabetes, and Chronic Kidney Disease datasets. The experimental results demonstrate prediction accuracies of 99.3%, 99.5%, and 99.3% for heart disease, diabetes, and chronic kidney disease, respectively. The framework also lowered latency, communication overhead, execution efficiency, and security compared to current techniques. Component-wise study shows that feature optimization, geometric feature embedding, graph-aware federated learning, and adaptive hyperparameter tuning improve predictive performance. Experimental results show that the BCFL-FGMEAN-GWCA framework provides a secure, privacy-preserving, and precise multi-disease prediction solution in distributed healthcare settings, enabling next-generation intelligent healthcare systems.

papers.title: SafePay: A Privacy-Preserving Multi-Layer AI Framework for Real-Time Financial Fraud Detection
papers.abstract: Digital payment fraud keeps growing worldwide, while many consumer payment platforms still depend on static identity checks and rule engines that act only after a transaction is complete. Such approaches are reactive, confined to single institutions, and hard to audit when a genuine customer is blocked. This paper presents SafePay, a multi-layer fraud detection framework that places behavioural biometrics, gradient-boosted machine learning, explainable artificial intelligence, blockchain-based sharing of hashed fraud signals, and federated learning inside one real-time payment pipeline. The platform was built as containerised microservices using Next.js, FastAPI, PostgreSQL, Redis, XGBoost, Solidity with Hardhat, and Flower. Its machine-learning component was evaluated on the IEEE-CIS Fraud Detection benchmark of 590,540 transactions with an 80/20 stratified split. The centralised XGBoost baseline obtained 97.55% accuracy, 88.78% precision, 36.37% recall, 51.61% F1-score, and 91.16% ROC-AUC, whereas Random Forest reached the highest ROC-AUC of 92.77% among the four classifiers compared. A three-client federated simulation reached a validation AUC of 0.846 without exchanging raw transaction records. Explanations are produced for challenged and blocked payments. On a development laptop, the complete fraud-enabled payment pipeline needed a mean latency of 309.89 ms with a 95th percentile of 348.47 ms. The study is limited by benchmark-only training data, a simulated federation, a local blockchain testnet, and heuristic behavioural and device scoring that has not been tested in a controlled ablation.

papers.title: A Review on Low-Latency AI-Based Architectures for Real-Time Disaster Prediction Systems
papers.abstract: A Review on Low-Latency AI-Based Architectures for Real- Time Disaster Prediction Systems Nidhi Raghav1 Dr Manish Ranjan Pandey2 Research Scholar, Department of Computer Science and Applications, IFTM University, Moradabad, India1 Associate Professor, Department of Computer Applications, IFTM University, Moradabad, India2 nidhi.mbd002@gmail.com1 manish_pandey@iftmuniversity.ac.in2 Abstract—Natural disasters pose persistent threats to human life, infrastructure, economic stability, and public safety. Conventional disaster prediction systems often depend on centralized cloud infrastructures, which can introduce communication overhead and processing delays that limit their effectiveness in time-critical situations. Recent advances in Artificial Intelligence (AI), Internet of Things (IoT), and edge computing have created opportunities to develop more responsive disaster prediction systems by enabling data collection and processing closer to the source. This study presents a structured review of AI-based disaster prediction approaches, with particular emphasis on low-latency computing architectures for real-time applications. Published studies are categorized according to disaster type, AI techniques, sensing technologies, and deployment architectures, including cloud, fog, edge, and hybrid computing environments. The review identifies several important research gaps, including limited real-world deployment, inconsistent evaluation of latency and real-time performance, computational and resource constraints, and insufficient integration with emerging communication technologies. Based on these findings, the study proposes a conceptual low- latency architecture integrating IoT-based sensing, edge intelligence, fog coordination, and cloud-assisted learning to support timely disaster prediction and response. The study further highlights future research directions involving lightweight AI models, federated learning, adaptive resource management, and advanced communication technologies. Overall, the findings provide a foundation for developing scalable, efficient, and latency-aware AI-based frameworks for real-time disaster prediction. papers.title: Secure Deployment of Neural Networks in Edge and IoT Devices
papers.abstract: Secure deployment of neural networks (NNs) on edge and Internet of Things (IoT) devices is essential for real-time intelligence. However, it is challenged by latency variation, energy limits, adversarial attacks, privacy risks, memory scarcity, and hardware heterogeneity. This paper presents a secure NN deployment framework for edge/IoT using MATLAB-based simulation over 200 epochs and 200 inference requests. The framework evaluates latency, energy consumption, adversarial robustness, federated learning (FL) convergence under Differential Privacy (DP), compression-based memory reduction, side-channel power leakage, and throughput variability across 100 devices. Results show stable yet noisy latency of 80-88ms, centered near 83-84ms, and consistent energy demand with a mean of 1.07197×10^6mJ. At ε=0.1, unsecured model accuracy drops from 85.51% to 35.05%, while the defended model retains 75.50%, a 40.45 percentage-point gain. With DP noise of σ=0.03, FL global loss declines from 1.92 to about -0.05 by round 200, indicating convergence. Pruning and quantization from 20% to 50% reduce memory from 410.68 MB to 255.59 MB. Peak side-channel leakage reaches 1.62 V, and throughput varies from 4.24 to 16.50 million Ops/s. Despite simulation-only evaluation and limited adaptive-threat coverage, the study offers a practical metrics-driven blueprint for balancing security, privacy, and efficiency in edge/IoT AI deployment.

papers.title: Personalized Rollout Allocation for Federated LQR Policy Optimization under Heterogeneous Process Noise
papers.abstract: We study federated model-free learning of a common linear quadratic regulator (LQR) gain under a limited uplink communication budget, with clients that share dynamics and costs but experience different process-noise levels. Conventionally, clients transmit gradient matrices whose dimension equals the number of controller parameters. Exploiting the structure of two-point zeroth-order estimates, we consider an implementation in which clients transmit only one scalar cost-difference coefficient per rollout pair, while the server regenerates the associated perturbation directions from shared seeds. Communication thus scales with the number of rollout pairs rather than the controller dimension, turning the uplink budget into a rollout budget. Because noise heterogeneity produces gradient estimates of widely differing variance and every client carries equal weight in the fleet objective, uniform rollout allocation allows noisy clients to dominate the aggregated update and increases the probability of destabilizing updates. We propose a rollout-allocation scheme that assigns rollout pairs in proportion to the standard deviation of each client's estimates and show that it minimizes the variance of the aggregated update. The scheme is implemented exactly through a greedy integer allocation rule whose weights are estimated from the communicated scalars. We further prove that a single allocation factor quantifies its improvement over uniform allocation in a one-round instability bound, the certified step size, and the error floor of a joint stability and convergence guarantee. Simulations show that, under the same communication budget, personalized allocation reduces the one-step instability rate from $37\%$ to $0.3\%$.

papers.title: Neanderthal introgressed ancestry reveals human genomic regions enriched with recessive deleterious mutations
papers.abstract: Abstract Negative selection on deleterious mutations plays a key role in shaping human genetic variation, yet the dominance effects of these mutations remain poorly understood because existing statistical methods often cannot distinguish dominance effects from the overall selective effects. In this work, we take a fundamentally different approach by leveraging the distribution of Neanderthal ancestry across the human genome. Simulations show that recessive deleterious mutations can increase archaic introgressed ancestry through heterosis in the absence of positive selection, in contrast to the depletion expected under additive effects. We use this signal to develop DominL , a machine learning classifier trained on simulations of human demography with Neanderthal introgression to identify megabase-scale genomic windows enriched with recessive mutations. DominL demonstrates robust accuracy, with particularly high power in exon-dense regions. Applied to 7 non-African populations from the 1000 Genomes Project, DominL identifies approximately 3-9% of the genome as enriched for recessive mutations, with most high-confidence regions shared across populations. Predicted regions show patterns consistent with expected signatures from recessive mutations, including weakened background selection, depletion of runs of homozygosity, and enrichment of non-additive trait-associated variants. These regions also contain genes associated with metabolic and immune-related functions.

papers.title: AI-driven discovery and engineering of human-derived protein scaffolds for mRNA delivery
papers.abstract: Safe and effective gene delivery remains a central challenge for therapeutic applications. While non-viral and viral vectors have enabled substantial progress, their reliance on non-human components often triggers immune responses, limiting their use in chronic treatments. Here, we develop DeepDelivery, an artificial intelligence-driven platform to identify human proteins with scaffold potential for mRNA delivery. Proteome-scale screening nominated 512 candidates, and experimental validation show that 12 of 15 selected human proteins functioned as scaffold components that facilitated particle formation and mRNA delivery within a modular engineering framework. Notably, several tripartite motif (TRIM) family proteins, typically linked to antiviral responses, exhibit strong assembly and delivery activity. Model interpretability and perturbation analyses identify TRIM domain features that influenced prediction scores and guide TRIM25-specific domain engineering to improve delivery. Together, these results establish a framework for mining the human proteome for scaffold components of programmable mRNA delivery systems and for further exploring the design space of human-derived delivery architectures. Protein-based carriers could provide biocompatible options for mRNA delivery. Here, authors develop an AI-guided platform to identify and engineer human-derived protein scaffolds that assemble into particles and support mRNA delivery in cultured cells.

papers.title: Connectivity-Aware Client Selection in Decentralized Federated Learning
papers.abstract: Decentralized federated learning (DFL) has emerged as a scalable alternative to centralized federated learning, removing the single point of failure and communication bottleneck at the server. However, most existing decentralized approaches rely on full-neighborhood broadcasting, where each client transmits its model update to all of its neighbors in each communication round. While effective, this results in significant communication overhead and high energy consumption. This paper applies spectral graph tools as lightweight client selection methods that leverage the graph topology by analyzing the spectral properties of the graph Laplacian over a fixed communication graph. Specifically, we exploit eigenvector embeddings and heat/diffusion kernel similarities to guide each client in selecting only a subset of structurally relevant neighbors, i.e., those that are most beneficial for the convergence of the federation process. This topology aware randomization matches or outperforms uniform neighborhood subsampling and approaches the accuracy of full broadcasting. The largest gains, about $3$ percentage points, emerge under strong data heterogeneity on larger, structurally rich graphs, while the total number of transmitted messages is reduced by $50\%$ compared to naive broadcasting.

papers.title: AuditFL: A Contract-Backed Clearing Layer for Open Federated Learning
papers.abstract: Federated learning (FL) keeps raw data local, but most deployments still rely on a trusted coordinator for client admission, checkpoint distribution, update collection, aggregation, and rewards. This paper presents AuditFL, a contract-backed clearing layer for auditable FL in open settings. AuditFL keeps training and aggregation off chain, stores model artifacts in an assumed reliable off-chain artifact store, and records only content identifiers and economic state on chain. Clients reserve update tickets with deposits, publish update identifiers, and later claim refunds or rewards; the task coordinator publishes global checkpoints and finalizes rounds through deterministic settlement rules. The design does not remove the aggregator, but makes its on-chain round decisions attributable, replayable, auditable, and economically constrained. We implement AuditFL as both a deterministic state-machine prototype and a Solidity contract on a local Ethereum-compatible Anvil chain. On full MNIST with Dirichlet non-IID splits, 12 rounds, and up to 200 clients, AuditFL preserves the Plain FL learning trajectory while its overhead follows closed-form control-plane models. At 200 clients, the contract run issues 5,026 transactions, stores 2,413 off-chain artifacts (144.9 MiB), and consumes 829.7M EVM gas, dominated by per-client reserve and publish calls. Controlled dropout, invalid-update, and artifact-unavailability stress tests reduce inclusion nearly linearly but still finalize rounds, with final-accuracy changes remaining within a few tenths of an accuracy percentage point even under high injected failure rates.

papers.title: Role-Aware Server Optimization for Multimodal Federated Learning with Missing Modalities
papers.abstract: Multimodal federated learning (MFL) trains a shared model by aggregating client updates without exchanging raw data. Under missing modalities, clients adapt active modality encoders and a shared prediction block (fusion and classifier) to different input subsets. This raises two server-side questions: which clients should contribute to each component, and how should their aggregates be incorporated across rounds? We observe that an absent-modality encoder can still adapt through missing-input handling. Availability- based aggregation can therefore omit its update while retaining jointly learned prediction-block updates. Contributor selection also shapes server momentum, a weighted history of aggregated updates. We observe that prediction-block momentum can improve or reduce performance depending on the encoder update policy. We therefore propose Role-Aware Server Optimization (RASO), which coordinates contributor selection with role-specific server updates. RASO selects contributors through prediction dependence and inclusion in local optimization, retains encoder momentum, and synchronizes the shared prediction block to its current aggregate. Experiments across datasets and fusion architectures demonstrate the effectiveness of RASO under missing modalities.

papers.title: Graph-Based Deep Learning for Financial Crime Detection: A Review of Transaction Networks, Fraud Patterns, and Explainable AI.
papers.abstract: Financial fraud and money laundering now operate through networks of accounts, devices, merchants, and identities, and rule-based systems and conventional machine learning models that score transactions one at a time often miss them. This narrative review examines how Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) detect suspicious connections among entities in transaction networks. It explains how financial data is represented as graphs and how message passing works, then reviews applications to money laundering and crime rings, synthetic identities and account takeover, and merchant fraud. It compares GNNs with conventional methods on accuracy, class imbalance, scalability, and interpretability. The reviewed studies report that GNNs can find structural patterns, such as hubs, cycles, and dense closed loops, that attribute-based models miss, and that sampling and label-balancing techniques help with imbalanced fraud data. The evidence is not one-sided: on the Elliptic Bitcoin benchmark, a random forest outperformed a graph convolutional network, and GNNs can struggle when labels are heavily skewed. Computational cost, camouflaged fraudsters, and the difficulty of explaining graph-based decisions to regulators remain open problems. The review concludes that GNNs should be evaluated against strong conventional baselines and paired with explanation tools, federated learning, and human oversight. The article follows no formal search protocol.

papers.title: Federated Transfer Learning with Attentional Graph Neural Networks for Zero-Day IoT Botnet Detection and Secure Edge Orchestration
papers.abstract: Internet of Things (IoT) devices are increasingly appearing in a wide variety of edge environments, and these environments have become cybersecurity hot spots due to the increased vulnerability of them to sophisticated Zero-Day botnets propagation and Distributed Denial-of-Service (DDoS) attacks. However, traditional centralized intrusion detection system (IDS) is not capable of dealing with privacy constraints, communication overhead and dynamic topological structures of modern IoT networks. To solve these problems, a novel federated transfer learning framework, with the support of Attentional Graph Neural Networks (AGNN) is proposed for decentralized zero-day botnet detection at resource-constrained edge nodes. Proposed architecture includes federated learning to achieve collaborative model training, without sharing raw telemetry data and graph-based spatial modeling for capturing complex inter-device communication anomalies. Moreover, a transfer learning mechanism fine-tunes pre-trained threat intelligence on newly emerging edge sub-networks with limited fine-tuning. Empirical results on the benchmark IoT intrusion datasets (N-BaIoT and BoT-IoT) show a detection accuracy of 98.6%, 0.97 in ROC-AUC, a reduction of false alarm rate to 0.42% and a reduction of communication bandwidth overhead of 45.3% when compared to the traditional centralized deep learning paradigms. The results of ablation experiments indicate that the base GNN, the base GNN with attention and the base GNN with federated attention, together with the full transfer-learning setup, gradually improves the ablation results.

papers.title: INTELLIGENT DECISION SUPPORT SYSTEMS FOR IDENTIFICATION OF CULTURAL VALUES: MODERN APPROACHES AND DEVELOPMENT PROSPECTS
papers.abstract: The relevance of the research is determined by the rapid digitalization of cultural heritage, the growing volume of digital images, textual descriptions, metadata, and the increasing need for accurate, adaptive, scalable, and explainable automated identification and classification of cultural heritage objects. The problem addressed in the study is the limited effectiveness of traditional and partially integrated approaches based on k-NN, manually designed descriptors, convolutional neural networks, and static knowledge graph representations when processing heterogeneous, incomplete, and semantically complex cultural heritage data. The purpose of the research is to analyze modern approaches to intelligent decision support systems for cultural heritage identification and to substantiate an improved multimodal architecture capable of integrating visual, textual, and semantic information. The research methods include comparative analysis of existing approaches, analysis and generalization of previous research results, conceptual modeling, and evaluation of modern deep learning, multimodal learning, and graph-based methods. Particular attention is given to Graph Neural Networks, Graph Attention Networks (GAT), Relational Graph Convolutional Networks (R-GCN), Vision Transformers, BERT-based language models, self-supervised learning, and Explainable AI. The results demonstrate that replacing static graph representation methods with GAT and R-GCN enables more effective consideration of relationship types and weights, contextual information, and incomplete or noisy data. A multimodal architecture integrating Vision Transformer for image processing, a BERT-based model for textual information, and GNNs for Knowledge Graph representation is proposed. Their integration into a shared embedding space enables cross-modal analysis, semantic search, and zero-shot and few-shot classification. The study concludes that the transition from isolated classification models to integrated multimodal intelligent decision support systems can significantly improve the accuracy, robustness, adaptability, and interpretability of cultural heritage identification. Further research should focus on adaptive decision-making, self-supervised learning, Explainable AI, automatic Knowledge Graph enrichment, integration with national and international cultural heritage databases, human-in-the-loop approaches, and federated learning.

papers.title: Deep Learning Frontiers: Advanced Architectures and Intelligent Applications
authors: Dr. L. Lakshmaiah, Dr. Sudhakara Reddy M, Dr. Raju Anitha, Dr. K. Nageswara Reddy.
papers.abstract: The rapid advancement of Artificial Intelligence (AI) has transformed the way information is processed, knowledge is generated, and intelligent decisions are made across diverse domains. Deep Learning, as a major branch of machine learning, has emerged as a powerful technology for developing intelligent systems capable of learning complex patterns, understanding multimodal information, generating content, and solving challenging real-world problems. Recent developments in neural network architectures, foundation models, large language models, generative AI, intelligent agents, and autonomous systems have significantly expanded the scope and applications of deep learning. Recognizing these developments, the multi-author book Deep Learning Frontiers: Advanced Architectures and Intelligent Applications has been designed to provide a comprehensive understanding of advanced deep learning concepts, computational methodologies, emerging technologies, and practical applications. This book brings together contributions covering the theoretical foundations, advanced architectures, optimization techniques, representation learning methods, intelligent AI systems, and industry-oriented applications of deep learning. It is intended to support undergraduate and postgraduate students, research scholars, faculty members, academicians, software developers, and industry professionals who wish to strengthen their understanding of contemporary deep learning technologies and their practical implementation. Chapter 1, Advanced Foundations, Optimization, and Deep Learning Architectures, introduces the evolution of deep learning from traditional neural networks to modern intelligent learning paradigms. It discusses advanced neural network architectures, including deep feedforward networks, residual networks, and dense connections. The chapter further explores optimization algorithms such as AdamW and RMSprop, learning rate scheduling, regularization techniques, and generalization strategies. Advanced training methodologies, including transfer learning, fine-tuning, curriculum learning, and self-supervised learning, are examined alongside hyperparameter optimization approaches. The chapter also introduces popular deep learning frameworks, GPU acceleration, distributed training, model evaluation, cross-validation, and robustness testing. Chapter 2, Advanced Deep Learning Architectures and Representation Learning, focuses on the architectural developments that enable deep learning systems to process images, sequences, structured relationships, and complex data representations. It covers convolutional neural networks, recurrent neural networks, LSTM, GRU, attention mechanisms, and transformer architectures. Vision transformers and hybrid architectures are discussed in the context of image classification, object detection, and image segmentation. The chapter also examines graph neural networks, autoencoders, variational autoencoders, generative adversarial networks, and diffusion models, highlighting their importance in representation learning, image synthesis, and generative applications. Chapter 3, Foundation Models, Multimodal Learning, and Intelligent AI Systems, presents the emerging landscape of large-scale pretrained models and intelligent systems. It explores foundation models, large language model architectures, pretraining strategies, scaling laws, and model adaptation techniques such as instruction tuning, parameter-efficient fine-tuning, LoRA, and quantization. Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), embedding models, vector databases, semantic search, and grounded generation are discussed as important approaches for knowledge-intensive AI applications. The chapter further addresses multimodal learning, vision-language models, speech and audio intelligence, deep reinforcement learning, and intelligent AI agents. Explainable and trustworthy deep learning, including feature attribution, attention analysis, fairness, interpretability, and model transparency, completes the discussion. Chapter 4, Advanced Intelligent Applications of Deep Learning, examines the application of deep learning across major sectors. It discusses healthcare and biomedical intelligence, including medical image analysis, disease prediction, drug discovery, and clinical decision support. Computer vision and smart surveillance applications such as object tracking, facial analysis, activity recognition, and anomaly detection are also covered. Further topics include natural language processing, conversational AI, autonomous systems, robotics, smart manufacturing, financial intelligence, risk analytics, smart agriculture, environmental intelligence, and edge AI. Particular attention is given to practical techniques such as model compression, pruning, knowledge distillation, quantization, and real-time inference for intelligent IoT environments. Chapter 5, Emerging Frontiers, Deployment, and Industry Case Studies, explores advanced research directions and the practical deployment of deep learning systems. It introduces neuro-symbolic AI, continual learning, few-shot learning, meta-learning, sustainable deep learning, green AI, and carbon-aware computing. The chapter discusses MLOps, model serving, containerization, cloud deployment, edge deployment, and the operational requirements of intelligent applications. Security and privacy considerations, including adversarial attacks, data poisoning, differential privacy, and federated learning, are examined alongside responsible and ethical AI practices. Industry case studies illustrate the use of deep learning in healthcare, manufacturing, transportation, generative AI, and intelligent agents. Additional emphasis is placed on enterprise-scale agent operations, multi-tenant architectures, policy enforcement, identity management, sandboxing, incident response, lifecycle management, latency optimization, batching, and resource allocation. Capstone-oriented discussions provide practical perspectives on designing and deploying secure multi-agent research assistants, enterprise workflow automation platforms, cybersecurity investigation systems, and intelligent decision-support applications. A major objective of this book is to bridge the gap between theoretical understanding and practical implementation. The chapters collectively emphasize the importance of selecting appropriate architectures, preparing and managing datasets, optimizing model performance, evaluating reliability, and deploying intelligent solutions in real-world environments. The inclusion of contemporary topics such as foundation models, multimodal intelligence, generative AI, retrieval-augmented generation, and autonomous AI agents makes the book relevant to the rapidly evolving research and industrial landscape. The multi-author contributions provide diverse academic and technical perspectives on the subject, encouraging readers to explore both established deep learning methodologies and emerging research opportunities. The book is expected to serve as a useful reference for academic coursework, laboratory learning, research activities, project development, and professional knowledge enhancement. It also aims to encourage further investigation into efficient, secure, explainable, scalable, and responsible intelligent systems. We sincerely acknowledge all the contributing authors, reviewers, academicians, researchers, and professionals whose knowledge and efforts have supported the preparation of this book. Their contributions have helped bring together a broad range of concepts and applications within a unified academic resource. We also express our gratitude to the institutions, colleagues, and well-wishers who have encouraged the development of this work. We hope that Deep Learning Frontiers: Advanced Architectures and Intelligent Applications will provide readers with valuable insights, strengthen their technical foundations, inspire innovative research, and support the development of next-generation intelligent applications.

papers.title: FeDLRT: Federated Dynamical Low-Rank Training
papers.abstract: Abstract. We propose a federated dynamical low-rank training (FeDLRT) scheme to reduce client compute and communication costs—two significant performance bottlenecks in horizontal federated learning. Our method builds upon dynamical low-rank time integration schemes for manifold-constrained optimization to create a global low-rank basis of network weights, which enables client training on a small coefficient matrix. This global low-rank basis allows us to incorporate a variance correction scheme and prove global loss descent and convergence to a stationary point on a low-rank manifold. FeDLRT features dynamic augmentation and truncation of the low-rank bases to optimize computing and communication resource utilization. Notably FeDLRT only trains a small coefficient matrix per client. We demonstrate the efficiency of FeDLRT in an array of computer vision benchmarks with both independent and identically distributed (IID) and non-IID data and show a reduction of client compute and communication costs by up to an order of magnitude with minimal impacts on global accuracy. FeDLRT performs as well as classical methods such as FedAvg and FedLin, with a fraction of the memory and compute requirements.
papers.venue: SIAM Journal on Mathematics of Data Science

papers.title: Just Talk Once: Communication-Efficient Split Federated LLM Fine-Tuning on Edge Devices
papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) fine-tuning is increasingly shifting toward data generated on edge devices, where memory, computation, bandwidth, and connectivity constraints make conventional federated learning difficult to sustain. Split federated fine-tuning (SFT) improves client-side efficiency by offloading most model parameters and computation to the server but requires step-by-step bidirectional communication loop across the split interface and forces continuous client involvement throughout training. In this paper, we present L-shaped SFT, a split fine-tuning framework that removes this bidirectional bottleneck. Our key insight is that weight tying in modern LLMs enables server-side hidden activations to be directly supervised using target embeddings, allowing the training loss to be computed on the server without returning server outputs to the client. To further eliminate the need for continuous client participation, based on L-shaped SFT, we introduce one-shot SFT, in which clients upload activations once and then go offline while the server continues optimization over cached representations. We implement our design in a real system testbed with heterogeneous edge clients, including commercial smartphones and NVIDIA developer boards. Experiments demonstrate that our schemes significantly reduce communication costs and client online time compared with existing SFT baselines.

papers.title: Optimizing Stochastic Gradient Push under Broadcast Communications
papers.abstract: We consider the problem of minimizing the convergence time for decentralized federated learning (DFL) in wireless networks under broadcast communications, with focus on mixing matrix design. The mixing matrix is a critical hyperparameter for DFL that simultaneously controls the convergence rate across iterations and the communication demand per iteration, both strongly influencing the convergence time. Although the problem has been studied previously, existing solutions are mostly designed for decentralized parallel stochastic gradient descent (D-PSGD), which requires the mixing matrix to be symmetric and doubly stochastic. These constraints confine the activated communication graph to undirected (i.e., bidirected) graphs, which limits design flexibility. In contrast, we consider mixing matrix design for stochastic gradient push (SGP), which allows asymmetric mixing matrices and hence directed communication graphs. By analyzing how the convergence rate of SGP depends on the mixing matrices, we extract an objective function that explicitly depends on graph-theoretic parameters of the activated communication graph, based on which we develop an efficient design algorithm with performance guarantees. Our evaluations based on real data show that the proposed solution can notably reduce the convergence time compared to the state of the art without compromising the quality of the trained model.
